Our Next Energy was ahead of the curve when it came to battery makers shifting away from EVs and toward other markets. Nearly two years into that strategy, we spoke with CEO Mujeeb Ijaz about how it’s going.
October 15, 2026
A dominant trend in the US battery industry this year has been
battery makers’ increasing pivot away from EVs
to focus on energy storage, defense, industrial, and other markets for their products. Big battery names like Ford, GM, LG, and more have jumped on the bandwagon. It’s no surprise that this shift was a hot topic at
The Battery Show
in Detroit, North America’s leading event for the battery industry.
Our Next Energy (ONE), headquartered in the nearby suburb of Novi, was on site with a big, flashy booth. Three years ago, the battery maker was touting an
anode-free cell it said could help EVs travel 750 miles on one charge
. Then came
and ultimately an exit of the EV market altogether. It’s approaching two years since ONE announced it would shift to building batteries for energy storage, defense, and rail.
Battery Technology caught up with
ONE founder and CEO Mujeeb Ijaz
to talk about how that strategy is playing out.

title: Beyond Telematics: Building Intelligent Transport Operations

Beyond Telematics: Building Intelligent Transport Operations
Prioritise Us

Microlise is helping fleet operators turn visibility into action. Credit: Getty Images
Data collection is a critical part of fleet management, but Microlise is working to transform it into a process of intelligent action
In recent years, leaders have been working to
increase visibility
in their fleets, but these insights do not always translate into solutions.
As global logistics becomes increasingly complex, driven by pressures to operate with more sustainable processes, or cut costs, Microlise is operating in a way that
transforms fleet management
The platform is using its strong capabilities to translate the data into intelligent action, allowing managers to unlock new value across their operations.
Industry concerns
Fleet operations
are incredibly complex, working with a vast number of vehicles, drivers and routes. Alongside this, managers need to operate alongside legislation and safety regulations – which becomes even more difficult when operations are across borders.
They are a necessary part of a supply chain, ensuring products can move safely to their destination, but they are not as simple as moving from one place to another.
Due to the vast number of moving parts, fragmentation occurs, meaning that teams cannot get full oversight, nor can they take valuable action.
In some cases, the visibility is there, but teams lack the collaborative capability required to turn the insights into a strategy plan.
Microlise, however, is moving to close the gap between insights and action, using its AI capabilities and platforms in order to help its customers unlock new opportunities. It has a seamless ecosystem which
enables fleet operators
and product manufacturers to remotely monitor, manage and maintain their business. With many drivers on the road at once – often in various countries – being able to see everything remotely is crucial for looking after your fleet.
Microlise offers a vehicle calendar which helps with maintenance. Credit: Microlise
At a glance
Microlise technology can operate across fleet telematics; safety, health and compliance; journey management and transport management
Its technology has more than 933,000 subscriptions
Data is collected from more than 195 countries
Microlise found that more than 80% of transport and logistics managers use AI tools in their fleet operations
The average daily cost associated with manual proof of delivery processing has risen to £172.40 (US$230)
A collaborative solution
Part of Microlise’s efforts include a customer forum, Microlise Labs. This was launched in June 2026 as a means to bring customers and product teams together. By doing this, it looked at the future of transport technology and some of the current issues that the industry is facing.
The Labs are built around open discussion, real-world operational insight and shared experience. The forum means that Microlise staff have the opportunity to work with the people their company is meant to help.
As the industry continues to change, it can be difficult for the technology providers to keep up. This acts as an opportunity to work in tandem in order to fix the modern issue.
Dean Garvey-North, Chief Technology Officer at Microlise, said: “Bringing together transport operators from different sectors created exactly the kind of open, honest discussion we hoped for.”
“The alignment across both workshops reinforced a clear opportunity to make transport operations more connected, proactive and informed.”
Microlise Labs acts as a space for customers to explore where time is being lost, or where processes still feel disconnected. Through workshop-style sessions, leaders can work together to shape practical solutions.
In doing this, Microlise is helping solve an active issue, hoping to help its customers unlock
cost savings and efficiency gains

title: DHL Freight Adds Chinese Electric-Truck to Dutch Network
content:
DHL Freight Adds Chinese Electric-Truck to Dutch Network
Prioritise Us
on Google
DHL Freight has begun commercial operation of the first European-built eTopas 600 electric truck in its Netherlands network. Credit: DHL
DHL Freight has begun commercial operation of an electric truck in its Netherlands network, reducing emissions on cross-border routes into Belgium
DHL Freight has begun commercial operations of a battery-electric truck built in Europe to its fleet of vehicles in the Netherlands.
The electric-truck is operating cross-border deliveries to Belgium, in addition to handling domestic distribution within the Netherlands.
The electric-truck is the first model of Chinese manufacturer's SuperPanther eTopas 600 range to be assembled in Europe.
DHL Frieght's SuperPanther eTopas 600 Electric Truck. Credit: DHL Freight
Reducing emissions in Benelux
The truck was introduced after successfully completing a period of real-world testing.
Arjan van Weelden, Carrier & Sustainability Manager at DHL Freight, says: "Our experience from daily operations has been positive so far. The vehicle meets the requirements of the planned deployment profiles and achieves high productivity within the network."
“Feedback from drivers has also been very positive, and we are seeing clear interest from customers in transport solutions that reduce greenhouse gas emissions."
The truck can travel up to 500 kilometres on a single charge, which makes it well suited to medium-haul work.
It is used flexibly across a range of routes rather than being committed to a fixed shuttle service or a single terminal.
The vehicle covers around 2,000 kilometres per week, giving DHL Freight first-hand experience of how electric heavy-duty trucks can fit within existing network structures and cross-border operations.
Arjan van Weelden, Carrier & Sustainability Manager at DHL Freight
The commercial deployment follows a step-by-step partnership between DHL Freight and SuperPanther.
After an initial memorandum of understanding in September 2024, the eTopas 600 was tested in Austria under real-world conditions.
A two-week trial in spring 2026 saw the vehicle cover around 1,900 kilometres, with an average daily mileage of 238 kilometres.
Recorded electricity consumption was 102 kilowatt-hours per 100 kilometres, and compared with the reference case for the trial around 930 kilograms of CO₂e were saved against an equivalent diesel-powered heavy-duty truck on the same route profile.
In July 2026, the first eTopas 600 produced in Europe by the Chinese manufacturer came off the production line for DHL Freight, and the vehicle has been in regular operation in the Dutch network since September.
At IAA Transportation in Hanover, DHL Group and SuperPanther also signed an MoU on autonomous driving, aimed at testing under real-world operating conditions how the technology can be advanced and brought into practice.
Heidi van Eldik, CEO of DHL Freight Netherlands & Belgium, says: "Our customers are looking for practical ways to
reduce greenhouse gas emissions
Heidi van Eldik, CEO of DHL Freight Netherlands & Belgium
Key facts about SuperPanther’s eTopas 600
Propulsion: two electric motors (axle drive)
Power performance: continuous power 394 kW (535 hp); peak power 692 kW (941 hp)
Curb weight: 10.8 t
Gross combination weight: 42 t
Range: 500 kilometres
Battery: lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery from CATL
Battery capacity: 621 kWh
Charging time: appx. 38 minutes from 20 to 80 percent (dual CCS2 charging port)
Battery lifetime: 4,500 full charging cycles, mileage over 1.2m kilometres
Braking system: five-level energy recuperation brake
Electrification's role in DHL's decarbonisation plans
As part of DHL Group's decarbonisation objectives, DHL is seeking to reduce its emissions from road transport, which accounted for 22% of DHL Group’s emissions in 2025.
One of the main ways that DHL intends to contribute to meet this target is by increasing the proportion of sustainable fuels in its fuel mix to 30%. For road transportation, HVO (hydrogenated vegetable oil) is expected to account for the majority of the investments.
Within the road transportation segment, 16% of emissions were generated by heavy duty line haul trucks while 6% were generated by smaller trucks or vans used for pickup-and-delivery operations, as part of DHL’s eCommerce distribution network.
Supply Chain Digital has reported that DHL is monitoring the possibility of electrifying the larger vehicles used for longer distance line hauls, but notes that the current limitations of battery capacity, which have recently increased from 400kW to 600kW, as well as the challenges of both securing recharging capacity on long distance line hauls, and managing the impact of recharging on scheduling are factors that DHL Freight is examining.
DHL signed a memorandum of understanding with Chinese battery supplier Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) in September 2026 in which DHL was appointed CATL's strategic logistics partner, with the aim of developing and scaling sustainable freight solutions across Europe, including CATL's European supply chain operations.

title: Hapag-Lloyd Revises ZIM Acquisition Bid
content:
Hapag-Lloyd Revises ZIM Acquisition Bid
Prioritise Us
on Google
Hapag-Lloyd has made substantial improvements to the terms of a proposed acquisition of Israel-based liner operator ZIM in order to satisfy the Israeli authorities’ concerns about the viability of a carved-out container liner business.
Rolf Habben Jansen, CEO of Hapag-Lloyd, explains how a revised bid for ZIM will satisfy Israeli security of supply concerns
Hapag-Lloyd has made substantial improvements to the terms of a proposed acquisition of Israel-based liner operator ZIM in order to satisfy the Israeli authorities’ concerns about the viability of a carved-out container liner business.
“The substantially improved proposal gives Israel materially more maritime independence and addresses all its national security needs, which is critical as we were reminded again the past three years,” says Rolf Habben Jansen, CEO of Hapag-Lloyd.
The revisions add an additional liner route to Asia and provide the carved-out container liner business, ZIM Israel, with a new modern fleet. In addition, the revised proposal addresses concerns about the retention of maritime expertise in Israel by including significant investments in Israeli maritime personnel.
“We are enhancing Israel's shipping capabilities very significantly.”
“I am genuinely convinced that the proposal we are presenting offers real solutions to the issues faced by the Israeli State and boosts Israel´s maritime capabilities and is a reflection of the longstanding relationship of Israel and Germany.”
Rolf did not provide any further update on the expected timeline for the conclusion of the negotiations with ZIM, noting only that “the negotiations are complex and highly detailed.”
When the deal was originally announced in February 2026, the deal had been expected to be concluded in late 2026, subject to regulatory approvals.
Rolf Habben Jansen, CEO of Hapag-Lloyd
Carveout for ZIM’s Israeli connections
The original proposal agreed between Hapag-Lloyd and ZIM in February 2026 would have seen Hapag-Lloyd acquire 100% of Zim’s shares for approximately USD4.2bn.
The current Golden Share held by the State of Israel in ZIM would be devolved to a standalone container line handling trade with Israel, which would be owned by FIMI, Israel's largest private equity fund.
The new carved-out container line would retain full responsibility for the ZIM brand.
Hapag-Lloyd ZIM merger to expand Hapag-Lloyd fleet
Rolf reiterates that the logic of the proposed merger between Hapag-Lloyd and ZIM remains clear.
“There are not many shipping companies left that have the necessary scale and could therefore take us a significant step forward. ZIM is also quite similar to us and is well managed. This would bring us another step closer to the global top four in our industry. The synergies would generate annual savings of up to half a billion euros,” Rolf estimates on 12 October.
When the combination between Hapag-Lloyd and ZIM was first proposed in February 2026, it was suggested that the deal would secure Hapag-Lloyd’s market position as the fifth-largest container shipping company worldwide with a modern fleet of over 400 vessels, a standing capacity of over 3 million TEU, and an annual transport volume of more than 18 million TEU.
The combination would also significantly strengthen Hapag-Lloyd’s network on the Transpacific, Intra Asia, Atlantic, Latin America and East Mediterranean routes.
ZIM is the world’s tenth-largest container liner shipping company with established operations in more than 90 countries serving approximately 33,000 customers in over 300 ports worldwide.
Hapag-Lloyd: Key facts and stats
Operates a fleet of 300 modern container ships, representing a total transport capacity of 2.5m twenty-foot-equivalent units (TEU).
Transports 13.5m TEU annually, connecting to more than 600 ports.
Maintains a workforce of 15,200 employees in its Liner Shipping segment and 4,400 employees in Terminal & Infrastructure.
Reaches globally, with 400 offices located across 140 countries worldwide.
Possesses equity stakes in 22 marine terminals across Europe, Latin America, the US, India and North Africa.

title: Exploring Competitiveness and Resilience in the Supply Chain
content:
Exploring Competitiveness and Resilience in the Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
on Google
Sam Stark, CEO at Green Project Technologies, explores how sustainability and resilience work together
Sam Stark, CEO and Founder of Green Project Technologies, discusses how sustainability and compliance help strengthen business resilience
The way in which organisations approach sustainability has shifted significantly. It was once seen as a bonus – good to have but not necessary for operations. Now, a strong sustainability initiative is a driver of resilience and customer satisfaction – businesses with visible strategies in place are more attractive to customers, especially as they think about their own emisisons.
As ongoing climate disruption has forced organisations into a state of constant reaction, operating with a
thorough sustainability agenda
is key to limiting operational risk.
Supply Chain Digital spoke with Sam Stark, CEO and Founder of Green Project Technologies. Green Project Technologies, an ACT Group company, is an AI-powered climate management platform, helping organisations manage and reduce emissions across their value chains.
How are corporate climate priorities focusing on resilience instead of sustainability?
Corporate climate priorities are undergoing a real reset as boards shift from a values-led sustainability agenda to proactive resilience. World events such as physical climate shocks and geopolitical instability have made climate exposure a core operational risk. As such, companies are forced to treat decarbonisation as a competitiveness strategy rather than a reputational exercise.
The new corporate climate agenda is defined by resilience because investments that reduce volatility and futureproof operations are rewarded. Of course, sustainability still matters, but only when it contributes to strengthening resilience by cutting compliance risk, reducing long-term costs or protecting the business from disruption. In the current environment, resilience is not a softer rebrand of sustainability, it is the commercial framework that now determines which climate actions survive budget scrutiny, and which do not.
The implementation of this shift varies globally. In the United States, resilience has overtaken sustainability as the dominant boardroom language. This is largely driven by the focus on compliance and risk avoidance but is also driven by the absence of federal climate mandates. In the United Kingdom and EU however,
regulatory expectations
and a continued moral commitment to decarbonisation mean sustainability retains stronger resonance, even as resilience becomes the strategic backbone of delivery.
Organisations are implementing decarbonisation strategies. Credit: Unsplash
What does this mean for global supply chains and their leaders?
For global supply chain leaders, the shift from sustainability to resilience fundamentally changes how climate action is prioritised and executed. The implications of this also differ greatly between regions. In the US, with no federal decarbonisation mandate,
resilience has become the dominant principle
. As such, boards expect supply chain leaders to minimise volatility and build systems that can adapt quickly to climate shocks and geopolitical disruption. In the UK and EU, sustainability and resilience now operate in tandem. Legally enforceable reporting regimes and mechanisms like CBAM, combined with corporate net zero commitments, mean European leaders must deliver both emissions reduction and operational stability, by redesigning networks around climate risk and regulatory alignment.
Across markets, supply chain leaders are being judged less on the ambition of sustainability commitments and more on their ability to reduce exposure and ensure compliance under unstable conditions. This requires diversifying suppliers and investing in audit ready data infrastructure that can withstand shocks rather than simply report them. That shift is what elevates supply chain leadership into the centre of corporate climate strategy, not as a support function, but as the commercial strategy that determines competitiveness.
Supply chain leadership is prioritising climate strategy more. Credit: Getty Images
How can businesses create long term resilience in supply chains?
Building long-term resilience in global supply chains requires businesses to shift from efficiency-optimised networks to systems designed for volatility and regulatory complexity. This is where climate management platforms become resilience tools because they give companies
real-time Scope 3 visibility
and automated compliance readiness to enable procurement teams to identify vulnerabilities early and act accordingly.
The starting point is quality supplier-specific data, mapping each supplier's geographic footprint, reliance on fossil-based energy, and supply chain concentration, since this is what actually reveals where procurement risk sits. The suppliers with lower-emitting profiles are often the same ones with less exposure to fossil fuel volatility, global logistics disruption, and travel, so emissions data becomes a proxy for resilience risk, not just a compliance metric. The leaders making real progress are the ones building this into standard practice, not something reserved for when a crisis is already underway.
Resilience also depends on embedding climate risk intelligence into operations, using AI and continuous monitoring, with a human in the loop, to anticipate disruption before it hits. Crucially, companies must treat compliance as a strategic, not an administrative, burden. Businesses that get this right treat resilience as infrastructure, not initiative, something built once and relied on for years, not revisited every budget cycle.
Emissions tracking is key for resilience. Credit: Unsplash
Why is it important that these changes have been made, and do you think this can boost the integration of sustainability?
The shift toward resilience is important because it finally aligns climate action with the commercial realities that determine whether initiatives survive budget scrutiny. By reframing climate strategy around risk reduction and competitiveness, businesses are grounding sustainability in the metrics executives actually care about and can rally behind across finance, operations, sustainability, compliance and legal functions. This makes climate action harder to dismiss as reputational or optional. In practice, resilience becomes the gateway to deeper sustainability integration. Once companies build traceable supply chains and adopt real time climate intelligence, they create the infrastructure that makes decarbonisation cheaper and more defensible.
Resilience doesn’t replace sustainability
, but it operationalises it. In doing so, it gives sustainability a stronger business case and far more durable future inside organisations.

title: 4flow: AI Decision Intelligence and Supply Chain Execution

4flow: AI Decision Intelligence and Supply Chain Execution
Prioritise Us
on Google
4flow is turning visibility into execution with its AI-native platform. Credit: Getty Images
Soeren Hagen, Chief Operating Officer of 4flow, explains how optaire is helping turn supply chain visibility into meaningful strategy and optimisation
Supply chain visibility has increased significantly in recent years, as more leaders understand that it
drives long-term resilience
Despite this, many teams still lack the ability to translate visibility into clear action in a timely manner.
4flow, however, uses its AI-native platform to connect visibility and disruption in order to develop a coordinated execution.
Increasing supply chain risk
Supply chains are at their most complex, meaning they are also at
their most vulnerable
. Changing regulations, ongoing climate events and increasing demand have all put pressure on supply chains.
With this, they are under more scrutiny – are they operating with ethics and sustainability in mind, are they being as efficient as possible, do they show long-term resilience? However, the scrutiny adds an extra layer of complexity, as supply chains are becoming more intricate and interconnected, visibility becomes an issue.
Recent years have demonstrated why visibility is key. As ESG reporting is becoming more standard, organisations need to be able to demonstrate their own capabilities with speed. Moreover, increasing cyber attacks has meant that business leaders want more insights into their tiers.
The awareness has increased, due to rising
technology and AI solutions
, but these insights do not always translate into action. As a result, organisations have the information they need, but cannot unlock value from it.
“The demands placed on leaders today look nothing like they did five years ago,” Julian Schulcz, COO at 4flow said on LinkedIn.
Julian Schulcz, COO at 4flow
“Markets shift faster, teams are more global and the expectations of every decision-maker keep rising. Leaders have to evolve at the same pace.”
4flow is using its
AI-native optaire
platform to unlock insights and convert them into a coordinated execution plan. This is helping organisations around the world react faster to disruption and operate with more efficiency and clarity.
Key numbers
4flow has more than 25 years of supply chain experience
It operates across more than 20 locations
Its 15,000+ team members help drive transformation
4flow has solutions across a range of industries, including automotive, consumer goods, retail, technology and defence
It has worked on more than 300 projects around the world every year
Real-time action
As a global provider of supply chain consulting, software and fourth-party logistics services, 4flow has a strong track record of helping customers optimise their supply chains. It has been working with leading businesses for more than 25 years, working amid the constantly changing market in order to maintain competitiveness and resilience.
4flow has a modular, AI-native platform, optaire, to drive end-to-end
supply chain and logistics
optimisation. It connects network, logistics and risk management, which results in more agility and resilience across the supply chain.
The platform is powered by AI agents, which means it is continuously scanning for changes in the market, or supply chain. Through this, it analyses scenarios and is capable of acting. As a result, it supports decision making and execution, allowing leaders to strategically use the real-time insights the agents discover.
“In successful transformations, strategy is just the beginning,” explains Soeren Hagen, Chief Operating Officer of 4flow said on LinkedIn.
Soeren Hagen, Chief Operating Officer of 4flow
“4flow has always taken an end-to-end approach to supply chain optimisation, working closely with our customers from strategy through to implementation, go-live and beyond.”
Optaire allows organisations to expand without disrupting existing systems, meaning no overhaul is needed and operations can continue without issue. As it is AI-native, the AI is built in and uses
real-time information
which allows it to work across the entire network, from planning to execution.
Through this, leaders can see less money spent on logistics, increased service level and faster issue resolution. This means the organisation is no longer playing catch-up – instead, it is operating within the changes, without any delays or further risk.
In successful transformations, strategy is just the beginning.
Soeren Hagen, Chief Operating Officer of 4flow said on LinkedIn
4flow gained recognition by Gartner for optaire, included in the “Coolest Vendor Innovations for Cross-Functional Supply Chain Technology (2026)” list. This is due to its capabilities of resolving issues and accelerating critical business decisions.

title: Kia launches first-of-its-kind remote driving car-sharing service with the PV5 EV van
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 16 2026 - 8:15 am PT
Kia launched a first-of-its-kind remote car-sharing program in Korea using
electric van.
Kia is using the PV5 EV van for remote car-sharing
The pilot program began operations on Thursday in Pangyo, Gyeonggi Province, using the Kia PV5, and it will run until the end of the year.
Kia said the new car-sharing service is the first of its kind in South Korea to use remote driving technology.
How does it work? Those interested can reserve a vehicle through a dedicated app. Once reserved, Kia’s electric van will drive itself to the requested location without a driver, using remote driving technology.
Users can drive the PV5 as they please and then park it at a desired location when they are finished. A remote driver will then move the vehicle back to its garage using 4G or 5G wireless technology.
Kia said the program can help businesses improve efficiency and reduce the burden of owning a fleet of vehicles. It’s also convenient to pick up and drop off the vehicle as you please.
A remote driver operating the PV5 remotely (Source: Kia)
The PV5 remote car-sharing pilot program is the latest in Kia’s push to advance remote driving technology.
Last April, Kia received a special exemption for the remote driving regulatory sandbox from the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport. In November 2025, it formed a
Remote Driving Consortium
with Socar, KT, and autonomous driving startup SUM, showcasing Korea’s First Remote Driving Demonstration on public roads by a domestic brand.
Most recently, Kia
signed an MOU
with KT and SUM in July to promote the commercialization of remote driving tech and aims to launch the service within a year.
Kia launches Korea’s first remote car-sharing using the PV5 (Source: Kia)
For the pilot service that launched this week, Kia, SUM, Mobiops, and the Korea Road Traffic Authority are participating in a consortium. Gyeonggi Province, KT, UMOS ONE, the Next Generation Convergence Technology Research Institute, and the Gyeonggi Automobile Rental Business Association are supporting the project as partner organizations.
Kia will provide PV5 vans and oversee the project. SUM will develop the remote driving solution, while Mobiops will handle service operations. Meanwhile, the Korea Road Traffic Authority assists with regulatory reviews.
During the pilot period, the partners will verify the remote driving technology and the feasibility of service operations under real-world conditions.
Using the data gathered during the trial, Kia plans to continue advancing the technology and expand the service in 2027 to accelerate the commercialization of PV5-based remote driving services.

title: Solar panels are bringing idle cranberry bogs back to life
content:
Two Massachusetts cranberry bogs that had stopped making financial sense to farm are growing berries again – with solar panels overhead helping pay the bills.
The Black Cat project in Plymouth and the Ring Road project in Kingston combine cranberry farming, community solar, and battery storage. Distributed Energy Infrastructure (DEI), which built the projects, says income from leasing the land for solar has made it viable to cultivate the long-idle bogs again.
It’s a particularly challenging form of agrivoltaics because cranberry bogs have soft, peaty soil and established vines that need to survive construction. You can’t just roll in with heavy equipment and start installing panels.
So the solar had to fit the farming. In a September article in North American Clean Energy, DEI cofounder and executive vice president Prateek Tare described panels raised 10 feet above the ground, leaving room for farm machinery underneath. Rows have more than 18 feet of clear space between them, and solar panel angles let sunlight reach the cranberry bogs.
Farmer Iain Ward helped work out those details, along with how construction could proceed without damaging the bogs. Even the protective mats needed changing: Black ones absorbed too much heat, so crews used white ones instead.
That care added time. Tare said construction took around eight months – roughly twice as long as a comparable conventional solar project.
“The DEI team was phenomenal at understanding and adapting solar construction so that energy production could coexist without damage to the perennial cropping system,” Ward said.
Greenbacker Renewables owns both sites. Black Cat pairs 1 megawatt (MW) of solar with 2.7 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery storage, while Ring Road has 4.4 MW of solar and a 13.5 MWh battery.
The money reaches both sides of the farming arrangement, too. The landowner receives solar land lease income, and Ward is paid to manage the bogs, in addition to his earnings from selling the berries.
DEI’s October announcement celebrates what it calls the first-ever agrivoltaic cranberry harvests, which Tare’s earlier account dates to fall 2025.
Top comment by Mckillio
Considering how tough farming is in general for independent farms, they're in huge debt on average, getting renewables on their properties for another income stream seems like a no brainer in general. If having panels can help their plants grow better and/or reduce water usage, even better. With that amount of renewable onsite electricity, and the wild cost of diesel, switching to EV equipment also seems like a no brainer if they have to get new equipment anyway.
The announcement doesn’t say how many cranberries were picked or how yields compare with growing them without panels. Those numbers might help other farmers decide whether solar could help keep their own bogs in business.

title: This cool accessory turns your bike electric in just three seconds
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 16 2026 - 6:58 am PT
There are plenty of e-bike conversion kits designed to turn your existing bicycle electric, but most involve at least a bit of wrenching. Spiny 2 takes a different approach, using a removable friction-drive system that can apparently snap onto your bike in just three seconds.
Now let me start by saying that this is a crowdfunding project on Kickstarter, so it’s a “buyer beware” situation. My long-time readers will know I have a rule about crowdfunding campaigns. I don’t cover them unless they either A) come from a company that has a track record of delivering products in the past, or B) I personally test out the product in advance to confirm it’s legitimate and works. In this case, I haven’t personally tested the Spiny 2 e-bike kit, but the brand does appear to have delivered hundreds of their previous version of the kit, so this isn’t a brand new, fly-by-night company.
The newly unveiled second-generation system combines its motor and battery into a compact 2.2 kg (4.9 lb) package. Once the mounting hardware and sensors are initially installed on the bike, the entire drive unit can be clicked into place before a ride and removed afterward.
It’s a friction drive kit, which isn’t the most elegant way to drive an e-bike, but it does get the job done quickly and simply.
That could be particularly useful for riders who want to keep the feel of their favorite pedal bike, but occasionally want a little electric help.
Instead of replacing a wheel or integrating with the drivetrain, Spiny 2 uses a roller that contacts the rear tire. Cadence and speed sensors detect when the rider begins pedaling, at which point the motor moves against the tire and begins providing assistance in around 0.25 seconds. Stop pedaling and the roller lifts away again, allowing the bike to roll without additional motor drag.
Keeping the whole kit street lega, the US version is rated at 250W nominal but can produce up to 750W of peak power and assist riders up to 20 mph (32 km/h). Canadian models peak at 500W, while versions intended for most other markets are limited to 250W and 25 km/h (15.5 mph).
A 266Wh battery is built into the removable unit, with Spiny claiming up to 90 km (56 miles) of range under ideal conditions. As always with e-bike range figures – especially one that ambitious from a relatively small battery – expect real-world range to depend heavily on assist level, terrain, rider weight, and speed. Suffice it to say though that unless you’re doing pro-level pedaling by yourself, the 266Wh battery isn’t going to net normal folks like you and me anywhere close to 56 miles of range on average day.
There are five pedal-assist levels controlled through a smartphone app or optional Bluetooth handlebar remote. Charging is handled via USB-C PD, while the unit carries an IP65 weather-resistance rating. That USB-C charging is perhaps one of the nicest features on the whole kit, allowing convenient recharging from a typical laptop charger or even a powerbank, and helping the kit join
a very limited club
of USB-C rechargable e-bikes.
Compatibility is fairly broad, including many road, city, hybrid, and touring bikes with either rim or disc brakes. Adapters are also available for some tighter-clearance bikes and Bromptons, though rear-suspension bicycles are excluded.
There are some limitations, with a major one being that you can’t operate a normal rear fender (though the
higher floating style rear fenders
should likely still work).
Spiny 2 recently
launched on Kickstarter
, with deliveries currently estimated for April 2027.
As with any crowdfunded hardware product, those delivery dates aren’t guarantees. But if Spiny can deliver on its promises, the ability to electrify your existing bike for Monday’s commute and turn it back into a normal lightweight bicycle three seconds later is certainly an interesting proposition.

title: Waymo picks Toronto as first Canadian city, targets riders in 2028
content:
autonomous driving
Fred Lambert
| Oct 16 2026 - 5:07 am PT
Waymo is bringing its robotaxis to Canada, and Toronto is first. Its cars will start driving the city’s streets in the coming days, and the company wants its first public riders on board in 2028.
That makes Toronto Waymo’s fourth announced market outside the US, after London, Tokyo, and Singapore. But there’s a catch: Ontario doesn’t have rules for a commercial driverless service yet.
Mapping first, riders in 2028
announced the expansion
on its blog today. As in every new city, its cars will start out manually driven. Specialists behind the wheel will build high-definition maps and validate the software on Toronto streets before anything runs without a human.
For operations, Waymo is bringing in Element Fleet Management, which is headquartered in Toronto, to run end-to-end fleet management. It also pointed to two Canadian companies already in its corner: the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, a long-term investor, and Magna International, its manufacturing partner.
Co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana called Canada “an important milestone in Waymo’s global journey.”
Waymo also says it and its partners will create “hundreds of roles” over time in fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and operations. That line is there for a reason. In April, Mayor Olivia Chow’s office told the Toronto Star it wouldn’t support Waymo if the service cost jobs, and that the company “must demonstrate this will not happen.”
Ontario’s rules run out before Waymo’s launch
Waymo’s post doesn’t mention a single permit or approval.
Ontario has allowed automated vehicle testing since 2016 under a pilot regulation, O. Reg. 306/15, and added driverless testing in 2019. According to
Ontario’s e-Laws database
, that regulation is revoked on October 13, 2027, months before Waymo wants to carry riders, and the province hasn’t said what replaces it.
It’s also a testing framework, not a ride-hailing licence. Transport Canada told Canadian Affairs last week that self-driving vehicles on public roads are limited to “temporary pilot projects” run by the provinces. So Waymo’s 2028 date depends on Doug Ford’s government writing rules that don’t exist today.
The safety case Waymo is bringing
Waymo’s pitch rests on its US record. The company says it has driven more than 400 million fully autonomous kilometres (roughly 250 million miles) and that its vehicles were involved in 95% fewer crashes causing serious injury or worse than human drivers in the cities where it operates.
reported last month
, Waymo now claims its cars have prevented 841 injuries. It’s carrying more than 500,000 paid rides a week across over a dozen US metros, and it
went driverless in Las Vegas
this summer with Denver, San Diego, and Tampa following.
Denver matters here. It’s Waymo’s first real snow city, and Toronto’s winters, with slush, road salt, and freezing rain coating sensors for months, are exactly what the long manual-driving phase is meant to test. Waymo calls its system “all-weather.” Toronto will check that claim.
Compare that to Tesla. Its “Robotaxi” service runs in seven US cities, Tesla still doesn’t disclose how many cars operate without a safety monitor, and
the fleet has been barely running
for much of the year. Tesla hasn’t put a date on carrying riders in a single Canadian city.
Electrek’s Take
This is the right way to enter a new country. Waymo isn’t promising driverless rides next month. It’s giving itself more than two years and at least two Toronto winters of data before anyone pays for a ride, which is exactly how it built a US service that now does half a million paid trips a week.
Queen’s Park and City Hall might give them trouble. Ontario’s only legal framework for these cars expires next October, there’s no path yet from a testing permit to a paid service, and Toronto’s mayor has already made jobs the condition for her support. Waymo clearly read that, which is why Element and “hundreds of roles” are front and center in its announcement.
I think Waymo gets there, but 2028 is Ontario’s deadline to hit as much as Waymo’s. If the province lets the pilot lapse without a commercial framework, Canada’s biggest city ends up watching London and Tokyo get robotaxis first.
And for those of us in Montreal: Quebec, your move.

title: U.S. trade commission finds solar imports from India, Indonesia and Laos are harming domestic industry - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Following affirmative dumping and subsidy findings by Commerce, the International Trade Commission’s final vote secures the issuance of federal antidumping and countervailing duty orders.
Ryan Kennedy
16 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
United States
The U.S. International Trade Commission building
The U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) has issued a
final affirmative injury determination
in its Solar IV investigation targeting crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells, whether or not assembled into modules, imported from India, Indonesia, and Laos.
The decision clears the final legal hurdle for federal trade protection, finding that dumped and subsidized imports from the three Asian nations cause material injury to domestic solar manufacturers. As a direct result of the ruling, the U.S. Department of Commerce will issue official antidumping (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders, establishing high tariff barriers and permanent cash deposit requirements across all three import corridors.
The upcoming duty orders will impose combined tariff rates as high as 249% for India, 268% for Indonesia, and 219% for Laos. These case-specific remedies, governed by the Tariff Act of 1930, will stack directly on top of existing executive tariffs and Section 232 minimum import price floors rather than replacing them.
Finalized duty rates
The USITC vote locks in the final margins established by Commerce last month. For Indian suppliers, Commerce set final dumping margins at 123.04% for all producers alongside a countervailing subsidy rate of 126.09%. Indonesian exporters face final dumping margins set at 94.36% for all producers, with countervailing duty rates ranging between 73.2% and 173.7% depending on the specific supplier. For imports originating in Laos, Commerce established final dumping margins at 65.43% for all exporters, accompanied by countervailing subsidy rates ranging between 82.03% and 153.67%.
The trade cases were originally brought by the Alliance for American Solar Manufacturing and Trade, a coalition represented by lead petitioners First Solar, Hanwha Qcells USA, and Mission Solar Energy. The litigation follows earlier Solar III duty orders targeting Southeast Asian manufacturing hubs in Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam.
Next steps
Following the USITC’s final injury determination, Commerce is scheduled to issue its official AD and CVD orders in early November 2026. Upon publication, U.S. Customs and Border Protection will be instructed to require final duty cash deposits on all incoming entries of cells and modules from India, Indonesia, and Laos.
The Commission’s full public report,
Crystalline Silicon Photovoltaic Cells, Whether or Not Assembled Into Modules, from India, Indonesia, and Laos
(Inv. Nos. 701-TA-772-774 and 731-TA-1756-1758, USITC Publication 5804) detailing its factual findings and legal analysis, will be published on the USITC website by November 23, 2026.

title: China proposes ban on exports of perovskite, tandem solar manufacturing technology - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
China has proposed banning exports of selected high-efficiency perovskite and tandem solar manufacturing technologies, alongside new restrictions on advanced polysilicon, wafer and crystalline-silicon cell production processes. The proposed measures would cover 12 photovoltaic technologies, with public consultation open until Nov. 15.
Vincent Shaw
16 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
UtmoLight’s tandem solar cell production line
Ministry of Commerce
(Mofcom) and Ministry of Science and Technology have proposed prohibiting exports of selected high-efficiency perovskite and tandem solar manufacturing technologies, alongside new restrictions on advanced polysilicon, wafer and crystalline-silicon cell production know-how.
The proposals, published on Oct. 16 under Joint Announcement No. 48 of 2026, would add 12 photovoltaic technologies to China’s Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. They are part of a broader consultation covering 40 technologies across sectors including solar energy, artificial intelligence and biomedicine. The public consultation runs until Nov. 15.
The proposed export bans cover production processes and related equipment manufacturing technologies for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells based on wafers measuring at least 182 mm and achieving conversion efficiencies of 30% or higher. They also include slot-die coating processes for perovskites with coating widths of at least 1.1 meters.
Additional thresholds apply to large-area modules, including single-junction perovskite modules measuring at least 1 square meter with conversion efficiencies of 18% or higher, and perovskite tandem modules of the same minimum area with efficiencies of at least 28%. The proposed controls target manufacturing technologies meeting these specifications rather than exports of finished modules.
Other technologies proposed for prohibition include cold-hydrogenation fluidized-bed processes for trichlorosilane production with annual single-line capacities of at least 250,000 metric tons, and silane-based fluidized-bed processes with annual capacities of at least 20,000 metric tons. The draft also covers processes for manufacturing silicon wafers no thicker than 70 micrometers and certain edge-passivation technologies for thin crystalline-silicon cells, along with related equipment manufacturing know-how.
The proposed restricted-export category includes polysilicon plant engineering technologies for production lines with annual capacities of at least 30,000 metric tons, as well as advanced crystal-pulling and wafer-cutting processes.
It also covers specified high-performance manufacturing processes for tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon), back-contact (BC) and heterojunction (HJT) solar cells, including deposition, passivation, diffusion and metallization technologies. The HJT provisions include certain p-type technologies evaluated under air mass zero (AM0) illumination conditions relevant to space applications.
Under China’s technology import and export regulations, prohibited technologies cannot be exported, while restricted technologies can be transferred overseas only with government approval and the necessary licenses.
The proposed export bans and licensing requirements have not yet taken effect. However, a separate interim registration requirement took effect on Oct. 16, when the announcement was issued.
Companies must register planned exports of the listed technologies, including qualifying key equipment, through the Mofcom’s online system before transfer. The requirement covers intellectual property transfers, overseas technology licensing, changes in ownership or control involving foreign entities, and transactions that are underway but have not yet been completed.
The Mofcom said the proposals address national security concerns as photovoltaic technologies increasingly find applications in aerospace, defense and other sensitive sectors. The ministry said technologies that fall below the specified thresholds, as well as finished products manufactured using controlled technologies, are outside the proposed scope. It added that the measures do not target any particular country, region or company.
If adopted, the controls could reinforce China’s position in advanced PV manufacturing by limiting overseas access to some of its most sophisticated production technologies.
Although exports of finished solar cells and modules would not be directly affected, transfers of controlled manufacturing know-how through technology licensing, overseas production-line installation and commissioning, equipment exports and on-site technical support could be prohibited or subject to government approval.
In the near term, the measures could delay overseas PV manufacturing projects, increase compliance costs and limit the deployment of advanced Chinese production technologies abroad. Over the longer term, the restrictions could strengthen China’s influence over the international diffusion of next-generation PV manufacturing technologies, potentially slowing efforts by overseas manufacturers to close the technological gap.
However, tighter controls could also complicate Chinese manufacturers’ international expansion plans and heighten trade tensions or prompt retaliatory measures.

title: Scientists develop air-source heat pump system for broiler houses - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Turkey have tested an air-source heat pump for heating commercial poultry houses, combining experimental measurements with numerical simulations. The system reduced annual heating costs by approximately 44% compared with conventional coal-fired heating.
Lior Kahana
16 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Heat pumps
The heat pump system
A research team in Turkey has assessed the potential of air-source heat pumps (ASHPs) to replace coal-fired heating in commercial poultry houses in cold climates. Combining experimental measurements, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, and cost analysis, the researchers found that an ASHP system could reduce annual heating costs by approximately 44% compared with coal-fired heating, while maintaining suitable indoor conditions for broiler chickens.
“The main novelty of this research lies in its integrated experimental, numerical, and techno-economic evaluation of an ASHP as a direct replacement for conventional coal-fired heating in commercial broiler houses,” corresponding author Zekeriya Parlak told
pv magazine
. “This work combines real-world energy consumption measurements from three identical broiler houses on the same farm, analytical heat-demand calculations, experimentally validated computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, and comparative heating-cost assessments.”
Parlak said his team also plans to investigate the integration of heat recovery units, PV panels, and battery storage with ASHPs in poultry houses. “The objective will be to evaluate the potential energy savings, system performance, and investment costs of these integrated technologies,” he said. “In particular, we aim to develop a calculation methodology for determining the appropriate heat pump capacity by considering the contribution of heat recovery systems to the overall heating demand.”
The researchers conducted the study at a commercial poultry farm in Sakarya, Turkey, using three identical broiler houses, each measuring 90.3 meters by 15 meters, with a wall height of 2.1 meters and a capacity of 21,000 chickens. Two houses were heated by coal-fired boilers, while the third used an ASHP connected to a hot-water storage tank and fan coil units (FCUs). During a production cycle that began in January 2024, the team measured indoor and outdoor temperatures, heating-system water temperatures, energy consumption, and ventilation parameters.
The researchers also calculated heating requirements and developed a CFD model using Ansys Fluent to simulate five FCU configurations featuring six or seven units. The simulations assessed temperature and airflow distribution at different heights and were validated against experimental measurements. “The analytical method predicted coal consumption with an error of only 0.14% and heat pump electricity consumption with an error of 2.21% compared with measured values,” said Parlak.
“Perhaps the most interesting numerical finding was that the number and operating mode of the fan coil units significantly affected thermal uniformity, even when the total heating capacity was kept constant,” Parlak said. “Operating all seven FCUs in heating mode produced the most homogeneous temperature and velocity distributions among the five investigated configurations, with standard deviations of 2.28 K for temperature and 0.28 m/s for air velocity. Moreover, the proportion of the cross-sectional area with air velocities below 0.1 m/s remained below 1% in all simulated cases. This indicates that appropriate air-distribution design is essential for minimizing stagnant zones and improving thermal conditions around the birds.”
The researchers also compared actual heating costs and estimated annual expenses over six production cycles. “The annual cost comparison showed a reduction from $15,506.26 for coal heating to $8,692.48 for the heat pump system, corresponding to approximately 44% lower annual heating costs,” Parlak said. “The comparative analysis also indicated that the heat pump offered additional cost savings of approximately 18% relative to coal, 42% relative to natural gas, 48% relative to fuel oil, and 65% relative to direct electric resistance heating under the evaluated conditions.”
The findings are presented in “
Performance evaluation of an air source heat pump heating system in broiler houses: Experimental measurements, CFD analysis, and cost comparison
,” published in
Case Studies in Thermal Engineering
. The research team included scientists from Sakarya University and ETA4 Engineering, both in Turkey.

title: Big highs and lows across Asia in September - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, Solcast, a DNV company, reports that September 2026 saw extreme solar irradiance variations across Asia, with Japan and Borneo experiencing up to 30% below-normal levels, while China, Korea, the Philippines and eastern Indonesia recorded significant surpluses. Typhoons drove much of the variability, while strengthening El Niño is expected to bring sunnier conditions to Southeast Asia and increased cloudiness to Japan and eastern China through year-end.
16 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Utility-scale
September brought unusually large swings in solar irradiance across Asia, with few regions experiencing a typical month and some areas around 30% above or below normal breaking records, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
. Japan and Borneo were notably cloudier, while parts of China, Korea, the Philippines and eastern Indonesia recorded much sunnier conditions. An active typhoon season contributed to the sharp contrasts, while the outlook for the final three months of 2026 remains brighter across much of Southeast Asia and cloudier in parts of eastern China and Japan as El Niño continues to strengthen.
Japan and Borneo experienced notably below-average irradiance in September with both close to 70% of normal. Japan suffered under a tropical storm and typhoons which each brought extensive cloud , while Borneo was affected by wildfire smoke followed by stronger cloud cover later in the
month. In contrast, northern China, Korea, the Philippines and eastern Indonesia recorded substantially above-average irradiance. The Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau in southern China saw particularly strong positive anomalies, reaching up to 30% above normal, the greatest increase across Asia.
The historical ranking map below puts these differences into context by comparing September irradiance at each location with previous Septembers. Each quintile represents 20% of historical years, from the lowest fifth to the highest fifth. Unlike the anomaly map, which shows the size of the departure from average, this map shows how this September ranks compared with past years. Notably large portions of the map, such as in Japan and Borneo, or Korea and southern China saw the highest or lowest September on record.
September continued an already active 2026 typhoon season, with three typhoons, Dujuan, Surigae and Choi-wan. Extreme sea surface temperatures have contributed to the particularly active season. Dujuan and Surigae impacted the Japanese islands in close succession, consistent with the substantial irradiance reductions observed there. Less powerful tropical storms and depressions also brought extensive cloud and rainfall across parts of the region, particularly Vietnam, Thailand and Japan, further suppressing irradiance during affected periods.
The daily maps show how tropical storms and typhoons moved across the region, with multiple systems present simultaneously in the Pacific between 20 and 23 September.
Looking ahead to the final three months of 2026, weather agencies show a strong consensus for sunnier conditions across most of Southeast Asia. Farther north, eastern China and Japan are forecast to experience cloudier-than-average conditions, while the outlook farther west is more mixed. This
regional divide comes as El Niño continues to strengthen, with measures already close to record levels.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: Electrifying everything - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
COP31 aims to increase electricity’s share of global final energy demand from 20% to 35% by 2035, accelerating the transition to clean, affordable energy through electrification. Australia is leading with rapid growth in solar, wind, batteries and EVs, demonstrating how renewable energy can lower electricity costs, reduce fossil fuel dependence and support decarbonisation.
International Solar Energy Society (ISES)
16 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
The UN Climate Change Conference COP31 will take place in Türkiye in November 2026. A flagship target is to raise the share of final energy demand met by electricity
Rising electricity demand signals rising affluence in developing countries, and progress towards “electrification of everything” via solar and wind. Dramatically cheaper, cleaner and more reliable domestic energy is a result.
Most industrial economies (including USA, China, the European Union, Japan and Australia) have annual per capita electricity consumption in the range 6-12 MWh compared with the global average of 4 MWh. For Latin America, India and ASEAN the figure is 1-3 MWh.
In an affluent advanced economy, about 20 Megawatt-hours (MWh) of clean electricity per person per year is required for decarbonisation of land transport, heating & cooling in buildings, water heating, and industrial process heat. This is relatively straightforward using off-the-shelf technology.
Another 5-25 MWh per person per year is required for decarbonization of the chemical industry, which includes metals, plastics, cement, precursor chemicals, and synthetic shipping & aviation fuels. This needs substantial technology development over the next decade.
The “Final energy” mentioned in the COP31 target refers to energy products delivered to the consumer, including vehicle fuel, natural gas and electricity. This is a silly measure of energy because it conflates chemical energy with electrical energy. The electricity used in a heat pump or electric vehicle is 3-5 times smaller than fossil fuel energy delivering the same service.
Rapid domestic electrification in Australia
COP31 is led jointly by Türkiye and Australia. Australia has a good electrification story to tell.
Australia is the global n. 1 for per capita solar generation, and n. 8 for wind. The Government target for 2030 is 82% of electricity from renewables (mostly solar and wind), up from 50% today.
The state of South Australia is tracking towards 100% net supply of electricity from solar and wind in 2028. South Australia has become an attractive destination for companies wishing to manufacture using clean energy.
More than 40% of Australian dwellings have rooftop solar (global n. 1 per capita), tracking towards 50% by 2030. The average size of new systems is 10 kW with turnkey cost of $10,000. This low cost arises from very smooth Government approvals, an experienced workforce, and absence of tariffs.
About 7% of Australian dwellings have home batteries, which is expected to triple by 2030, making Australia the global n. 1 per capita. The typical size of new home batteries is 25 kWh. Home battery uptake is driven by Government support, which is gradually reducing as it does its job of kick-starting the industry.
A revolution in domestic energy is underway. Home batteries coupled with rooftop solar, heat pumps and an EV allows families to enjoy abundant, clean, reliable and permanently cheap domestic energy: below $800 per year for electricity (and zero natural gas and vehicle fuel bills).
Completion of the 350 GWh Snowy 2.0 system around 2029 will deliver 13 kWh of long duration rechargeable pumped hydro energy storage per person (global n. 1).
EV uptake is rising rapidly, driven by the war on Iran. It’s currently at one quarter of new car sales (similar to the global average), although well behind the global leader Norway at 98%.
The rise of solar and batteries is having a remarkable effect on wholesale electricity prices. The graph shows inflation-adjusted average wholesale spot market prices in Australia’s national electricity market since 2012 (blue bars) and the renewable energy fraction of generation (red line). Expensive fossil gas is being pushed out of the market for both ancillary services and peak period power – gas dropped from 13% of generation a decade ago to 3% today.

title: China could produce the cheapest green hydrogen - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
China could produce green hydrogen at an average cost of $120/MWh, significantly less than Germany, the United States and Japan, according to researchers at the University of Cologne. The analysis highlights China’s cost advantages and the supply security risks associated with hydrogen imports.
Ralph Diermann
16 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Hydrogen
China has a significant cost advantage over Germany, the United States and Japan in green hydrogen production, with average costs projected at $120/MWh, according to a
recent analysis
Germany ranks second, with average costs of $175/MWh, based on a combination of domestic production and imports from North Africa and other European Union countries.
The United States could also meet its entire hydrogen demand domestically, but at a higher cost of $225/MWh. Japan, meanwhile, has limited and expensive domestic production potential. With no pipeline connections to the mainland, the island nation would have to rely on seaborne hydrogen imports, adding an estimated $80/MWh in transport costs.
Despite these additional costs, imports from China would remain cheaper than domestic production in Japan, averaging $190/MWh, according to EWI. Without Chinese supplies, Japan’s hydrogen import costs would exceed $300/MWh.
Import dependence raises supply security concerns
EWI attributes China’s cost advantage to favorable wind and solar resources, lower investment costs for renewable energy installations and electrolyzers, and lower labor and financing costs.
For Germany, the researchers identify import dependence as a potential risk to security of supply.
The analysis is based on EWI’s Global PtX Cost Tool, which calculates technically feasible green hydrogen supply worldwide, along with production and transport costs. The tool also covers hydrogen derivatives, including ammonia, methane, methanol and Fischer-Tropsch fuels, and accounts for transport by pipeline and ship.
For its 2026 update, EWI revised key assumptions, including capital expenditure for renewable energy installations and electrolyzers, as well as country-specific weighted average costs of capital (WACC).
The updated tool also offers higher geographical resolution and a revised classification of solar photovoltaic potential. New features include cost-potential curves and a “seasonality factor” that measures fluctuations in production throughout the year.
The tool is available free of charge on EWI’s website. Users can compare two cost scenarios through 2050 and two different supply profiles when running their own calculations.

title: Germany recommends eliminating direct internet access to PV plant control systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) recommends eliminating direct internet access to PV plant control systems to reduce cybersecurity risks. It also calls for secure remote connections, multifactor authentication, regular software updates and periodic security checks.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
16 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) has published
cybersecurity recommendations
to protect industrial control systems accessible via the internet. The agency strongly recommends securing networked control systems. The guidance targets operators of small and very small facilities, including hydropower plants, wind farms, waste-to-energy facilities and PV installations of all sizes.
The main recommendation is to eliminate direct internet access to plant control systems. In PV installations, these systems may include industrial controllers, communications equipment, monitoring gateways, inverters, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems and remote monitoring platforms.
Connecting these systems directly to the internet increases their exposure to cyberattacks. Systems accessible via public networks may be vulnerable to unauthorized access attempts, exploitation of known security flaws or manipulation of operating parameters. The risks extend beyond the loss of monitoring data, as incidents affecting operational technology (OT) systems can disrupt plant control and operations.
The BSI recommends replacing direct internet access with secure remote connections using virtual private networks (VPNs) and multifactor authentication. VPNs establish encrypted connections between authorized users and plant networks, while multifactor authentication requires an additional form of identity verification beyond a password. Although these measures do not eliminate cybersecurity risks, they reduce the likelihood of unauthorized access resulting from stolen credentials or weak passwords.
The agency also recommends keeping equipment up to date and promptly installing security patches and software updates. This applies to supervisory systems and connected field devices, including routers, firewalls, controllers, inverters and communications gateways. Failure to install updates can leave systems vulnerable to known security flaws for which fixes are already available.
The BSI also calls for periodic checks to identify devices and systems exposed to the internet. Operators should maintain inventories of connected assets, identify their communications interfaces and verify that remote services are not unnecessarily accessible. When exposed systems are identified, operators should implement appropriate mitigation measures.
For PV plants, the recommendations underscore the importance of separating corporate and operational networks, restricting remote access to authorized users and service providers, and establishing regular update and security review procedures. The BSI recommends integrating these practices into routine plant operations to strengthen the cybersecurity of connected control systems.

title: Nitric-acid-free process recovers more than 98% of silver from PV waste - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
French researchers have recovered silver, the most valuable material in end-of-life silicon PV modules, in two steps using a reusable leaching solution.
Brian Publicover
16 Oct 2026
Research & Development
recycling
Researchers at France’s Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA) have developed a leaching route that strips base metals from end-of-life solar cell waste in under 10 minutes while leaving the silver behind, avoiding the nitric acid used in most current recovery processes.
The process combines selective leaching with density-based separation and recovers more than 98% of the silver at laboratory scale, the researchers said. It produces a silver and silver chloride composite of 97.2% purity, and the team has validated it in a 20-liter pilot reactor.
Most hydrometallurgical routes dissolve silver in nitric acid and then precipitate it as silver chloride, a method that generates nitrogen oxides and nitrate-rich effluents, the researchers said. Alternatives such as methanesulfonic acid perform comparably but face high reagent costs and complex regeneration. Because the CEA process leaves the silver undissolved, the leachate can be reused over several cycles.
The leaching step uses 3 M hydrochloric acid with 10% hydrogen peroxide at 80 C. It dissolves more than 98% of the aluminum, copper, lead and zinc in the waste. Rather than dissolving, the silver forms an insoluble silver chloride shell around a metallic core, which shields it from further attack and limits silver losses during leaching to 1.7%. A density-based separation step at a 10% solid-to-liquid ratio then separates the silver from the silicon, leaving residual impurities below 0.5% by weight.
The feedstock is a metal-rich powder produced by sanding delaminated end-of-life modules layer by layer, a mechanical process the group described in a separate paper. The composite still needs downstream refining, such as chemical reduction or electrowinning, to become metallic silver.
Silver makes up only 0.1% to 0.5% of the waste by weight but accounts for about 60% of a module’s economic value, the researchers said, citing earlier literature.
The work was funded by the European Union’s Horizon Europe EVERPV project, which CEA coordinates. The same research group recently reported a
mild oxalic acid process for recovering indium
PV recycling economics
, and a University of Newcastle team reported
97% silver recovery
using froth flotation in January.
The scientists described their findings in “
A simplifie
d hydrometallurgical process for silver recovery from photovoltaic waste
,” which was recently published in
Hydrometallurgy
Recyclers’ silver recovery rates have risen as the sector has scaled. In data compiled by the International Energy Agency’s Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme (IEA-PVPS), US recycler Solarcycle reports
recovering nearly 92% of silver
at commercial scale and Italian pilot-scale recycler 9-Tech 90%. Alongside the EU-funded Photorama project, EVERPV is among the EU projects
developing multi-step pilot lines
that target 95% to 98% metal recovery.

title: US Army plans laser weapons that can be mounted on almost any vehicle
content: The US Army is making efforts to advance a new generation of high-energy laser weapons designed to counter drone threats across the battlefield. Through its Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) programme, the service aims to develop modular systems that can be transferred between different military vehicles to expand air defense capabilities beyond specialized units.Directed-energy weapons, such as E-HEL, can be used to take out drones at a much lower cost than using more expensive kinetic weapons like missiles. Powered by electric energy, E-HEL generates a lethal high-energy laser beam, offering a low cost-per-shot against critical unmanned aircraft system threats, and a magazine that regenerates with the system’s power supply.Scalable, affordable directed energy capabilitiesThe E-HEL program represents a significant step forward in the Army’s effort to deliver scalable, affordable, and adaptable directed energy capabilities to soldiers.The Army’s emerging concept focuses on separating laser weapon systems from the specific vehicles on which they are installed. Rather than developing a dedicated laser-equipped vehicle for every mission, the service wants modular systems that can be integrated onto different platforms according to operational requirements.During a panel discussion held recently at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention it was revealed that the Army could soon integrate laser weapons on multiple vehicles.Brigadier General Guy Yelverton, the Army’s Capability Program Executive for Defensive Fires, explained that the programme is exploring ways to integrate future laser capabilities across the service’s vehicle fleet.The concept could allow laser systems to be mounted on tactical vehicles, light utility platforms and other suitable military transport assets. It could also make it easier to relocate a weapon system when a vehicle requires maintenance or when operational priorities change.The program also aims to make the systems easier for soldiers to operate, potentially allowing units outside traditional air defence formations to employ laser weapons against incoming drones.The LOCUST family has already been explored in vehicle-mounted and palletised configurations. Some earlier variants have also been deployed in support of US operations along the southern border.The LOCUST X3 combines a laser projector with electro-optical and infrared cameras used to identify, track and engage targets. Additional sensors, including radar and passive radio-frequency detection equipment, can provide information to help cue the weapon toward potential threats.The system is primarily intended to counter small unmanned aircraft. Its relatively compact configuration makes it a candidate for deployment on light tactical vehicles, although integrating it onto smaller platforms presents challenges involving payload capacity, electrical power, cooling and overall system weight.Laser systems to be mounted on tactical vehiclesThe Army’s broader objective is not simply to acquire a new laser weapon, but to establish a flexible architecture that can accommodate improvements in performance and reliability over time.In September, the US Army announced the award to AeroVironment Inc. of an other-transaction-agreement for production under the Enduring-High Energy Laser program. This was the Army’s first production contract for a high energy laser weapon system.Developed using a modular open systems approach design consisting of 11 major interfaces, E-HEL is not locked into a single platform or vehicle. The system is designed for operational flexibility, capable of deployment from fixed bases, semi-fixed tactical sites, and mobile combat vehicles, ensuring broad applicability across the operational spectrum. This approach will enable onboarding of cutting-edge capabilities and continuous technology upgrades as they mature to address emerging Army requirements.

title: Perovskite solar modules reach 18.2% efficiency with safer solvents
content: A new, greener, lower-toxicity method could help manufacture flexible perovskite solar panels at an industrial scale using a roll-to-roll printing.The University of Surrey has proposed this safer method for producing high-efficiency perovskite solar modules. It uses a low-toxicity, bio-derived solvent formulation that operates at room temperature and reduces the use of hazardous industrial chemicals. The process uses continuous printing techniques similar to newspaper printing, which could make large-scale production both eco-friendly and cost-effective. “The potential impact of our innovation extends beyond simply replacing a hazardous solvent. A process based on easy-to-use, non-toxic solvents and simpler coating steps reduces the need for solvent handling, waste treatment and the safety infrastructure that goes with them,” said Professor Ravi Silva, Distinguished Professor, Director – Advanced Technology Institute (ATI) and Head of NanoElectronics Center. Roll-to-roll printing. Credit: Surrey University. Ditch toxic chemicalsLightweight, flexible perovskite solar cells have long promised to replace silicon panels. But hazardous production processes have hindered their commercial potential. Typically, creating printable perovskite inks requires large quantities of toxic solvents, including dimethylformamide and acetonitrile. These chemicals endanger factory workers and create severe environmental burdens. Surprisingly, just a single gigawatt-scale manufacturing line can consume over 90,000 liters of toxic solvent.Now, that chemical barrier is crumbling. The researchers discarded the hazardous legacy chemicals. And formulated a “Significantly Reduced-Toxicity” (SRT) ink system built on bio-derived ingredients. The team created a quick-drying formulation using a combination of ethanol and 2-methyltetrahydrofuran, a eco-friendly solvent derived from agricultural and forestry waste. This bio-derived mixture eliminates the need for anti-solvent processing steps. Skipping those harsh steps saves energy and conserves raw materials during manufacturing.Flexible mini-modulesGoing green did not mean sacrificing performance.Using a roll-to-roll compatible bar-coating method, the team printed solar mini-modules with an active area of 11.5 square centimeters. Coated at room temperature and dried with a quick gas jet, these flexible panels reached power conversion efficiencies over 18.2 percent while maintaining rock-solid stability under continuous illumination.The mini-modules feature an inverted architecture with bar-coated, self-assembled monolayers as hole-transport layers. This structure cuts the need for additional interlayers. According to the study, the team used a laser-based P1-to-P4 scribing process to monolithically link individual solar cells for industrial module patterning. The scientific paper further added that the development tested the eco-friendly solvent using a gas-blown bar-coating method. But the team also made sure it works with standard slot-die coating machines used in factories.As a result, the process could be integrated into high-throughput factory floors in the future. It would ensure that the eco-friendly manufacturing technique is ready for large-scale industrial deployment.“We want to help make clean energy available across the world, and if we can support decarbonization at scale in the same step, that is a double win for society,” Silva added. Integrating green chemistry into high-speed printing techniques makes the large-scale production of flexible solar cells a practical near-term reality. Flexible perovskites could soon power everything from portable consumer electronics and building-integrated windows to ultra-lightweight solar arrays launched into space. The study findings were published in the journal Nano Energy.
