title: New US Navy drone tech enables ship landings without GPS guidance
content: The U.S. Navy has demonstrated a new way to land drones on moving ships without using GPS, satellite navigation, or a pilot. In a recent test, the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division (NAWCAD) showed a drone carrying out its mission and landing on a moving ship using onboard cameras, motion sensors, and software.This demonstration could help the Navy fly drones in areas where enemies try to block satellite signals. NAWCAD, located in Patuxent River, Maryland, said the technology is ready for testing on Navy aircraft.Software guides drones onto moving ship decksLanding on a moving ship is hard because the deck moves with the waves. In the past, systems used ship-mounted radar, special recovery gear, and changes to the ship to help guide aircraft safely onto the deck.NAWCAD engineers have developed a software-based approach that uses cameras already installed on the drone. The team at its Maritime Autonomous Guidance-Navigation-Control Intelligent Coupled Systems Lab combined these cameras with guidance, navigation, and control algorithms.During flight, the software identifies the ship’s shape and visual features to determine its position. It then guides the aircraft toward the deck while predicting the deck’s movement, helping the drone time its landing as the vessel rises and falls.“In contested areas where satellites and communications are jammed, autonomy gives significant advantage to our sailors,” said Rear Adm. Todd Evans, commander of NAWCAD.New approach reduces reliance on costly equipmentThe Navy’s earlier autonomous shipboard drone landings required additional hardware. In 2006, the RQ-8A Fire Scout made the service’s first autonomous landings on a moving ship aboard USS Nashville, using ship-mounted radar to track the aircraft relative to the flight deck.The latest approach shifts much of that work into onboard software. It uses commercial-standard cameras, motion sensors, and electronics, potentially reducing the need for expensive radar installations and extensive ship modifications.The system is also designed to work with nearly any drone flight computer, according to NAWCAD. This could allow the Navy to introduce the capability through software upgrades, including on ships with limited room for additional equipment.“In a high-end maritime conflict, GPS is the first operational link an adversary attempts to sever,” said Peter Arslanian, a NAWCAD aerospace engineer.Technology could support larger combat dronesNAWCAD plans to extend the technology to larger uncrewed aircraft, including drones designed to transport supplies to tactical forces. The center is working to transfer the capability to several programs, including the Navy’s Small Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems program office and its Collaborative Combat Aircraft program for uncrewed wingmen.The work could also support DARPA’s EVADE, or Early VTOL Aircraft Demonstration, project. The initiative aims to develop drones that can take off from and land on ship decks without launch or recovery equipment. Five companies, including AeroVironment and Sikorsky, are developing designs for the effort.Fleet testing is the next stepThe Naval Innovative Science and Engineering Program and the Office of Naval Research funded the development. With the flight demonstration complete, the technology is moving toward operational testing on fleet aircraft.If testing proves successful, the system could give the Navy more flexibility to deploy drones from ships operating in environments where satellite navigation is unreliable or deliberately disrupted.

title: Scientists smash speed limit in superconductors, probe Cooper pairs
content: A collaboration of researchers from the Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter in Germany, the Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology in China, ETH Zurich in Switzerland, and the University of Oxford in the UK has achieved a major breakthrough by smashing the ‘speed limit’ in a superconductor to probe the depairing of entangled pairs of electrons, or Cooper pairs. Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity while offering zero electrical resistance and give out a magnetic field when cooled down to temperatures below a certain threshold.These unique properties have enabled technologies like particle colliders and medical devices such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), which sounded like something straight out of science fiction just a century ago. While we have succeeded in attaining these superconducting states in various materials, scientists are well aware of the fragility of these systems. An increase in temperature or changes in the electric current or magnetic fields are also sufficient to knock the material out of its superconducting state. Ripping off superconductivityWhile magnetic fields and electric current can be measured, there is yet another limit that is difficult to measure, given that it can cause disruptions in just a billionth of a second. This is the depairing limit, where entangled pairs of electrons, also known as Cooper pairs, can be ripped apart, and superconductivity can be lost immediately. Given the quick pace of disruption caused by crossing the depairing limit, scientists need to be even faster in their investigation to probe if it is being crossed, and the multinational team of researchers figured out a novel way to do so, which was akin to breaching the speed limit on the quick transition that occurs when the limit is reached. Type II superconductors, which are used for a wide range of applications, are actually a physical compromise. Unlike Type I superconductors, which have fragile magnetic limits, Type II superconductors boast higher limits but thanks to their internal magnetic fields, or quantum vortices, within them that allow electricity to flow and maintain superconductivity even through extreme conditions. A strong electric current can whip these quantum vortices and generate resistance in the material, thereby bringing an end to its superconductivity. So, the team of researchers decided to use this information to learn more about the depairing limit. Smashing the speed limitThe team worked with two different types of superconducting materials, niobium nitride (NbN) and a member of the yttrium barium copper oxide (YBCO) family, both of which exhibit high-temperature superconductivity. NbN is known to have s-wave gap symmetry, while YBCO has a d-wave gap symmetry, which determines how easy it is to rip apart their superconductivity. To outrun the quantum processes that occur within a few billionths of a second, the team built a optical-electrical circuit that surpasses the velocity of tens of kilometers per second at which quantum vortices move by several orders of magnitude. The researchers found that NbN remained superconducting until the applied current reached a threshold and then abruptly lost its superconductivity. The YBCO material, on the other hand, lost its superconductivity gradually. The team attributes this different to the gap symmetries of the two materials, where NbN’s energy gap is the same in all directions, while that in the YBCO material varies significantly and therefore cannot be snuffed out in one go. The difference in the behavior of the two materials gave the researchers a very fundamental understanding of superconductivity, which ultimately boils down to Cooper pairs and their stability. Exceeding the speed limit of the transition of the superconducting material has given researchers new ways to study and access these properties in the future. The research findings were published in the journal Nature Physics.

title: Tiny atomic flaws could make metal alloys stronger, resistant to heat
content: US scientists have used tiny defects in crystals to make stronger and more heat-resistant metal alloys that could be incorporated into future aircraft jet engines and power plants.The research was led by Andreas Bezold, PhD, an assistant professor of materials science and engineering at the Ohio State University. He believes the approach could lead to more durable materials that withstand extreme heat.Crystal defects are irregularities caused by imperfectly arranged atoms. But rather than a weakness, these defects could reportedly form complex three-dimensional (3D) structures. When carefully arranged, the imperfections could strengthen metals without altering their chemical composition.“Defects are very important to learn more about, because by understanding how they interact with a material’s internal structure helps us design stronger materials,” Bezold pointed out. When flaws become usefulAll crystals contain tiny defects that disrupt their atomic structure and can change their properties. Although crystal defects are usually associated with damage or weakness, but arranging them correctly can actually make metals stronger.To prove this, the research team worked with two materials: a cobalt-nickel-based superalloy and a cobalt-chromium-tungsten alloy. They first deformed the metal crystals and then aged them through heat treatment. This formed dense networks of atomically thin structures inside the alloys.To the team’s surprise, the structures altered the arrangement of the atoms within the metals. And even made them better at withstanding stress and handling extreme heat. “We wanted to make these strengthening structures a deliberate part of the material’s design,” Bezold stated. “So it was fascinating to see how defects could have such a positive effect on the overall durability of the alloys.”To better understand these changes, the team combined transmission electron microscopy with computer simulations. The results showed that the way atoms surround defects could determine how strong a metal becomes. Jets and power plantsAccording to Michael Mills, PhD, a professor of materials science and engineering at the university and co-author of the study, the discovery could be particularly useful for technologies that operate under extreme heat and stress. These can include aircraft turbine engines or power plant machineryJet engines need metals that resist deformation at temperatures often exceeding 1,832 degrees Fahrenheit (1,000 degrees Celsius), while power plant components must withstand prolonged exposure to extreme heat.“Seeing the strengthening process on the atomic scale was quite stunning, since despite being associated with damage, the right defects with the right structure and chemistry can actually make a material stronger,” Mills said in a press release. The effort builds on earlier Ohio State research into defects that strengthen metals. It involved researchers from Ohio State, the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg, and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, with support from the NSF, DOE, and other organizations. The team hopes the findings will lead to better ways of designing stronger, high-performance materials.“This is a field that is quickly becoming very exciting,” Bezold said. “We hope that this idea becomes a new lever that strengthens and pushes the limits of material engineering even further.”The study has been published in the journal Science.

title: Humanoid robots play table tennis doubles, rally for over 10 shots
content: Researchers have developed PingpongDuo, a robotic framework that enables humanoid robots to play table tennis doubles through coordinated movements and alternating strikes. The system addresses the challenges of sharing limited space, repositioning quickly, maintaining striking accuracy, and avoiding collisions between teammates. It combines coordinated positioning with learned movement and racket-control skills to help robots respond to changing ball trajectories while working together. In experiments, the framework improved ball-return performance in simulation. It demonstrated that two humanoid robots could sustain consecutive rallies while following the strict alternating-strike rule required in doubles play.Humanoid robots rallyResearchers from the University of Hong Kong, Shanghai Innovation Institute, Archon Robotics, and NVIDIA have developed PingpongDuo, a control framework that enables two humanoid robots to play table tennis doubles while coordinating their movements and alternating shots.The system combines AI, motion learning, and risk estimation to help robots strike the ball, clear space for teammates, and reposition for subsequent returns without colliding.Unlike conventional humanoid table tennis systems designed for individual play, PingpongDuo coordinates two robots operating in the confined space on one side of the table. Each robot must strike in strict alternation, moving away from the central hitting area after its shot while its teammate prepares to return the next ball.The framework uses a hierarchical control system that combines team-level positioning with individual movement and striking skills. At the team level, a planner selects positioning targets for both robots. A learned risk estimator evaluates potential movements for collision risks involving their hands, feet, and bodies. A safety filter adjusts risky positioning plans while prioritizing the robot preparing to strike, helping preserve its ability to return the ball.At the individual level, the system uses separate artificial intelligence policies for footwork and racket control. Researchers trained the movement policy using human table tennis doubles footage, creating a library of approximately 200 footwork sequences covering different movement distances.The robots learn to transition between striking, clearing space, recovering, and waiting. Training each skill using the body positions and movements produced by the other helps the robots respond to new shots without first returning to a standard posture.Humanoids sharpen strikesThe researchers also developed a racket-arm refinement policy to improve ball returns after rapid movements. The policy adjusts seven arm joints based on the robot’s current state and the estimated position and velocity of the ball.To train this component, the team calibrated a physics simulator using real measurements of ball flight, table bounces, and racket contact. The resulting model allows the system to learn how changes in racket movement affect whether a ball clears the net and lands on the opponent’s side.In simulation, PingpongDuo improved ball-return success by 13.2 percent over the state-of-the-art baseline. The researchers also reported a positioning error of approximately 2 centimeters during clearance.In real-world experiments, two Unitree G1 humanoid robots sustained more than 10 consecutive alternating strikes. A robot also completed a 2.15-meter clearance-and-recovery movement cycle in 2.4 seconds, reaching a peak speed of 2.23 meters per second.The researchers noted that the current system relies on external motion-capture equipment and does not account for ball spin. Future work will investigate onboard perception, spin estimation, and autonomous attacking and defensive strategies.

title: Hanwha tests 30 kW laser weapon, develops vehicle-mounted 50 kW system
content: South Korea’s Hanwha Systems has demonstrated its laser air defense weapons intercepting drones during a military exercise, while developing a more powerful, vehicle-mounted system aimed at international defense customers.During the South Korean Army’s Army TIGER+ future warfare exercise on October 14, the company’s Cheongwang laser weapon and a mobile, 30-kilowatt-class laser cannon intercepted all three target drones. The demonstration was attended by around 500 military, academic, and industry representatives.Hanwha is also pursuing exports of a 50-kilowatt laser-equipped armored vehicle, designed to combine greater mobility with higher laser output. The system is still under development, and the company has not announced a confirmed export order.Cheongwang targets low-cost drone threatsSouth Korea’s Cheongwang, also known as Laser Air Defense Weapon Block-I, was developed by Hanwha Systems and the country’s Agency for Defense Development. It became operational in December 2024, with South Korea describing it as the world’s first operationally deployed laser air defense weapon. The Korea Times and ChosunBiz reported the latest demonstration.The system focuses a high-energy laser beam on a target to damage critical components, such as its battery, rather than launching a conventional interceptor. Hanwha says each engagement costs about 2,000 South Korean won, or around $1.50, and the system can keep operating as long as it is electrical power.That cost structure could be useful against inexpensive drones, which can otherwise force defenders to expend costly missiles to defeat relatively cheap threats. Laser weapons don’t consume a separate projectile for each engagement, though they still require power, cooling, and suitable conditions to operate effectively.The October exercise followed another demonstration in September, when Cheongwang reportedly intercepted four drones and two unmanned aerial vehicles in succession. These demonstrations highlight the system’s potential against small aerial threats, but do not establish its effectiveness against every type of drone or under all battlefield conditions.A more powerful laser moves onto an armored vehicleAlongside Cheongwang, Hanwha has developed a mobile 30 kW-class laser cannon intended for installation on combat vehicles. The system uses miniaturized, lightweight components and phase-change-based cooling technology to manage heat generated during high-power operation.The company is also developing a separate 50 kW Laser Armored Vehicle for overseas customers. The higher-output vehicle was displayed at the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland in September and at South Korea’s Defense Drone Technology Exhibition.The 50 kW configuration is designed to offer greater mobility and laser power than the existing fixed Cheongwang system. Defense News reported in September that Hanwha planned to begin serial production by the end of 2027. That remains a company target, not a confirmed production milestone.Hanwha targets international defense marketsHanwha Systems is positioning both Cheongwang and the vehicle-mounted laser for export as militaries seek more affordable ways to counter small drones used for surveillance, reconnaissance, and attacks.The company has said it is in discussions with potential customers in Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, although it has not publicly identified a buyer for the 50 kW vehicle.Laser weapons still face limitations. Rain, fog, moisture, and other atmospheric conditions can reduce the energy reaching a target, while maintaining a laser on a moving or maneuvering drone requires accurate tracking and sustained beam control.

title: BMW opens third Gen6 EV battery site for next-gen electric cars
content: BMW Group has begun series production of its sixth-generation high-voltage batteries in Shenyang, China, to power future Neue Klasse electric vehicles built in the country. The new technology offers up to 30 percent longer range and faster charging compared with the previous generation.Shenyang becomes the third production location in BMW’s global Gen6 battery network, following Debrecen in Hungary and Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Germany. Manufacturing batteries near vehicle plants shortens transport routes and supports local supply as the automaker expands production of its latest electric-vehicle technology.“The high-voltage battery is a key component of our all-electric vehicles and one of the BMW Group’s most important technologies for the future,” said Dr. Raymond Wittmann, BMW AG’s board member responsible for Production.New cells offer higher energy densityThe Gen6 batteries use newly developed cylindrical cells with more than 20 percent higher energy density than the previous cell generation. BMW mentioned that the technology also delivers up to 30 percent faster charging and longer range.A cell-to-pack design integrates the cylindrical cells directly into the battery housing, removing the conventional module level. This arrangement makes better use of the available installation space and allows BMW to adapt the battery for different vehicle models.The battery also incorporates BMW’s Energy Master, a central control unit mounted directly on the high-voltage pack. It brings together essential power-supply and battery-management functions.The Shenyang batteries are intended for China-built Neue Klasse models, making local battery manufacturing a key part of the company’s regional vehicle production plans.Battery network expands across marketsBMW’s Gen6 manufacturing strategy places battery assembly close to the vehicle factories it supplies. The company says this approach supports stable supply and strengthens the resilience of its production network.Battery assembly facilities in Woodruff, United States, and San Luis Potosí, Mexico, are also preparing to begin series production in the coming months.All locations operate under common production, quality, and safety standards and contribute regional manufacturing and supplier expertise.“Production in Shenyang exemplifies our global approach: We manufacture locally, efficiently and close to our markets, in line with uniform global standards and the highest quality,” Wittmann said.Laser welding meets digital quality checksProduction starts with cell inspections before the cells are joined with cooling units to form clusters. Following laser cleaning, those clusters and the cell contact system are precision-welded together.A specialized foaming process then bonds the components into a single mechanical unit, contributing to the battery’s safety, stability, and longevity. Workers and production equipment complete the housing closure, sealing, and riveting before the Energy Master is installed.Digital quality controls accompany the manufacturing process. Production data is captured and analyzed throughout assembly, while digital twins, data analytics, and AI-supported inspections help identify deviations early and maintain traceability.Inline inspection systems monitor laser-welded joints in real time. Every completed battery then undergoes comprehensive end-of-line testing for quality, safety and functionality.With Shenyang now producing Gen6 batteries, BMW has established a local source for the energy systems underpinning its China-built Neue Klasse vehicles.

title: SpaceX delivers 6,300 pounds of supplies and science gear to the ISS
content: Orbiting 250 miles above the planet, NASA astronaut Anil Menon marked his 50th birthday in a way few could ever. He received a special delivery package.After a 51-hour orbital pursuit that began with a dazzling pre-dawn launch, SpaceX’s cargo Dragon spacecraft successfully docked with the International Space Station’s Harmony module on October 15. The mission was designated Commercial Resupply Services CRS-35. It brought over 6,300 pounds of vital supplies, cutting-edge science experiments, and a surprise birthday delivery for Menon, who served as the prime crew member monitoring the automated rendezvous.Menon launched to the ISS in July on Soyuz MS-29 for an eight-month stay. Hence, he was midway through his extended mission when CRS-35 arrived. Chasing the stationThe journey began two days earlier at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, where a Falcon 9 rocket roared to life and climbed into the morning sky. Launched near dawn, the rocket lit up the upper atmosphere and gave spectators along the US East Coast a glowing “space jellyfish” from its expanding exhaust plumes.Traveling at a high 17,500 mph, Dragon executed a series of precise thruster burns to catch up with the station as both spacecraft sped over South Africa. Docking proceeded flawlessly. Dragon autonomously attached to the space-facing zenith port on the station’s Harmony module, bringing a fresh supply line to the newly arrived Crew-13 astronauts, who took over station operations earlier this month.The Dragon spacecraft is delivering a diverse range of operational equipment and advanced scientific experiments to support the orbital laboratory. Its primary payload includes the eighth and final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays (IROSAs) to complete the station’s power-grid expansion, along with maintenance components for the Canadarm2 robotic arm and replacement hardware for the station’s toilet systems. Research and upgrades to ISSOn the scientific side, the shipment carries materials to produce 3D-printed artificial retinas to treat vision loss on Earth, and 3D heart tissue models to improve drug testing.On Earth, gravity causes cells to settle and deform. In zero gravity, cells grow in 3D structures similar to how they form inside the human body, allowing scientists to cultivate far more realistic heart tissues and brain organoids.Furthermore, researchers will study brain organoids to help pinpoint potential therapies for neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis. It also includes experimental materials to observe how a new type of glass forms without the interference of gravity.The arrival marks a transitional moment for the orbital laboratory. As the Crew-13 team unpacks fresh food and scientific instruments, outgoing Crew-12 members are ready to share stories from their nearly eight-month stint in space.SpaceX’s Cargo Dragon stands out as a key asset for international space operations because it can return to Earth. It features a protective heat shield and parachute system that let it land safely. Dragon will remain tethered to the station for about a month. Astronauts will pack its pressurized cabin with completed research, waste, and spent hardware before the spacecraft detaches for a powered re-entry and splashdown in the ocean.

title: Factory-built modules could speed up 10MW data center construction
content: A proposed 10-megawatt AI data center in Indiana could use factory-built modules to shorten its delivery schedule to within one year. Data center company Brightray announced the project on October 14 after its subsidiary signed a letter of intent with a US mission-critical infrastructure partner.The agreement outlines plans to manufacture and integrate data hall modules while foundation and supporting construction work proceed at the site. The approach aims to accelerate deployment of infrastructure for high-density AI computing, with planned compatibility with Nvidia’s GB300 platform.The proposal remains at an early stage. Its principal cooperation arrangements are nonbinding, and construction depends on final technical specifications, commercial terms, approvals, and a definitive contract.Moving construction into the factoryBrightray intends to complete pre-installation and integration of the data hall modules and related functional systems during manufacturing. On-site work would then focus on placing modules, connecting interfaces, and commissioning the completed facility.The planned single-story layout would accommodate AI equipment alongside the space needed for operation and maintenance. Power distribution, cooling, and the arrangement of the data halls are being planned around high-density computing requirements.Brightray’s proposed scope includes design, manufacturing, integration, delivery, and other services agreed with its partner.“Our entry point is delivery: with Brightray’s prefabricated data center solution, we move more of the work into the factory and run manufacturing in parallel with on-site works, with the aim of shortening the delivery period for this project to within one year,” said founder Bin Wang in the latest press release.One-year target covers the entire projectThe proposed delivery period extends beyond manufacturing and shipping prefabricated modules.It covers design finalization, permitting, international shipping, foundation and ancillary construction, installation, and commissioning in the United States. That date and the implementation schedule remain subject to the subsequent definitive contract.The facility is planned around Tier III design standards, with a target annual power usage effectiveness, or PUE, below 1.2. These remain design objectives rather than demonstrated operating results.Final specifications and delivery arrangements also depend on site conditions, available power, required approvals, and equipment supply. Those dependencies remain relevant even when manufacturing and site preparation proceed simultaneously.First US opportunity awaits a firm agreementThe letter of intent is Brightray’s first for a US project, giving the company an opportunity to establish local delivery and partnership experience.Under the proposed arrangements, the unnamed partner intends to issue a purchase order by November 15, 2026. However, neither party is obligated under the principal cooperation provisions to purchase equipment, provide supplies, or make payments.The letter expires 12 months after signing unless a definitive agreement replaces it earlier. Brightray said there is no assurance that a purchase order or final contract would follow, or that the project would proceed as planned.If finalized, the Indiana-based development could serve as a reference for future US projects.For now, the proposed 10MW facility offers a test of whether factory integration can accelerate AI infrastructure delivery while meeting the site’s power, cooling, and construction requirements.

title: Alef flying car takes on Tesla Roadster with new flight demonstration
content: California-based Alef Aeronautics released a video on Thursday showing its electric flying car soaring over a Tesla Roadster, welcoming the automaker to what it calls the “flying car race.” The company said the demonstration marked its 1,000th logged flight. It follows an earlier video showing Alef’s Model Zero Ultralight driving and flying, including a flight over a Tesla Cybertruck.Alef used the latest demonstration to highlight the differences between its aircraft and Tesla’s proposed thruster-equipped Roadster, while promoting its progress toward limited customer deliveries.An airborne welcome for Tesla“Welcome, Tesla, to the flying car race; we’ve been here alone for eleven years,” said Jim Dukhovny, Alef’s CEO.The company also claimed that the “Tesla Roadster today became the second flying car in history, following Alef.” Both vehicles use electric powertrains and all-wheel drive, according to Alef. They also share an early investor, Tim Draper. Their approaches to getting airborne differ. Alef uses distributed electric propulsion, while the Tesla Roadster is expected to use thrusters.Alef’s design incorporates a wing-forming body and a rotating cabin. The company said its vehicle uses air for liftoff rather than relying on stored compressed gas. According to Alef, its lower vehicle weight also allows it to incorporate a “full-vehicle ballistic parachute.”A vehicle for roads and flightAlef’s concept combines road travel with vertical takeoff and landing. Its intended ability to drive and park gives it a different use case from aircraft designed solely for flight.The company developed its first flying-car prototype in 2019. In 2022, it unveiled its first full-size Model A prototype and announced a driving range of 220 miles and a flight range of 110 miles. Those figures describe the Model A’s announced capabilities, rather than the distance covered during the Roadster flyover.In 2023, Alef received an FAA Special Airworthiness Certification for its flying car. That milestone should be distinguished from full type certification or authorization for unrestricted customer operations.The company subsequently released public footage of its Model Zero Ultralight operating on the ground and in the air. Its latest video continues that demonstration-led approach, placing another recognizable Tesla vehicle beneath its aircraft. Dukhovny described competition as beneficial to the emerging market.“It proves the market, establishes a separate flying car category, creates industry for lobbying specific regulations, brings investor focus, helps compare technology, and creates a benchmark to measure against,” he said.Limited deliveries targeted for 2026Alef revealed that it has received more than 3,600 pre-orders worth $1 billion. Its first flying car is expected to start at $299,999. The company began hand-building its first customer vehicles in December 2025 at its Silicon Valley facility in California.Its initial delivery target covers a limited number of early buyers by the end of 2026. According to Alef, these vehicles are intended for “the purpose of testing flying cars in the real-world environment, under very controlled conditions.”The company plans for increase production in 2027 and provide training and support to early adopters. For now, Alef’s path toward customer use centers on controlled testing, with the Roadster flyover serving as its latest public demonstration.

title: New robot brain lets humanoids tackle multi-step tasks autonomously
content: NEURA Robotics has introduced Neuron AI, a robot foundation model designed to help robots understand and interact with their surroundings using multiple sensory inputs. The system combines visual perception with touch, sound, language, robot-state information, and memory to support a range of tasks. The German company aims to deploy the model across different robot platforms, allowing customers to adapt its capabilities to specific applications. NEURA plans to demonstrate the technology through its humanoid robots, showcasing its approach to developing adaptable robotic systems for real-world environments.Advances robot IntelligenceNeuron AI is a robot foundation model designed to combine visual perception, touch, sound, language, and memory to help robots perform complex tasks. The German robotics company described the system as a Perception-Language-Action (PLA) model that processes sensory information and translates it into physical actions. The architecture is designed to support multiple robot platforms, allowing skills to adapt to different applications rather than being developed separately for each machine.Neuron AI integrates several information sources, including 3D vision, tactile and force measurements, audio, robot-state data, and language. According to NEURA, the model aligns these inputs over time to help robots interpret their surroundings and maintain context as tasks progress.The inclusion of tactile and force data could help robots determine whether physical interactions have produced the intended results. For example, changes in contact forces could indicate whether a screw has engaged correctly, while audio cues could help identify when a mechanical latch has clicked into place. These examples illustrate the intended capabilities rather than independently verified performance results.Memory is another component of the architecture. NEURA noted that the system can retain information about earlier events and objects that have moved out of view, potentially helping robots coordinate actions across multiple stages of a task.The approach combines perception, contextual information, and action within a common model. However, the company has not published comparative benchmarks demonstrating how much memory or additional sensory inputs improve performance over vision-based systems.Furthering humanoid automationNEURA said Neuron AI supports five robot embodiments, including the 4NE1 Gen 3 and Gen 4 humanoids, a wheeled 4NE1 platform, and two additional bimanual robot platforms. This approach aims to transfer learned capabilities across different hardware configurations while allowing customers to adapt skills to their specific requirements.The company’s product information states that inference runs locally on the robot without requiring a cloud connection. On-device processing could allow robots to execute learned skills without continuous access to remote computing infrastructure.Neuron AI’s training process combines real-world robot experience, simulated variations, and human demonstrations recorded using sensor-equipped suits. NEURA’s training infrastructure, called NEURA Gyms, supports data collection, skill training, and benchmarking. The company also identifies industrial data partnerships with Schaeffler and Bosch.NEURA plans to use its Neuraverse platform to help customers fine-tune robot capabilities for particular workflows and distribute them across fleets. Customers can keep their trained skills private or choose to share capabilities and deployment data with the wider ecosystem.The company identifies Time-to-Skill—the time required to teach a robot a task and achieve reliable execution—as a key measure of progress. However, the announcement does not include measured results for this metric.NEURA plans to demonstrate Neuron AI using its 4NE1 humanoid at NVIDIA GTC Berlin from October 20–22. The planned 11-minute autonomous sequence involves sorting laundry, loading a washing machine, closing and reopening it, unloading the clothes, and transferring them to a dryer without human intervention.The demonstration is intended to show how the system coordinates multiple actions while maintaining context throughout a task. The announced sequence covers laundry handling rather than a complete washing and drying cycle.

title: Elon Musk showcases 'flying car' Tesla Roadster at SpaceX facility
content: Growing up, every vision of the future featured flying cars. Elon Musk seems determined to finally make it happen. At a product reveal staged at a SpaceX rocket development facility in Texas, the billionaire CEO showcased a prototype of the long-delayed Tesla Roadster. The event featured high-flying stunts, air-pumping cold thrusters, and a driverless demonstration that looked straight out of a sci-fi movie. “Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk wrote shortly after on X.Turns out the future does have flying cars pic.twitter.com/6fexPp6SXI— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 16, 2026A rocket-fueled spectacleThe highlight was brief, wild, and entirely experimental. Propelled by 10 ultra-high-pressure air nozzles fed by internal compressed tanks, the prototype used underbody suction to cling to a steep ramp, hang upside down, and spin off. It leaped over a line of parked Teslas, flipped mid-air, and used bursts of compressed gas to break its fall before landing safely in a cloud of white smoke.The specs sound absurd. Musk claims the production model will reach 0 to 60 mph in under a second — and the credit for this goes to rocket-thruster technology. “Success is not guaranteed,” Musk told the crowd, explaining that the test ran autonomously for safety. “I mean that. It’ll probably work, but if it doesn’t work, we’re at a safe distance.”Tesla’s next-generation electric Roadster features an all-wheel-drive powertrain, seating for four, 10,000 Nm of wheel torque, a 620-mile range, and a top speed exceeding 250 mph. The standard model costs $50,000 to reserve.Upgrading to the Thrust Variant requires a $245,000 follow-up payment and adds SpaceX cold-gas rear thrusters alongside an active multi-mode fan system for downforce, cutting acceleration down to under a second. An invite-only Rocket Variant replaces standard features with a single-seat configuration and perimeter thrusters for true flight, rendering it non-road-legal.The long road to 2028While the spectacle was undeniable, aviation experts remain skeptical that the vehicle can serve as both a practical road car and a true aircraft.Aircraft design prioritizes minimal weight to generate lift and maintain stability. Hence, heavy components are detrimental to performance. Also, passenger road vehicles use safety features like steel bumpers and crumple zones to absorb impact forces during collisions. Heavy safety parts protect cars during crashes, but that extra weight makes it hard to fly.“Inevitably, something that is a hybrid between the two is going to be a poor performing aircraft and a poor performing vehicle, and also quite expensive,” Roger Conner, vertical flight curator at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum, told CNN. Thursday’s demonstration did not show long-range flight capabilities. “We’re not talking about sustained flight,” he emphasized. “We are literally talking about hopping.”Musk pitched the car as the direct result of a collaboration between “the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company.” The current tentative production target has been set for 2028. Still, Musk has a track record of setting optimistic release targets for Tesla products, only to miss them by years.Whether drivers will ever legally hover over morning traffic jams remains an open question. Nevertheless, watching a sports car flip upside down and land on cold-gas jets was proof enough that flying cars are moving out of science fiction and onto the runway. Way to go, Musk.

title: Directed-energy weapon integrated on vehicle to neutralize threats
content: A San Francisco-based company has showcased that laser-based counter-drone weapon can easily offer aerial protection for autonomous military logistics vehicles. Aurelius Systems recently mounted its Archimedes autonomous laser weapon on an American Rheinmetall unmanned ground vehicle at AUSA 2026.Aurelius Systems revealed that by combining high-power directed energy lasers, advanced sensors, and AI autonomy, Archimedes tracks, targets, and neutralizes aerial threats in seconds. When deployed in numbers, Archimedes units form a resilient defense grid, creating persistent protection for forces, facilities, and critical infrastructure.Directed-energy counter-UAS systems offer precise engagementThe integration brings together an autonomous ground platform and a directed-energy weapon designed to detect, track and engage small aerial targets. The concept addresses an increasingly important battlefield challenge: how to sustain military forces when conventional supply vehicles and personnel face persistent surveillance and attacks from inexpensive drones.Directed-energy counter-UAS systems offer precise engagement with multi-drone threats. They provide a compact, low-SWaP-C platform that reduces costs and logistical burden compared to traditional systems.Built for rapid deployment without heavy logisticsThe system is small, compact, and field-portable and built for rapid deployment without heavy logistics. It also integrates optical sensing paired with machine learning for real-time detection and targeting — no operator required.Aurelius Systems’ partnership with Rheinmetall was announced in July. The partnership brings together Aurelius’ directed-energy platform, Archimedes, with American Rheinmetall’s robotic combat vehicles to address one of the most urgent challenges in modern defense: mobile, cost-effective, scalable protection against multi-drone threats.Archimedes is being integrated first on the Ox, the unmanned ground vehicle American Rheinmetall has entered in the U.S. Army’s Ground Optionally Autonomous Transport competition for a vehicle that hauls supplies and equipment over rough terrain. With a laser on board, a cargo-carrying vehicle can defend itself against drones during resupply runs, a role Rheinmetall has described as protection for autonomous logistics missions.“The battlefield demands mobility, autonomy, and resilience. By integrating autonomous directed-energy with robotic combat vehicles, we’re delivering force-multiplying technologies that operate in the most dangerous environments, helping protect warfighters while enhancing mission effectiveness,” said CEO of Aurelius Systems Michael LaFramboise in July, . “This partnership with American Rheinmetall supports a future where forces can sustain operations in contested environments, reduce warfighter risk, and maintain freedom of movement.”The laser is being integrated with American Rheinmetall’s Ox unmanned ground vehicle, a platform entered in the U.S. Army’s Ground Optionally Autonomous Transport competition.The vehicle is intended to transport supplies and equipment across difficult terrain, supporting military logistics operations where sending crewed vehicles could expose personnel to unnecessary danger.Integrating Archimedes could expand the Ox’s role beyond transporting cargo. Equipped with a counter-drone capability, the platform could potentially detect and engage aerial threats while supporting supply movements.This would be particularly relevant in contested environments where drones can observe roads, locate logistics convoys and attack vehicles carrying ammunition, fuel, food and other essential supplies.

title: US Military drones tap 150,000 radios to counter jamming threats
content: L3Harris Technologies and Skydio are integrating military drones with tactical radio technology to help U.S. forces maintain communications under electronic warfare threats. The partnership combines Skydio’s X10D drone with L3Harris radios and specialized waveforms designed to protect command links in contested environments.The integration could help American troops operate uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) when adversaries attempt to disrupt battlefield communications. It also connects drone operations with tactical radio networks already deployed across U.S. and allied forces.The X10D is a compact drone designed for military reconnaissance, giving troops an aerial view of potential threats without exposing personnel to the same risks.Drone integrates tactical radiosThe companies have integrated L3Harris’ Falcon IV embeddable radios and Wraith waveform into Skydio’s X10D drone. The combination provides layered protection against jamming and adds electronic warfare capabilities to the aircraft.Radio integration gives the drone access to communications technology designed for military operations. Maintaining command-and-control links matters when troops rely on aerial sensors to gather information beyond their immediate positions.Electronic interference can disrupt the connection between operators and unmanned aircraft. Losing that link can complicate flight control and limit the delivery of useful battlefield information.L3Harris and Skydio aim to reduce that vulnerability through their integrated system. The setup is designed to help warfighters continue flying drones and communicating in environments where electronic warfare threatens those functions.Existing radio networks expand reachThe partnership also draws on a substantial installed base of military communications equipment. More than 150,000 tactical radios in U.S. and allied inventories can host the Wraith waveform, according to L3Harris.That compatibility could help defense forces incorporate the capability into existing communications networks. It also offers a path to connecting autonomous aircraft with equipment already fielded by military units.The companies have also incorporated Wraith Shield, a waveform designed to scan radio-frequency spectrum and identify threats. The technology can detect and neutralize adversarial drones, adding another layer to the integrated electronic warfare capability.These functions extend the partnership beyond keeping a drone connected to its operator. They also address the electromagnetic environment in which military aircraft and communications systems must operate.Open systems support integrationThe collaboration relies on open-system architectures that allow different technologies to work together. Such designs can help militaries integrate new equipment without rebuilding their entire communications infrastructure around a single platform.Faisal Munir, president of mission-critical communications at L3Harris, said the partnership combines complementary technologies with resilient networks. He added that the integration helps warfighters communicate and operate unmanned aircraft in electronic warfare-constrained environments.The approach reflects a growing engineering challenge for modern militaries. Autonomous aircraft need reliable links to deliver information and support operations, but adversaries can target those links with electronic interference.Integrating drones with established tactical radios offers one way to address that problem. The effectiveness of the approach will depend on how well the systems perform under operational conditions and against evolving electronic warfare threats.

title: US funds world's first fast-spectrum molten chloride reactor test
content: A nuclear experiment backed by the U.S. Department of Energy could deliver crucial operating data for next-generation reactors as early as 2027. The Molten Chloride Reactor Experiment (MCRE) aims to test a fast-spectrum molten chloride salt reactor under sustained fission conditions. Its results could help engineers move the technology closer to commercial use.The DOE has approved additional cost-shared funding to accelerate the experiment’s final development stage. Southern Company, Idaho National Laboratory and CORE POWER are collaborating on the project through the department’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program.Testing a different reactor designUnlike conventional reactors, which typically use solid fuel, molten salt reactor designs can dissolve nuclear fuel in liquid salt. MCRE will investigate a chloride-based system that operates with a fast neutron spectrum.Fast neutrons retain more energy than the thermal neutrons used in many conventional reactors. This difference influences how nuclear fuel behaves and how a reactor sustains fission. Engineers need experimental evidence to understand those effects and refine their designs.MCRE aims to become the world’s first fast-spectrum molten chloride reactor experiment to achieve criticality. That milestone occurs when a reactor sustains a controlled nuclear chain reaction.Idaho National Laboratory will help researchers gather direct measurements of the reactor’s behavior during operation. Associate Laboratory Director Jess Gehin said engineers currently rely on models to predict how this reactor design will perform.“Enhancing those models with real-world operating evidence will reduce uncertainty for future reactor designers and regulators,” Gehin said.The measurements could help developers validate simulation tools and assess engineering decisions. They could also inform future reactor licensing efforts, although regulators will still need project-specific safety evidence.Reducing risks before deploymentAdvanced reactor developers face significant technical challenges before they can bring new designs to market. Experimental results can help engineers identify uncertainties before committing to larger, more expensive demonstrations.MCRE could provide data on fuel behavior and reactor performance during sustained fission. Those findings may help developers evaluate design choices and build stronger technical cases for future projects.Southern Company sees the experiment as an example of how federal funding and private-sector expertise can advance nuclear research. Senior Vice President Mark S. Berry said collaboration could help reduce technical uncertainty as developers pursue reliable and affordable energy.The research could also support applications beyond electricity generation. Fast-spectrum molten salt systems may eventually support industrial energy demands and medical isotope production. Developers are also exploring whether these reactors could extract additional value from used nuclear fuel.Maritime nuclear power prospectsCORE POWER sees potential applications in commercial shipping, where nuclear propulsion could provide long-duration power without onboard carbon emissions during operation.CEO Mikal Bøe said the company committed to building MCRE in 2020. The accelerated schedule now targets criticality as early as 2027.Bøe said the experiment could help establish the engineering knowledge, licensing approaches, and supply chains needed for commercial deployment. CORE POWER also wants to connect advances in nuclear fuel technology with its maritime nuclear development efforts.Nuclear-powered commercial vessels could eventually offer an alternative to conventional marine fuels. However, deployment would require substantial work on reactor safety, ship integration, regulation, and supporting infrastructure.MCRE’s immediate goal remains scientific, not commercial. Its experimental results could help determine whether fast-spectrum molten chloride reactors can progress toward practical applications, including future maritime power systems.

title: Nuclear waste sensor detects vibrations above 100 kHz in lab tests
content: Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh have demonstrated a fiber-optic sensing system capable of detecting acoustic signals above 100 kilohertz (kHz), roughly five times the frequency cited for conventional systems, in a step toward monitoring cracks and corrosion in nuclear fuel storage canisters.Developed with Pittsburgh-based startup Sensible Photonics, the system underwent field testing at Idaho National Laboratory (INL) in September. The researchers used a mock nuclear fuel canister to test whether the sensors could detect vibrations and locate their source.The technology is designed to monitor steel canisters that hold spent nuclear fuel. It could eventually be retrofitted onto existing storage casks, allowing operators to detect acoustic signals associated with developing cracks before they compromise the containers.The researchers conducted the tests from September 8 to 11, using different sensor configurations to assess the system’s sensitivity. The demonstration marked the completion of the project’s first phase, supported by funding from the US Department of Energy.Detecting damage through soundSpent nuclear fuel is typically cooled in water before being sealed inside steel canisters surrounded by concrete storage casks. These containers can remain at nuclear facilities for decades.Although the fuel has been removed from a reactor, it continues to generate heat. Storage casks therefore include ventilation openings that help dissipate heat.At coastal nuclear facilities, salty air can enter through these openings and contribute to corrosion of the steel canisters. Over time, corrosion may lead to cracks that threaten their structural integrity.The researchers developed their fiber-optic system to detect acoustic emissions, or small vibrations produced when materials undergo changes such as cracking.“People tend to think about fiber-optics as a way to produce faster internet speeds, but it can be used to continuously monitor everything from bridges to batteries to nuclear waste,” said Khurram Naeem, a research assistant professor at Pittsburgh and technical lead for the demonstration.According to Naeem, the system can detect signals above 100 kHz, compared with the 20 kHz capability he cited for most conventional counterpart systems.The higher detection frequency is a technical capability, not evidence that the system detects cracks five times earlier or more accurately.Testing sensors on canistersDuring the INL demonstration, researchers installed optical fibers outside a mock nuclear fuel canister and tested several arrangements to measure acoustic vibrations.They also conducted pencil-lead-break tests, a standard technique for generating repeatable acoustic signals that simulate the emissions associated with material damage.“Through a series of pencil-lead-break tests, we showed that the technology could detect the sound and find the source,” Naeem said.The team also evaluated methods for attaching sensors to storage casks, with the aim of developing installations capable of remaining in place for years under high-temperature and high-radiation conditions.However, the tests did not establish that the system could reliably identify actual corrosion or cracks in operating nuclear fuel storage canisters. Its long-term performance under nuclear storage conditions also remains to be demonstrated.The project involves researchers from Pittsburgh’s Swanson School of Engineering and Sensible Photonics, a startup co-founded by Pitt professor Paul Ohodnicki.Researchers also collaborated with scientists from INL, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory.The team is seeking further funding to evaluate the system’s durability and stability and advance it toward potential commercial use at nuclear storage facilities.

title: China completes world-first commercial green ammonia refueling at sea
content: A green-ammonia-powered ship departed on a ‘world-first’ commercial ocean voyage across the Pacific from the Chinese port of Zhoushan to Australia, carrying nearly 1,000 metric tonnes (t) of certified ammonia.The journey began earlier this week after the world’s first commercial ship-to-ship transfer of green ammonia as marine propulsion fuel. The transfer took place at an anchorage off Zhoushan on October 13, in open water away from port infrastructure, according to Chinese Energy Engineering Corporation (CEEC), a state energy firm.Bunkering at Chinese portThe bulk carrier Mineral Europa received green ammonia during the bunkering operation, a ship-to-ship fuel transfer. It has a carrying capacity of 210,000 deadweight tons (DWT), the estimated maximum weight the ship can safely carry.The fuel was pumped across a hose to Mineral Europa by a converted bunkering vessel, Shenghang Yongle, which entered service less than five weeks before the operation.CEEC Hydrogen Energy Co., Compagnie Maritime Belge Technology (CMB.TECH), a Belgium-based transport company, and Jiangsu Andefu Energy Technology Co. jointly handled the bunkering operation, according to China Global Television Network (CGTN), a Chinese media group.In a statement, Alexander Saverys, CEO of CMB.TECH, called Mineral Europa the beginning of a “propulsion revolution” and said it proves large ocean-going ships “can be powered by ammonia.”Green ammonia, sourced from CEEC’s Songyuan Hydrogen Energy Industrial Park nearly 1,240 miles north of Zhousan, had a voyage of its own. Before reaching the port of Zhoushan, the fuel traveled nearly 435 miles from Songyuan to Nanjing Port by road in a specialized tank. From Nanjing Port, the bunker vessel took over the rest of the journey, carrying 1,000 metric tons of clean fuel before transferring it safely to Mineral Europa.The bulk carrier now holds the liquid ammonia in two deck-mounted tanks of 106,000 cubic feet, keeping the clean fuel at approximately −27°F.Industry observers called these latest milestones the “missing link” in using green ammonia as a marine fuel.The event silenced critics who doubted the practicality of using ammonia as a zero-carbon fuel at sea. The success of the bunkering operation showed that end-to-end green ammonia supply chains can operate under commercial conditions.Before this, all the blocks of the green ammonia supply chain existed in isolation: ammonia-burning engines, vessels fitted to carry it, and offshore production facilities making it from renewable electricity. However, the latest operation connected them, marking a major commercial milestone.Ammonia as dominant fuel choice by 2042Going forward, the Belgian shipping company is expected to increase its ammonia-powered fleet, taking nearly 21 deliveries of such vessels over the next three years. According to CGTN, the fleet would comprise 18 dry bulk carriers, one container ship, and two chemical tankers, with most deliveries expected by July 2027.Norway, the US Gulf Coast, Southern Africa, and Australia are other regions that are advancing multiple ammonia production and bunkering projects to diversify supply over time.However, experts cautioned against considering ammonia a globally sustainable maritime fuel because its global fuel network is not yet fully developed. A Norwegian report forecasts that ammonia will become the dominant fuel choice for new ships by 2042. The analysis said this would represent about 25% of maritime fuel by 2050. This implies demand of roughly 120 million metric tons per year of green ammonia by mid-century.Not completely carbon-freeAs zero-carbon ammonia-powered ships set sail, technical experts cautioned against treating them as entirely free of fossil fuels.They noted that present-day ammonia marine engines burn 5% marine diesel oil. At best, 95 percent of the vessel’s propulsion energy comes from zero-carbon ammonia.Another challenge facing the industry is the need for bulkier vessels to transport sustainable ammonia fuel.Green ammonia has 2.4 times less energy content than conventional marine diesel. While marine pilot oil produces approximately 44 MJ/kg, ammonia generates 18.6 megajoules per kilogram (MJ/kg) of fuel burned. As a result, ammonia-fueled vessels need much larger fuel storage to cover the same voyage range, nearly 2.4 times that of traditional maritime fuels.

title: Human gut-inspired battery uses bacteria to generate 0.75 volts
content: Researchers at Binghamton University have developed a bacteria-powered battery inspired by the human small intestine that maintained an output of about 0.75 volts for at least 14 hours during testing.The device uses flexible, finger-like structures inspired by intestinal villi to provide more space for bacteria to grow while improving nutrient delivery and waste removal. These tiny projections, which normally help the intestines absorb nutrients, offer a model for improving electricity generation using spore-forming bacteria.A team of researchers fabricated the structures using a flexible polymer hydrogel and embedded Bacillus subtilis bacteria within them. The structures serve as the battery’s anode, where bacterial activity helps generate electricity.The team says the technology could eventually be installed in wastewater pipelines, using organic waste as a nutrient source to generate electricity for low-power devices.Overcoming flat electrode limitationsBacteria-powered batteries generate electricity by harnessing the metabolic activity of microorganisms. However, their performance depends partly on how effectively bacteria receive nutrients and release waste.Conventional two-dimensional electrodes provide limited surface area for bacterial growth. Porous materials offer additional space but can become clogged as bacteria form biofilms, restricting the movement of nutrients and waste products.“Porous structures can be easily clogged by biofilm formation, so we had a lot of problems with nutrient delivery, waste buildup or uneven biofilm growth,” said Seokheun “Sean” Choi, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Binghamton University.To address these problems, Choi and doctoral researchers Ruohan Zhang and Botian Wang turned to the structure of the small intestine.The intestinal villi provide a large surface area while allowing nutrients to move across relatively short distances. The researchers sought to reproduce these advantages in a flexible battery electrode.They created finger-like projections from a polymer hydrogel commonly used in biomedical applications. The material allowed them to build a three-dimensional structure capable of accommodating bacteria throughout the electrode.The bacteria-containing structures form the anode, while a modified carbon-cloth cathode sits on the opposite side of an ion-exchange membrane. Together, these components allow the device to produce electricity as the bacteria metabolize nutrients.Wastewater applications remain untestedThe researchers envision placing future versions of the biobattery inside wastewater pipes, where microorganisms could use organic matter in the water as fuel.“We can put this biobattery in a waste pipe, because it can easily be integrated with its surroundings,” Choi said.The flexible hydrogel could allow the battery to conform to different pipeline shapes and sizes. Such systems might eventually supply electricity to small sensors without requiring conventional batteries.However, the research remains at an early stage. The reported voltage was maintained with a continuous supply of nutrient medium, and the team has not demonstrated the system operating inside a wastewater pipeline.The researchers also want to simplify manufacturing through a single-step printing process that could make the structures easier to produce at scale.Another goal is to improve how bacteria are distributed within the device. In the human intestine, microorganisms are concentrated mainly in a mucus layer near the villi’s surface. The current design embeds bacteria throughout the hydrogel instead.Future work will examine whether reproducing more of the intestine’s physical and chemical conditions can help maintain bacterial activity and improve performance.The findings were published in the journal Small.

title: US team develops chip that directs fluid flow for targeted drug delivery
content: Researchers at Cornell University have developed a chip-based system that creates and controls hydrogen microbubbles on demand. By directing the bubbles to manipulate fluid flow, the technology could pave the way for applications such as targeted drug delivery.​In the experiments, they tapped the power of ultrasound, sound waves, to energize the bubbles set within a 3-millimeter area on a chip for manipulating the flow of liquids. The device produced these bubbles on a grid of electrodes that makes the electrical control possible.​Real-time microbubble control​The newly built system can be programmed in real time, and researchers are now able to produce individual bubbles exactly when and where they want, control their size and number, and steer them electronically. They exert control over the bubble movements, individually as well as in larger groups. This allows them to direct the flow of liquid as desired.​According to the researchers, the technology could have medical applications, as it opens the door to creating reconfigurable microfluidic devices that may enable precise drug delivery.​”With this bubble array, we can control the bubble size, numbers and position in real time, so we can program the flow direction,” said Zhiyuan Zhang, author of the new study published in Science Advances.​Size determines fluid flow​Zhang used a chip fabricated at the Cornell NanoScale Science and Technology Facility, consisting of nine tiny electrodes arranged in a square that generate bubbles between 10 and 100 micrometers.​To create a single hydrogen bubble, he split the water molecule by using electricity. The bubble grew larger if the voltage was applied for a longer duration. After producing the bubble, the researcher exposes the system to sound energy. These ultrasonic waves make the bubbles resonate, producing vibrations that move the surrounding fluid.​Researchers noted that, when controlling the fluid flow, the size of the bubble is critical. Bubble size determines the ultrasound frequency needed for resonance. Properly matched frequencies create strong fluid flow, they added.​”The size of the bubble determines the resonant frequency of the bubble,” said Itai Cohen, professor in the Department of Physics at Cornell University. “If you’re applying ultrasound at 40 kilohertz and the bubble is too small or too big, then it’s not going to oscillate significantly. But if it’s just the right size to resonate at 40 kilohertz, you get a lot of flow,” he added in a statement.​The study demonstrated that flow can be generated using a single or multiple bubbles. Single bubbles, when tuned to resonate, create fluid flow by transferring energy to neighboring fluid. Multiple bubbles can either work together, creating symmetrical flows if they all have the same size. With different-sized bubbles, the experiment showed that the size of the largest bubble governs the flow direction.​Programmable movements can also be attained by altering the placements of bubbles, shifting the flow from left to right or directing the movement in a curve by arranging five bubbles in an L-shape, the researchers said. Similarly, they could modify the flow by varying the voltage. They discovered that higher voltage produces a cloud of bubbles in a rapid flow. Hence, they can shoot the bubbles in a specific direction by simply turning on the ultrasound.

title: Vanilla’s Sweet Secret Could Help Heal Stubborn Wounds
content:
Scientists have discovered that the molecule responsible for vanilla’s sweet flavor could hold the secret to better wound care, with promising antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant properties. Credit: Shutterstock
Vanillin could help form wound-care materials while supplying antibacterial activity, a combination made more practical by its low-cost and abundant supply.
The compound behind vanilla’s sweet aroma could become an ingredient in wound-care materials. A team from Flinders University’s Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory has found that vanillin has pronounced antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial properties, making it a candidate for formulations designed to help wounds heal.
Vanillin could help deliver hard-to-dissolve drugs
The researchers examined vanillin through a food-to-function framework, connecting its chemistry with its biological activity and potential biomedical uses. Those possibilities include incorporating it into materials and using it to help deliver drugs.
Professor Krasimir Vasilev, Professor of Biomedical Nanotechnology at Flinders University and Director of Flinders’ Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory, says, “Because vanillin’s synthetic form is abundant and cost-effective, we believe vanillin-based formulations may offer safe and multifunctional solutions for ulcer treatment and targeted drug delivery, especially of hydrophobic compounds.
“Owing to its amphiphilic molecular structure, vanillin can interact with reactive oxygen species, cellular membranes, and polymeric matrices, providing a basis for its incorporation into functional formulations.”
Amphiphilic molecules contain both water-attracting and water-repelling regions, while hydrophobic compounds do not dissolve readily in water. In material design, vanillin can also serve as a dynamic crosslinker, helping form reversible connections between the long molecular chains that make up polymers. It can therefore contribute to a material’s structure as well as its biological activity.
Low-cost vanillin offers a manufacturing advantage
Vanillin is the primary chemical component extracted from natural vanilla pods, but it can also be produced synthetically from clove oil or rice. Its widespread use in foods gives researchers a familiar starting point for exploring other applications.
“Vanillin is among the most widely used flavor compounds in the global food system, valued for its sensory attributes, chemical stability, and long history of safety—and that can be transferred to other areas, such as medical uses,” says Vasilev.
The researchers see practical advantages in vanillin’s availability as a low-cost small molecule suitable for good manufacturing practices. These characteristics could support industrial-scale production, consistent formulations, and reliable supply chains.
Peppermint leaves inspired a protective coating
The laboratory’s interest in food-derived medical materials grew partly from Vasilev’s experience of eating peppermint leaves from a drink and noticing significant relief from a sore throat. That observation prompted him to investigate whether peppermint’s biological activity could be incorporated into a durable coating through plasma technology, a field he has researched for more than two decades.
In work published in the journal
in February 2026, the Flinders team created a nanoscale coating derived from peppermint oil. The coating protects against infection, inflammation, and oxidative stress while remaining compatible with human tissue and suitable for use on medical materials. The vanillin research continues this exploration of food compounds as potential ingredients in medical technologies.
“With coordinated engagement between academia, clinicians, and industry, vanillin has the potential to progress from an underutilized bioactive to a clinically deployable component of next-generation wound care and regenerative therapeutics,” says Vasilev.
Reference: “Vanillin as a bioactive component in biomedical formulations for chronic wound healing and tissue regeneration” by Borislav Stoilov, Vi Khanh Truong, Christopher Delaney and Krasimir Vasilev, 2 August 2026,
International Journal of Pharmaceutics

title: Scientists Uncover a Longevity Hotspot Where Reaching 100 Is Surprisingly Common
content:
Scientists are investigating whether lifestyle, genetics, and close community ties could help explain the exceptional longevity found in a remote Italian village. Credit: Stock
Turning 100 is unusually common in one Sardinian village, and centuries of records help show that its residents’ remarkable ages are real.
Women in Bolotana, a mountain community of about 2,300 people on the Italian island of Sardinia, have an exceptional pattern of survival after age 70. An international study suggests the village could qualify as a new “blue zone,” a community known for unusually long lives, although more observation is needed to establish that status.
Researchers estimated that women who reach 70 have a 13.8% chance of living to 100, compared with approximately 3.5% in Italy and 3.6% in the United States. That puts Bolotana’s estimate at nearly four times the U.S. figure.
The National Geographic-supported study was published in
Frontiers in Aging
and co-authored by S. Jay Olshansky, professor emeritus of epidemiology at the University of Illinois Chicago School of Public Health.
Checking the Centenarians
Bolotana first drew attention because six residents were at least 100 years old in 2024. Relative to the village’s population, the researchers estimated that centenarians were roughly 11 times as common as in the United States. But a high count alone cannot establish exceptional longevity, making reliable age records essential.
“What makes Bolotana extraordinary is that it has an incredible historical record that allows us to definitively evaluate ages at birth and death,” Olshansky said. “The municipal and baptismal records date back centuries and allowed us to independently verify ages.”
Sunset over Bolotana, a village on the Italian island of Sardinia. Credit: S. Jay Olshansky and Marisa Montibeller
The team reconstructed residents’ life histories across more than a century, matching birth, baptismal and death records. Among 3,060 people born in Bolotana between 1900 and 1925, researchers documented 38 who reached 100.
“Every single person that has made it past 100, we can validate,” Olshansky said. “There is no ambiguity.”
Women Lead Bolotana’s Longevity
Sardinia’s original blue zone, identified more than two decades ago, became famous for exceptional male longevity. Bolotana presents a different pattern: women showed the strongest survival advantage, with nearly 21 years of estimated remaining life expectancy at age 70.
The researchers examined both remaining life expectancy at 70 and the likelihood of reaching 100. Among the international benchmarks included, Bolotana’s women ranked second only to Hong Kong on both measures.
“Females almost always live longer than males anywhere in the world, but in Sardinia that wasn’t the case. It’s one of the things that made it so unusual,” Olshansky said. “We think this is the longest-lived female population in the world, or close to it.”
Blue zones, including Okinawa in Japan and Costa Rica’s Nicoya Peninsula, offer opportunities to investigate why some communities outlive surrounding populations. Bolotana may provide another setting, particularly for studying women’s survival in later life.
Strong Records, Open Questions
The village’s archives address a recurring criticism of longevity research: that extraordinary ages sometimes reflect inaccurate documentation. Researchers could check Bolotana’s centenarians against multiple independent sources rather than relying on a single record.
However, verified ages do not settle whether the village has a lasting survival advantage. Bolotana’s estimates varied with the calendar period analyzed, and earlier years showed a less pronounced advantage, particularly for survival to 100. Longer observation and continued demographic validation are needed before researchers can consider it an established blue zone.
The study also did not determine what causes the longevity pattern. Walking, food, family relationships, and genetics are possible contributors, but the demographic findings cannot establish how much each factor matters.
Everyday Clues To Longer Lives
Bolotana’s steep streets and hills make physical activity part of ordinary routines. Much of the food is grown locally, including olives used to produce oil rich in healthy fats. Families often live near one another, and social isolation appears uncommon.
“You’ve got this close-knit community where people take care of each other,” Olshansky said. “Movement is largely done by walking, not by driving.”
These features give researchers several connected possibilities to investigate. Daily movement, diet, and social support may work alongside inherited traits, making the village’s longevity difficult to trace to any single habit.
“If we can identify the characteristics behind this longevity and help people adopt them, the rest of the world can benefit from understanding the values practiced by these communities.”
Reference: “A new blue zone? exceptional late-life survival in Bolotana, Sardinia” by Giovanni Mario Pes, Steven N. Austad, Dan Buettner, Salvatore Pedde, Vittorio Romerio, Hiram Beltrán-Sánchez and S. Jay Olshansky, 8 September 2026,
Frontiers in Aging
DOI: 10.3389/fragi.2026.1951042
