title: Scientists Discover a Surprising New Way To Fight High Blood Pressure – Through the Ear
content:
A noninvasive device that stimulates nerves in the ear is being investigated as a potential new approach to stubborn high blood pressure. Credit: Shutterstock
A small ear stimulation device could offer a new way to tackle high blood pressure that stays elevated despite medication.
Researchers at
Queen Mary University of London
have tested a device that stimulates nerves through the ear in people whose high blood pressure remained uncontrolled despite medication. The trial, published in the American Heart Association journal
Hypertension
, found that the treatment was safe and practical to use at home.
Finding additional ways to control blood pressure matters because many people receiving treatment still exceed recommended targets. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, including heart attack and stroke.
Targeting Blood Pressure Through The Ear
The approach, transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), delivers electrical stimulation without an invasive procedure. It targets the autonomic nervous system, which helps regulate blood pressure through functions outside conscious control.
The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, delivers gentle electrical pulses through two clips attached to the tragus, the small piece of cartilage at the front of the ear. Patients can administer the treatment themselves at home.
Illustration of the SCRATCH-HTN treatment for hypertension. Credit: SCRATCH-HTN study team
The NIHR-funded SCRATCH-HTN trial included 63 participants whose hypertension remained uncontrolled while taking one or more blood pressure medications. They were randomly assigned to receive either active stimulation or a sham device, allowing researchers to compare outcomes between the groups.
Participants used their devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks, then once weekly for another 10 weeks. They followed the schedule closely, and treatment was safe and well tolerated during the trial. Those findings establish that the approach was practical to use but do not establish that it effectively lowers blood pressure compared to sham devices.
A Possible Benefit in More Severe Hypertension
Across the full study population, active treatment did not produce a significantly greater blood pressure reduction than the sham device. However, a subgroup analysis planned before the trial found a larger reduction with active treatment among people who began with more severe hypertension.
That result provides a direction for further research. Larger trials focused on specific patient groups will need to establish whether the difference holds up and identify who, if anyone, benefits.
Dr. Ajay Gupta, the chief investigator, a clinical reader at Queen Mary University of London and a consultant physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:
“This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham.
“As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension.”
Reference: “Safety, Acceptability and Efficacy of Noninvasive Transcutaneous-Autonomic Neuromodulation in Uncontrolled Hypertension” by Ajay Gupta, David Collier, James Steckelmacher, Jane Field, George Collett, Olivier Zongo, Mital Patel, Manish Saxena, Annastazia Learoyd, Amrita Ahluwalia and Peter Sever, 28 September 2026,
Hypertension

title: Scientists Discover Nature Has Far Fewer Backup Plans Than We Thought
content:
A sweeping global study challenges a long-standing assumption about how ecosystems withstand species loss. Credit: Stock
Nature may have fewer backup plans than we thought, leaving our food supply and climate more exposed when species disappear.
The largest global study of its kind suggests that losing species can steadily erode the benefits ecosystems provide, including pollination, clean water, carbon storage, and natural pest control. Led by
King’s College London
Imperial College London
, the research challenges the assumption that many species are interchangeable and that a few losses make little difference.
Working with the Natural History Museum and the Alan Turing Institute, the researchers combined 423 published studies and 222,829 data points from land, freshwater, marine, and estuarine ecosystems. Published in
Nature Ecology & Evolution
, their analysis produced a database more than twice the size of the largest previous effort.
Across 23 categories of ecosystem services and functions, most benefits kept increasing as biodiversity rose. They generally did not level off once a small collection of species was present, suggesting that ecosystems have less spare capacity than scientists previously assumed.
Why Losing Species Matters
The findings call into question the extent of “functional redundancy,” the idea that different species can perform similar jobs and compensate when one disappears. If that backup were widespread, additional species would eventually contribute little to a particular service. Instead, the study found that greater diversity usually continued to bring benefits.
Dr. Emma Moffett, the study’s lead author and a geography lecturer at King’s College London, said, “Our findings challenge the comfortable assumption has been that ecosystems carry plenty of backup, so losing a species here and there doesn’t change much. Across most of the benefits ecosystems provide that we looked at, the data doesn’t support that. The ecological benefits keep climbing as diversity rises, which means it is falling as we lose species.”
There were exceptions. Protection against coastal flooding, erosion, and similar hazards showed relatively little sensitivity to biodiversity overall. These functions often depend heavily on a few foundational species, such as shrubs whose roots stabilize sand dunes.
Conservation needs to account for both overall biodiversity and the outsized contributions of certain species. Protecting a wide range of species helps sustain many ecosystem benefits, while safeguarding foundational species preserves functions that others may be unable to replace.
Ocean Carbon Storage Stands Out
The strongest relationship between biodiversity and any measured service involved marine carbon sequestration, the capture and storage of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) in ocean waters and sediments. This suggests that species losses could have especially important consequences for the ocean’s contribution to climate protection.
Marine life helps move carbon through the ocean, from phytoplankton near the surface to microbial food webs involved in transferring it into deeper water. The findings point to the importance of diverse communities for blue carbon sinks in the ocean and coastal environments, including mangroves and salt marshes.
However, the striking ocean result came from only a small number of datasets. The researchers identify this shortage of evidence as an urgent research gap, so the finding warrants further investigation.
Dr. Moffett said, “The ocean result stopped us in our tracks. Carbon capture at sea responded to biodiversity more strongly than anything else we measured, and yet it’s one of the least studied areas we found. If the world is counting on blue carbon to help with climate change, marine life can’t be an afterthought.”
A Warning for Future Food Production
The team also explored how these benefits could change by connecting its database to biodiversity projections under the socioeconomic scenarios used by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. One focus was natural pest control on farmland, where predators and other enemies of crop pests provide a service farmers receive for free.
The model predicts that this protection would weaken under development driven by fossil fuels compared with a pathway less dependent on them. Countries experiencing rapid population growth and lower levels of development would face the sharpest losses.
Dr. Will Pearse, an associate professor in evolutionary ecology in Imperial College London’s Department of Life Sciences, said, “We’ve known that biodiversity supports humanity by providing us with food, clean water, clean air, and so many other ecosystem services. But what this model gives us is a precise, global picture: we can now predict the benefits biodiversity provides anywhere, making it even easier to recognize and take advantage of those benefits.”
The database and forecasts for all 23 categories are publicly available to support policy and planning.
Reference: “Biodiversity safeguards ecosystem services and functions worldwide” by Emma R. Moffett, Joel H. Gayford, Lexi Chen, Olivia F. Morris, Yuming Shi, Lucy Somekh, Nicole Stasik, Andy Purvis, Guy Woodward and William D. Pearse, 6 October 2026,
Nature Ecology & Evolution
DOI: 10.1038/s41559-026-03200-4

title: Climate Change Could Unleash an African Antelope Invasion Across the American West
content:
The African gemsbok (Oryx gazella) is a large, desert-adapted antelope native to the arid regions of southern Africa, particularly the Kalahari Desert. Recognized by its distinct black-and-white facial markings and long, straight horns, the gemsbok is exceptionally resilient to extreme heat and drought. Credit: Shutterstock
Climate change could give African antelopes an edge in the American West, with native wildlife facing tougher competition when drought leaves less to eat.
An antelope native to southern Africa’s Kalahari Desert has found a foothold in New Mexico’s dry rangelands, and climate change could give it far more of the American West to roam. Gemsbok were brought to the state for hunting in the 1960s and 1970s and have since spread more than 100 kilometers, or about 62 miles, from their release point.
A new study by researchers at the
University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
suggests that suitable habitat could expand well beyond New Mexico by 2100, reaching into Texas, Arizona, Utah, California, and even southern Washington and Montana. The same adaptations that help gemsbok survive in arid country could give them an advantage over native wildlife as those conditions become more widespread, raising concerns about the animals and grasslands that would have to support growing herds.
“Gemsbok are famous for being really well adapted to heat and drought. In addition to other heat adaptations, they can get all of their water from plants, so they don’t really need to drink. That’s really unusual for animals that big — they can weigh 450 pounds. They’re the poster species for dealing with the kind of changes we’re going to see in the Southwest,” said study co-author Bob Schooley, professor and head of the university’s Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences, or NRES.
Connected habitats could help gemsbok spread
The researchers built their forecasts around the places gemsbok already inhabit. For each recorded location, they examined precipitation, temperature seasonality, vegetation cover, terrain ruggedness, and human population density to identify the combination of conditions associated with the animals’ presence. People sharing wildlife photographs online supplied the sightings that made this analysis possible.
“We turned towards participant science to do this work. When people contribute photos to apps like iNaturalist, the occurrence records get scraped into something called the Global Biodiversity Information Facility. From that, we were able to use a statistical method called Maxent to find habitat associations for gemsbok,” said lead author Nathan Alexander. He began the research as a doctoral student in NRES, part of the College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences at Illinois, and is now a postdoctoral scholar at Southern Illinois University.
A new University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign study shows suitable habitat for introduced gemsbok could expand under climate change from their current range in New Mexico well into surrounding states. Credit: Jornada Basin LTER
Using those habitat associations, the team searched for similar environments elsewhere and projected where they could occur under future climate scenarios. The resulting maps suggest that gemsbok could gain more than additional land to occupy. Areas that are currently separated could become connected, potentially making it easier for the animals to move between them.
“When there are these isolated patches, there might be dispersal barriers that they can’t cross to get to the next patch. But when these patches coalesce and connect, there might be increased opportunities for gemsbok to invade and expand into these novel habitats. We see this particularly in western Texas, but also into western New Mexico and up into Arizona, and even some regions of California, like Death Valley,” said Kieran Andreoni. He began the research as a master’s student in NRES and is now conservation director at the Southern Plains Land Trust in Colorado.
When cattle leave, gemsbok keep grazing
Gemsbok would still have to reach that territory and establish populations for the projected habitat expansion to translate into a wider occupied range. If they do, larger herds could consume more of the forage that cattle and native grazers such as pronghorn and bison depend on, leaving less food to go around.
“Along with that diet overlap, gemsbok are able to forage on lower quality plant materials than some of our native species,” Alexander said. “So in drought years, we could imagine our native species might be a little bit more stressed and nutrient deficient, whereas the gemsbok are going to be able to move to less nutrient-rich plant material and still be able to persist in the environment.”
Gemsbok also left their natural predators, lions and hyenas, behind in Africa. Coyotes and mountain lions in the Southwest kill far fewer of the antelopes, according to Schooley. With relatively little pressure from predators and the ability to keep feeding as forage quality declines, growing herds could continue grazing land that is already struggling through drought.
“These desert rangelands are often used for cattle grazing. When there’s a severe drought, they pull the cattle off the landscape because there’s no food for them. Well, no one pulls the gemsbok off. Considering their ability to survive on low-quality forage, they could severely damage remaining grasslands. So I think that’s the kind of thing we worry about — what are the implications when they get to even larger numbers?” Schooley said.
Disease could follow expanding herds
Gemsbok in the Southwest have also tested positive for malignant catarrhal fever, bovine respiratory syncytial virus, and bovine para-influenza-3, all of concern to the cattle industry. Alexander said the antelopes could carry and spread diseases to domestic and native ungulates, or hoofed mammals, adding a potential disease risk to the competition for food.
Conservationists, ranchers, and hunting operations bring competing interests to decisions about gemsbok, making future population management difficult but critical, the researchers say. On New Mexico’s dry rangelands, and potentially far beyond them, keeping herds in check could help protect the food that cattle and native wildlife need when drought leaves less to share.
Reference: “Predicted range expansion of exotic Gemsbok (Oryx gazella) under climate change in the United States” by Nathan Alexander, Kieran J Andreoni and Robert L Schooley, 26 September 2026,
Journal of Mammalogy
DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyag083
Supported by the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture (Project 7006200) and the National Science Foundation (Jornada Basin Long Term Ecological Research Program, DEB 2025166 and DEB 2425143).

title: Scientists Say That a Honey Bee Colony May Actually Be a Single Living Organism
content:
Viewing honey bee colonies as superorganisms could reshape modern beekeeping, raising important questions about parasite management and practices that interfere with natural colony behavior. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study challenges traditional ideas about honey bee colonies.
A honey bee colony may be more than a society of thousands of insects. A new study proposes that the entire colony functions as a single living organism, with its own development, reproductive cycle, and biological lifespan. This perspective could challenge some of the most common practices in modern beekeeping.
Researchers Hannes Bonhoff of Lund University and Heikki Helanterä, a professor of evolutionary biology and genomics at the University of Oulu in Finland, argue that a queen and her colony together constitute a
superorganism
. Rather than treating the queen, 200 to 300 drones, and tens of thousands of workers as separate individuals, their framework considers the colony an animal whose members function much like specialized cells in a body.
A Honey Bee Colony That Grows, Ages, and Dies
“We have analyzed what it means for a bee colony to be a single organism, which opens up new insights into the fascinating life of the honey bee,” says Bonhoff.
Under this interpretation, a colony develops through stages comparable to those of a mammal, progressing from an embryo and fetus to a juvenile and adult. Bonhoff argues that colonies also undergo biological aging and eventually die after several years. The comparison treats the colony’s development as a whole, rather than focusing on the much shorter lifespans of its individual bees.
The superorganism concept is not new, but the researchers apply it to the colony’s life cycle, including how it reproduces and cares for its offspring. This approach raises questions about whether certain behaviors traditionally understood as collective insect activity might instead be viewed as functions of a larger biological individual.
Swarming May Be a Form of Parental Care
Honey bee colonies reproduce through swarming, when the established queen leaves the hive with roughly half the colony to find a new nesting site. A new queen remains in the original hive, where she becomes the reproductive center of the next colony generation.
In the researchers’ framework, this process resembles an animal producing offspring and providing extensive parental care. The developing colony inherits an established nest, food resources, shelter, and the support of experienced workers.
“When this superorganism reproduces, the offspring are cared for with great dedication by the parent, in some cases even at the cost of the parent’s life,” says Bonhoff.
The departing queen and her swarm face the risks of finding and establishing a new home, while the next generation develops in familiar surroundings. Established workers can also provide valuable foraging information through the honey bee dance language, which communicates the locations of food sources.
“Parental care therefore goes so far that the offspring inherits the mother’s nest, whilst she herself risks her life by swarming away to settle elsewhere,” says Bonhoff.
What This Could Mean for Modern Beekeeping
The proposed framework could have practical implications for managing honey bee populations. Beekeepers commonly replace queens and prevent swarming to maintain productive colonies. However, the researchers suggest that interfering with these natural processes may disrupt the colony’s reproductive and developmental cycle.
The study also raises questions about controlling Varroa mites, parasitic arachnids that threaten honey bee populations worldwide. Understanding the colony as an organism with distinct life stages could influence how beekeepers approach parasite management, although the proposed perspective does not itself establish a more effective treatment.
“Modern beekeeping methods are based on the idea of keeping the colony young and healthy indefinitely. Our study shows that such interventions fundamentally conflict with the natural reproductive strategy and the ability to cope with parasites,” says Bonhoff.
The research originated in Bonhoff’s master’s thesis at Lund University, supervised by Helanterä and Niklas Wahlberg, a professor of systematic biology at Lund. Wahlberg believes the work contributes to understanding how biological individuality can extend beyond a single insect.
“The concept itself has been around for a long time, but this is the first time it has been applied in a genuine biological context. It’s fascinating to think that, just as individual cells make up an organism, individual bees with different roles make up the superorganism,” concludes Wahlberg.

title: Scientists Uncover a 500-Year-Old Secret Hidden in a Book Henry VIII Wanted Destroyed
content:
Thomas Arundel, Archbishop of Canterbury. 19th-century copy of a 15th-century portrait. Credit: University of Cambridge
A Catholic book that survived the Reformation hints at a secret act of defiance by one of Henry VIII’s own enforcers.
Sir John Gage helped Henry VIII dismantle monasteries and dispose of their possessions for the Crown. Yet six fragile pages from a medieval religious book suggest that the trusted royal official also saved a Catholic text from the destruction he was expected to enforce.
Dr. Katie Walter of the University of Sussex and Dr. James Wade of Girton College, Cambridge, have linked the pages at The Keep archive in Brighton, U.K., to a manuscript held 3,500 miles away at Yale University in the United States. The manuscript is a copy of Nicholas Love’s early 15th-century
Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ
, and it bears Gage’s signature. Their study, published in
Notes and Queries
, connects him to a book that went from an approved bestseller to dangerous reading during the English Reformation.
An approved bestseller becomes dangerous
Love completed his English translation and adaptation of an earlier Latin text around 1409, when disputes over religious authority could carry deadly consequences. The Lollards, a proto-Protestant movement, argued that people should have access to the Bible in English and challenged the authority of the pope and priests. A law passed in 1401 sought to suppress heresy, with punishments for seditious heretics, including Lollards, that could include death by burning.
Pages 8-9 of The Keep fragment of Nicholas Love’s early 15th-century Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ, from Chapter 34, on the Raising of Lazarus. Image shows the manuscript’s thread binding. Credit: Courtesy of The Trustees of the Firle Estate Settlement and the University of Sussex
“In the early 15th century, having bible translations in English could get you killed,” Walter says. “Nicholas Love’s translation offered a safe alternative. It was considered orthodox and circulated with the seal of approval of Archbishop Arundel, the outspoken opponent of the Lollards.”
William Caxton published a printed edition of the
in 1486. It remained in print until publication abruptly stopped at the start of the Reformation, when teachings that had helped establish its religious credentials became contentious.
Love had appended a treatise defending the real presence of Jesus’ body and blood in the sacrament of Communion. He also included passages on oral confession to a priest and other orthodox Catholic sacraments. These became subjects of fierce debate during Henry VIII’s reign and the turbulent years of Reformation and counter-Reformation that followed. Some Catholics continued to prize the book illicitly.
Dr Katie Walter and Dr James Wade in The Keep archive, Brighton, with the fragment of Nicholas Love’s early 15th-century Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ. Credit: Courtesy of the University of Sussex
“65 copies of Love’s text survive today. That’s a lot for a 15th-century manuscript but so many could have been destroyed in the Reformation. It shows how popular it was, but it also shows how a work that became suspicious and dangerous for some could also be valued and preserved by others,” Wade says.
The king’s enforcer remained Catholic
Gage’s place among those owners brings together two sides of his life that readers of Hilary Mantel’s
Wolf Hall
trilogy may recognize. He appears in the novels as a religious conservative who nevertheless serves Henry VIII dependably as Constable of the Tower and a member of the Privy Council.
Depiction of the Lollard Richard Wyche being burnt at the stake in 1440. Credit: University of Cambridge
When the dissolution of the monasteries began in 1536, Gage was already vice-chamberlain of the royal household and gaining influence at court. He was also on good terms with Thomas Cromwell, whose power was rising. Having demonstrated his abilities as an administrator, Gage was assigned to organize the dissolution in Surrey, Kent, and Sussex. His work involved taking stock of everything the monastic houses owned and determining how to dispose of those assets for the Crown.
“Gage had a very long career in a highly turbulent court,” Wade says. “He survived when many other very shrewd people did not. And he made a fortune in the process. But he’s also this incredibly conflicted man, because he remained a Catholic throughout the Reformation. He’s got all this power and bureaucratic savvy combined with a risky conviction in his faith. Somehow he manages to reconcile these two things, and survive.”
John Gage’s signature in Takamiya MS 20. Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University. Credit: University of Cambridge
Six pages traced to Gage’s book
Connecting Gage to the six pages required Walter and Wade to resolve a cataloging puzzle that had frustrated scholars for nearly a century. Following clues left by archivists and earlier researchers, they reached the digitized
Takamiya MS 20 manuscript at Yale’s Beinecke Library
. As they scrolled through it, they found a gap immediately before a controversial passage about the importance of oral confession to a priest.
The missing text matched the content of The Keep’s pages, and the handwriting matched that of the manuscript’s scribe. Together, those features established that the separated pages belonged to the Yale volume. On its final page, Gage’s signature appears among a list of names thought to belong to its owners.
Portrait (unattributed) of Sir John Gage. Credit: Courtesy of The Trustees of the Firle Estate Settlement
Walter says, “The fact two possible owners before Gage were religious women suggests the manuscript might have been in a monastic house before it came into his possession. The dissolution of the monasteries led to the destruction of many books but others were taken and then circulated through informal networks. Considering Gage’s active role in the dissolution, it’s very possible he acquired the book during this chaos.”
Other monastic possessions certainly passed into Gage’s hands through his official work. He legitimately acquired the Battle Abbey sword, a treasure made for the abbot in the early 15th century. His house, Firle Place, was even built using stones removed from nearby Lewes Priory after its surrender to the Crown in 1537. The manuscript’s route into his possession remains uncertain.
“One possibility is that John Gage went to a monastic library and brought it home. Another is that someone else smuggled it out, and it briefly circulated from hand to hand until Gage acquired it. The key thing is – he kept it safe when he was meant to destroy books precisely like this one,” Wade says.
First page of The Keep fragment of Nicholas Love’s early 15th-century Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ. It shows the beginning of Chapter 34, on the Raising of Lazarus. Credit: Courtesy of The Trustees of the Firle Estate Settlement and the University of Sussex
Catholic books survived in private hands
Walter says, “We often associate this period with book burning and destruction, so this manuscript’s story goes a bit against that grain. It reminds us that people were also rescuing, valuing, and caring for books.”
After printing of the
ceased, Catholics played an important role in safeguarding its contents. “By keeping this book on his shelf, John Gage and his family were part of a much bigger secret effort to preserve Catholic literature and knowledge,” Walter says.
The researchers hope the findings will open new opportunities to trace Gage’s perilous course through the dissolution and the Reformation.
“It makes us think about the integrity that underlies subterfuge. There was a lot at stake for John Gage to perform tasks at court, but then secretly preserve the very thing that he’s meant to destroy,” Wade says.
Reference: “Nicholas Love’s Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ: A Missing Fragment from Takamiya MS 20 in the Holdings of the Keep” by Katie Walter and James Wade, 17 September 2026,

title: Zimbabwe’s Ancient Dinosaurs Were Nothing Like Scientists Expected
content:
Reconstruction of Musango. Credit: Mark Witton / The Trustees of the Natural History Museum
Scientists expected Zimbabwe’s fossil beds to yield familiar South African dinosaurs, but the newly named Musango is helping reveal a distinct prehistoric community.
Africa boasts up to 25% of Earth’s
animal and plant species
. This diversity is driven by diverse habitats: harsh deserts, vast grasslands, dense forests, towering mountains, lush coastlines, and teeming seas. It is also due to deep evolutionary roots, as many animal and plant groups originated here in the distant past. Paleontologists have been excavating this material for
nearly two centuries
Africa is most famous for spectacular hominid fossils that reveal our own ancestry. However, the continent boasts many fabulous fossil finds, including those of the most familiar extinct animals – dinosaurs.
The first African dinosaur fossils to be noted
scientifically
hailed from the Eastern Cape, South Africa, and were described in the 1850s. Since then, the African dinosaur map has expanded, with rich fossil beds in South Africa, Lesotho, Tanzania, Egypt, Niger, Malawi, Madagascar, and Morocco.
Zimbabwe is an important part of the African dinosaur puzzle, with dinosaur bones
reported since 1916
As a specialist on early dinosaurs who has worked on similar material from China, the UK and Africa, I’ve been drawn to these Zimbabwean fossils to see what they reveal about the first stages of their evolution.
Musango walked on two legs
Our latest
addition
to the Triassic zoo,
Musango matusadonaensis
, is a sauropodomorph dinosaur. (That’s the dinosaur subgroup that eventually gave rise to four-legged, long-necked giants like
Diplodocus
Its incomplete skeleton was found in the bank of the Nyamasango River close to Musango Island, as captured in the animal’s scientific name.
’s anatomy shows us that it was bipedal (walking on its hind legs only), reached about 4.5 meters in length, and weighed 220 kg. Growth marks in its bones reveal that it was a subadult when it died. Sadly, the skull wasn’t preserved, so its diet is unknown, but its close relatives were largely herbivorous (plant-eating).
Our new work reveals something unexpected about Zimbabwean dinosaurs. They’re not simply an extension of better-known South African faunas but include an array of species unique to the region. We’re now trying to work out why these differences exist. We suspect that environmental conditions might be the key.
Skeletal reconstruction. Credit: Brandon Stuart
New fossil finds revive Zimbabwe’s dinosaur research
Early fossil finds in Zimbabwe were overlooked by many scientists, and it was not until the 1970s that they became
more generally known
. This was thanks to pioneering work by Zimbabwean paleontologists Geoffrey Bond and Michael Raath, who discovered abundant material in the hinterlands of Bulawayo (south-west Zimbabwe) and the lower Zambezi Valley (forming the border with Zambia). Most of these finds were identified as belonging to known species named from neighboring South Africa.
Palaeontological work in Zimbabwe stalled for a few decades. However, a band of devoted fossil hunters kept searching. One of them, Steve Edwards, a local safari camp manager, found new, productive sites on the shore of Lake Kariba, the artificial lake which forms most of the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia. News of the discoveries eventually reached
Jonah Choiniere
at the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg. Jonah, an expert on early dinosaurs, immediately recognized the importance of the material. He assembled an international team of South African, Zimbabwean, and UK-based collaborators to explore them further.
This was a major task, as the sites on Late Kariba’s shoreline are deep inside Matusadona National Park. Our solution was to use one of the Kariba houseboats as a mobile hotel and laboratory, so that we could prospect the shoreline. We mounted two expeditions, in 2017 and 2018. We have been cleaning and studying this material ever since.
Both trips yielded a trove of material, collected from brick-red mudstones and sandstones that were laid down by ancient rivers around 210 million years ago, during the
Late Triassic period (237-201 million years ago)
. Geological evidence and plant fossils show that the Triassic landscape of Kariba was dry and dotted with stands of large conifer trees, with green corridors of vegetation following permanent watercourses.
Zimbabwe’s dinosaurs differ from South Africa’s
Sauropodomorphs are the most common Late Triassic dinosaurs. But what’s interesting about
and its relative
Musankwa
(which we described from the same beds in 2024)
is that they are unique to Zimbabwe.
We’d expected to find South African dinosaur species in these beds, given their similar age and geographic proximity, but surprisingly all the material we’ve collected so far has revealed animals that are distinct from those elsewhere.
These Zimbabwean dinosaurs are not even the closest relatives of their South African neighbors. We’ve also found other fossil animals, including lungfish and aquatic reptiles called phytosaurs, which are rare or absent in South African sites.
Following this, we’ve started to reappraise the historical dinosaur collections in Bulawayo. It appears that many of these fossils can’t be referred to South African species either, contrary to earlier assumptions.
Climate may explain the dinosaur divide
Then, as now, Zimbabwe was further north than South Africa and closer to the equator, so climatic differences might be responsible for these varied casts of characters (as climate is known to have a strong effect on the distributions of living animals). To probe this further, we’ll be going back to Kariba in search of more fossils.
We’ll also collect more information on the exact ages and environments of these dinosaur-bearing rocks, to compare them more precisely with sites elsewhere. Although the significance of these dinosaurs is only just coming to light, Zimbabwe is already taking a greater role in shedding much-needed light on early dinosaur evolution.

title: MIT Astronomers Catch a Star Slowly Eating Its Companion 300 Light-Years Away
content:
Artist’s impression of ZTF J0440+2325, a brown dwarf (right) and a red dwarf (left) that orbit each other every 86.65 minutes. The brown dwarf overflows onto its companion, and the stream of material strikes the surface of the red dwarf, heating a large hot spot at the point of impact. Credit: Aaron Householder (MIT)
Astronomers have discovered a star slowly eating its companion in an extraordinary cosmic feast that could last billions of years.
A small star about 300 light-years from Earth is feeding on a companion that circles it every 87 minutes. The two objects are remarkably close, yet the star is drawing away material slowly enough that the feeding could continue for hundreds of thousands or even billions of years.
The pair, named ZTF J0440+2325, lies within the Milky Way. Its smaller member is a brown dwarf, a planetlike object that falls between planets and stars in mass. The brown dwarf has about 25 times Jupiter’s mass, while the star has about 85 times Jupiter’s mass. Both are small by stellar standards, and the brown dwarf’s entire orbit could fit within the Sun’s diameter.
Most planets occupy stable orbits that keep them apart from their stars. Astronomers have observed plenty of these systems, along with a handful of stars rapidly engulfing planets that come too close. The new discovery reveals another possibility. Reported by scientists at MIT and other institutions in an October 5, 2026, paper in
Nature Astronomy
, it represents the first observation of a low-mass star slowly and steadily consuming material from another low-mass object.
A repeating triangle in the light curve
Several years ago, Kevin Burdge, an assistant professor of physics at MIT, noticed an unusual brightness pattern while reviewing data from the Zwicky Transient Facility, or ZTF. The facility uses a camera on a telescope at California’s Palomar Observatory to scan for rapid brightness changes that could signal a supernova, a gamma-ray burst, or colliding neutron stars. A supernova’s light curve, a record of brightness over time, resembles a bell as the exploding star brightens and then fades. The light curve that caught Burdge’s attention instead showed a repeating triangular pattern.
“I remember first looking at this and thinking, stars don’t make triangular waveforms like this,” he recalls.
At the time, Burdge and his colleagues were investigating a different signal, which they identified as a “black widow binary.” In that kind of system, an extremely dense, spinning neutron star slowly consumes a much smaller companion star, behavior that evokes its spider namesake. Burdge wondered whether the triangular signal came from another black widow. In those systems, however, the light shows a pronounced wobble as the lightweight companion whips around the much heavier neutron star.
“We weren’t seeing that whipping back and forth here,” Burdge says. “It didn’t make any sense. We couldn’t explain what this was.”
The wobble rules out a neutron star
Recently, Burdge returned to the unexplained signal with Aaron Householder, a graduate student in MIT’s Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences. They wanted to test an idea Burdge and his colleagues had considered years earlier.
“If you have less mass in the system overall, things can gently orbit each other without whipping back and forth,” Burdge says. “That was the idea. But we never had any proof. And this weird triangle just sat for years.”
Using the original ZTF signal to locate the source, the researchers directed multiple telescopes toward it. They measured several properties, including a small but detectable wobble, and compared the motion with that of black widows and similar binary systems.
“That was the real clincher for this system,” Householder says. “When we measured that wobble, we found we were not seeing a black widow. This was a low-mass star that’s orbited by a brown dwarf. The wobble was too small in amplitude to be anything else.”
Matter crashes directly onto the star
With the objects’ masses and tight orbit established, the team investigated whether one could be pulling material from the other. This process, called accretion, is most often observed around compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars, which pack enormous mass into a small space. When a black hole draws matter from a much smaller nearby object, the material gathers around it in a disk.
“The difference here is, the thing absorbing matter is not a tiny black hole but a star, which is relatively big in size,” Burdge explains. “So matter just pummels directly onto the surface, at very high speeds, like an asteroid hitting the moon.”
The researchers tested that possibility with simulations based on the properties of the star and brown dwarf. They modeled particles of matter on the brown dwarf and used the laws of physics and equations of motion to track where those particles would travel over time.
“When we track those test particles, we see they indeed fall right onto the surface of the star,” Householder says. “This is the first time we’ve caught a low-mass star actively accreting from another low-mass object.”
The team then considered how the steady stream would appear from a distance as the brown dwarf and its flowing material circled the star.
“It’s like you’ve got this continuous fireball onto one of the objects, and as one orbits the other, that hotspot comes in and out of view, and the peak of the triangle signal is when you’re looking right at the fireball,” Burdge explains.
Slow feeding could last billions of years
The researchers calculated that the brown dwarf must be supplying about 1/100,000 of Earth’s mass in material each year. To convey the scale, they compared the flow to about 40 million dump trucks’ worth of material, or roughly 1.3 trillion one-pound burritos every second. Even that enormous quantity represents only a small fraction of the brown dwarf’s mass, making the estimated transfer slow and steady relative to the available supply.
“When we think of stars interacting with planets or brown dwarfs, the picture is always that the star eventually swallows the other thing,” says Burdge. “This is what will happen to the Earth when the Sun becomes a red giant. But here, we’ve found an alternative: Instead of swallowing the thing up, the star can gradually eat it, for billions of years.”
Alongside Burdge and Householder, the study’s MIT coauthors include Kaitlyn Shin, Saul Rappaport, Joheen Chakraborty, and Emma Chickles. The collaboration also includes researchers from Caltech, the University of Hawaii, the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias and the Universidad de La Laguna in Spain, and the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics.
With an explanation for the triangular light curve, the team hopes to identify other nearby systems where stars gradually draw material from their companions.
“It’s inspiring a lot of new searches on our part,” Householder says. “I think we’re going to learn a lot about a different kind of way that planets and brown dwarfs interact with their host stars.”
Reference: “Stable mass transfer from a substellar object onto an M dwarf” by Aaron Householder, Kaitlyn Shin, Kevin B. Burdge, Thomas R. Marsh, Saul A. Rappaport, Kareem El-Badry, Joheen Chakraborty, Emma Chickles, Fei Dai, Matthew J. Graham, S. R. Kulkarni, Pablo Rodríguez-Gil, Andrew Vanderburg and Samuel Whitebook, 5 October 2026,

title: Eating Blueberries Linked to Subtle Gut Changes and Signs of Mood Improvement
content:
Blueberries are small, nutrient-rich fruits packed with fiber, vitamins, and anthocyanins—the pigments responsible for their deep blue color. Credit: Shutterstock
A small trial in older adults uncovered subtle gut changes and hints of mood improvement with daily blueberry powder, but no clear benefit over placebo.
Inside the gut, the fiber and dark pigments in blueberries encounter a crowded community of microbes. Those ingredients could change the microbes and the substances they produce, raising the possibility that eating the fruit might influence mood. Establishing whether those microscopic changes actually ease depressive symptoms requires evidence that reaches beyond the gut.
Courtney L. Millar, PhD, and her colleagues explored that possibility in a three-month pilot study of sedentary adults 65 and older with mild depressive symptoms. Participants who consumed blueberry powder daily showed a greater, more consistent reduction in symptoms than those given a placebo. The difference between the groups was not statistically significant, however, leaving the apparent benefit uncertain.
Two cups of blueberries versus placebo
“Fiber and anthocyanins in blueberries have potential to modify the gut microbiome and metabolites that are relevant to depression in older adults,” said Millar, the study’s lead author and an assistant scientist II at Hebrew SeniorLife’s Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research. Anthocyanins are the pigments that give blueberries their rich color, while metabolites are substances produced through chemical processes, including those carried out by microbes.
Participants were randomly assigned to consume either 48 grams, about 1.7 ounces, of blueberry powder each day or a matched placebo powder. The blueberry portion represented approximately two cups of fresh berries. The trial was double-blind, meaning neither the participants nor the researchers assessing them knew who was receiving which powder.
Millar’s team paired questionnaires measuring depressive symptoms with laboratory analyses of stool samples collected before and after the intervention.
“Our objective was to preliminarily determine the effect of blueberry consumption on the gut microbiome, metabolites, and depressive symptoms,” said Millar, who is also an assistant professor of medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School.
Reading microbial DNA allowed the researchers to measure which species and genes were present and how abundant they were. Separate chemical analyses measured short-chain fatty acids, substances produced by gut microbes. Together, these measurements let the team examine both the microbial community and some of its chemical products.
Small gut changes, uncertain mood benefits
Several categories of genes associated with microbial enzymes changed significantly within the blueberry group. One involved polyamine-transporting ATPase, which the researchers describe as participating in the production of the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid, or GABA. Changes in the abundance of those genes do not, by themselves, demonstrate that the microbes produced more GABA or that it affected participants’ mood.
Other measurements remained unchanged, including the abundance of microbial species, the metabolic pathways assessed, and the short-chain fatty acids measured in stool. The genetic findings therefore represented a narrow change within the gut microbiome, without a corresponding change in those measured chemical products.
Eighteen older adults completed the study, including 10 who consumed blueberry powder daily and eight who received a placebo. Researchers observed subtle shifts in microbial genes in the blueberry group, alongside greater reductions in depressive symptoms, pointing to a possible connection between blueberry compounds, the gut microbiome, and mood.

title: Scientists Discover Why Eating Fat Before Carbs Reduces Blood Sugar Spikes
content:
Eating olive oil before carbs reduced blood sugar spikes in mice, revealing a surprising way that food order could influence diabetes management. Credit: Shutterstock
A hormone that raises blood sugar may help put the brakes on a post-meal spike when fat reaches the gut before sugar.
An international research team found that giving mice fat before glucose slowed stomach emptying and reduced the early blood sugar spike. The experiments suggest that the response involves cooperation between gut and pancreatic hormones and nerve signals, offering clues to why food order may matter.
Human studies have already shown that eating vegetables, protein, or fat before carbohydrates can moderate post-meal blood sugar rises, an important treatment target in diabetes. Meal sequencing could therefore offer a practical dietary strategy that changes eating order without eliminating foods.
“Our group has long been interested in practical dietary approaches that people can continue in everyday life,” says corresponding author Daisuke Yabe of Kyoto University. “Meal sequencing is appealing because it merely changes how a meal is eaten rather than requiring people to avoid entire food groups.”
Olive oil administered before carbohydrates elicits early glucagon and GLP-1 responses that act in a partially redundant manner and, with involvement of vagal pathways, slow gastric emptying and attenuate the early post-meal glucose. Credit: KyotoU / Daisuke Yabe
How Food Order Changes Glucose Delivery
The stomach helps control how quickly nutrients reach the intestine. Slower emptying can spread out glucose delivery, tempering the early blood sugar rise. Researchers have also linked meal-sequencing benefits to increased release of incretin hormones, including GLP-1, which help lower blood glucose. Less clear was how these hormones interact with pancreatic hormones and nerve pathways.
To investigate, the team fasted mice overnight and compared three feeding sequences: water followed by glucose, olive oil followed by glucose 15 minutes later, and glucose followed by olive oil 15 minutes later. They tracked blood glucose and plasma levels of insulin, glucagon, GIP, and GLP-1. Blood measurements after oral acetaminophen provided an estimate of stomach-emptying speed.
When olive oil came first, the mice showed a smaller early blood sugar rise and slower stomach emptying than when it came afterward. Giving fat first also increased early secretion of glucagon, GIP, and GLP-1. These effects persisted in mice with type 2 diabetes and severe insulin deficiency.
Glucagon’s Unexpected Role
Glucagon is best known for raising blood glucose, making its contribution here particularly intriguing. Blocking either glucagon or GLP-1 signaling alone did not weaken the glucose-lowering effect of giving olive oil first, but blocking both did, indicating that both pathways contribute to the response.
The researchers also tested mice lacking the GLP-1 receptor and examined nerve involvement by tying off the vagus nerve below the diaphragm on both sides. The nerve experiments suggested that vagal pathways contribute to the response. Tests with other dietary fats helped establish that the findings were not unique to olive oil.
“Our findings suggest that the order in which nutrients reach the gut can engage a coordinated hormone-nerve response that changes how quickly the stomach delivers glucose to the intestine,” says Yabe.
Together with existing clinical evidence, the findings strengthen the case for testing practical meal-sequencing strategies in people with and without diabetes. The next challenge is to determine how reliably this hormone and nerve response translates into benefits during everyday meals.

title: The Secret Heart Benefit of a Common Diabetes Drug
content:
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are a class of prescription drugs used to treat type 2 diabetes, with popular brand names including Jardiance (empagliflozin), Farxiga (dapagliflozin), and Invokana (canagliflozin). These medications lower blood sugar by helping the kidneys remove excess glucose through urine, often producing modest weight loss. Credit: Stock
Researchers discovered that a diabetes medication altered how certain immune cells function, potentially reducing harmful inflammation.
A medication already used to treat diabetes may protect the heart by changing how immune cells behave in the bloodstream. In a small human clinical trial, researchers found that the drug reduced inflammatory cell clusters associated with cardiovascular disease, with measurable effects appearing after just two weeks.
The findings, published in the American Heart Association journal
Circulation
, provide the first direct evidence that sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors can alter specific immune cells in humans. These medications are known for lowering blood sugar, promoting weight loss, and providing cardiovascular and kidney benefits, but their effects on inflammation have been less clear.
A Rapid Reduction in Inflammatory Blood Cells
Researchers at Vanderbilt Health studied 16 women with obesity and prediabetes who received the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin for three months. Blood samples collected before treatment, after two weeks, and after 12 weeks allowed investigators to track changes in immune activity. The team also examined a separate comparison group of women who followed a low-calorie diet for three months.
Mona Mashayekhi, MD, PhD, Assistant Professor of Medicine in the Division of Diabetes, Endocrinology and Metabolism at Vanderbilt Health Credit: Vanderbilt Health
Using advanced genetic sequencing and cellular imaging, the researchers identified a significant reduction in monocyte platelet aggregates (MPAs). These clusters form when blood-clotting cells (platelets) attach to immune cells (monocytes), creating structures associated with inflammation in blood vessels and cardiovascular disease.
MPA levels declined significantly within two weeks of starting empagliflozin and fell further by the end of the study. The women in the diet comparison group did not show the same reduction, suggesting that the medication’s effects on these cells may extend beyond its influence on body weight.
Diabetes Medication Changes Immune Cell Behavior
The researchers also identified evidence of “metabolic reprogramming” in monocytes (immune cells). These cells shifted away from a highly inflammatory state toward a more stable metabolic profile associated with normal cellular energy production.
“There had been some suggestive studies in animals with these medications indicating they might be modulating the immune system — affecting inflammation — but that hadn’t really been shown in humans,” said Mona Mashayekhi, MD, PhD, Assistant Professor of Medicine in the Division of Diabetes, Endocrinology and Metabolism at Vanderbilt Health.
“This study provides the first direct evidence of SGLT2 inhibitors altering human immune cells, which may potentially reduce cardiovascular risk.”
A Larger Trial Will Investigate the Mechanism
“This finding is significant because it’s the first time this medication has been shown to have an immune effect at the cellular level with some specificity. If we understand how these medicines are reducing obesity-associated inflammation and heart disease and kidney disease, then we can identify the best patient for this treatment or discover other drug targets in that pathway that could really be beneficial.”
Mashayekhi and her colleagues have launched a randomized, placebo-controlled trial at Vanderbilt Health that aims to enroll 74 participants with obesity and metabolic syndrome. The study will examine immune changes over three months and analyze adipose tissue (fat) to investigate how the medication affects inflammation within the body.
The larger trial will help determine whether the immune changes observed in the initial study can be confirmed under more rigorous conditions and clarify how SGLT2 inhibitors influence inflammation associated with metabolic disease.

title: GCL’s perovskite modules installed in 500-meter expressway noise barrier in China
content:
GCL’s perovskite modules installed in 500-meter expressway noise barrier in China
GCL Perovskite
has supplied customized perovskite modules for a 500-meter photovoltaic noise barrier at the Douzhuang service area on the Shanghai-Chengdu Expressway in China. The installation is complete and uses 224 single-junction perovskite modules rated at 270 W each, for a total capacity of 60.48 kWp.
The Douzhuang service area on the Shanghai-Chengdu Expressway features a 500-meter PV noise barrier with perovskite modules supplied by GCL Perovskite.Image Credit: GCL Perovskite
The barrier has three sections: a 0.4 m curved sound-absorbing section, a 1.1 m PV section and a 2.9 m high sound-absorbing section. Its noise reduction coefficient is at least 0.70. The system also includes two inverters and an integrated energy-storage charging unit connected to the service area’s existing PV carport. Together they form a microgrid that combines roadside generation, on-site consumption and energy storage for peak shaving.
The project follows GCL Perovskite’s completion of the
first end-to-end production run on its GW-scale module line
in September. Perovskite noise barriers have been tried elsewhere. Japan’s JR Tokai
is testing perovskite solar cells on Tokaido Shinkansen noise barriers
developed with Sekisui Chemical.

title: Simulation shows the right hole transport layer could push a lead-free perovskite solar cell past 27% efficiency
content:
Simulation shows the right hole transport layer could push a lead-free perovskite solar cell past 27% efficiency
Researchers at the Renewable Energy Laboratory of India’s Maulana Azad National Institute of Technology (MANIT) in Bhopal have used simulations to show how the energy alignment at the hole transport layer (HTL) interface shapes the performance of lead-free, all-inorganic Cs
perovskite solar cells.
has attracted attention thanks to its environmental stability and promising optoelectronic properties, and being lead-free, it sidesteps the concerns about lead that continue to shadow the technology. Using the SCAPS-1D simulation tool, also used in an
earlier study of lead-free chalcogenide perovskites
, the team examined how the HTL’s valence band offset (VBO) affects the cell’s electrostatics, carrier transport, recombination and photovoltaic performance. They compared HTLs spanning cliff-type alignments, an intermediate spike regime and excessive spike-type alignments.
Performance depended strongly, and non-monotonically, on the VBO. Cliff-type alignment produced weak electric fields at the interface and diffusion-limited carrier extraction, which increased interfacial recombination losses. A balanced positive VBO instead generated an optimized depletion field that promotes drift-assisted carrier transport and suppresses interfacial recombination. At the other extreme, a large positive VBO caused carriers to accumulate at the interface and created a transport barrier, degrading performance.
The best result came from vanadium pentoxide (V2O5) with a +0.3 eV VBO, which delivered a simulated power conversion efficiency of 27.48%, with an open-circuit voltage of 1.26 V, a short-circuit current density of 25.1 mA/cm² and a fill factor of 87.3%. Quantum efficiency analysis also showed that optimized VBO engineering improves the collection of long-wavelength carriers by extending the effective drift region across the absorber bulk.
The researchers say the findings establish HTL VBO engineering as a key strategy for achieving high-efficiency lead-free Cs2PdBr6 solar cells. All efficiency figures come from the simulations.

title: 新能源资产如何保值增值？AI‌×专业运营构建护城河-索比光伏网
content:
当前，电价波动、消纳约束和市场交易规则变化，使新能源资产收益面临更多变量；与此同时，金融机构、产业基金、财务投资人等多元化投资主体加速进入新能源领域。对资产持有者而言，关注点从能否稳定发电，延伸到如何经营每一度电；对投资与收购方而言，还需要看清项目的收益基础、经营风险，以及未来的交易与流转条件。
10月14日，2026北京国际风能大会暨展览会（CWP2026）盛大开幕。协合运维以“AI×专业运营，让新能源资产更稳健”为主题亮相展会，将AI融入资产运营的真实场景，集中展示从投前判断、持有期经营到流转退出的的专业运营能力。他们从新能源资产持有者与投资者的视角出发，呈现在不断变化的市场中，专业运营如何贯穿资产价值链，助力资产长期稳健经营。
看清收益底盘与风险边界
在新能源投资回归理性、市场不确定性加大的背景下，准确评估项目风险与长期收益能力，是资产价值管理的起点。投前测算需要回答的，不只是模型中的回报率，更是这些收益假设在实际运营中能否成立。
依托多年积累的新能源资产运营数据、专业经验及市场分析能力，协合运维将资源、设备、限电、电价及运营成本等因素纳入整体的收益分析，致力于为投资与收购决策提供综合判断，助力投资者清晰识别资产价值与潜在风险。
让专业能力成为价值锚点
在生产保障方面，协合运维以HS系列资产运营解决方案，回应不同客户的组织能力与管理需求。对于已有运营团队的客户，可以按需接入专家顾问、技术支持与履约监督；需要专业组织承接更多运营责任的客户，则可选择相应深度的现场服务、运营统筹或资产托管，将人员、设备、备件及经营事项纳入相应的服务安排，帮助客户根据自身需求配置运营能力。
面对存量风电机组的长期运行及出质保后的服务需求，协合运维聚焦机组大部件维修、偏航与变桨等系统技改及备机备件保障，整合多方资源优势和自身技术实力，进行多品牌机型的定制化维修技改服务。以发电机维修为例，协合运维将备机置换与检测、运输、返厂维修及安装调试相衔接，有效解决停机等待周期长的问题，并结合机组实际状态开展修复与技改，持续守住发电能力。
让交易判断有依据、有复盘
发得出电，如何在市场波动中经营收益？协合运维展台中央的SISITrader智能体，吸引众多观众驻足交流。
SISITrader是协合运维面向电力交易领域打造的专业智能体平台，覆盖智能问数分析、日报周报月报、策略报告、自动化模块与电价预测评估等场景。平台致力于让AI进入“理解—数据—分析—决策—输出—复盘”的完整链路，让交易员的专业判断得到更稳定、更高效的支持，并让优秀经验沉淀为可执行、可复用、可迭代的业务资产。
在电力交易领域，还重点展示了聆风电力交易平台矩阵、储能资产运营以及咨询与数据服务等能力。截至目前，协合运维代管交易资产规模突破20GW，通过全面的市场数据分析、电价预测、交易策略优化与智能化决策支持，能够助力新能源资产更好地应对电价波动和交易风险，提升市场环境下的收益经营能力。
让可验证的运营结果支撑资产循环

title: REM Ocean arrives at Myklebust Shipyard
content:
DeepOcean has announced that the subsea vessel REM Ocean has arrived at
Myklebust Shipyard in Norway for final outfitting and completion ahead
of its planned delivery in 2027.
The milestone follows the vessel's initial construction at Song Cam Shipyard
in Vietnam.
Once completed, REM Ocean will offer 1,000 square metres of deck space
and accommodation for up to 120 personnel.
Designed for inspection, maintenance and repair (IMR) operations, the vessel
will be equipped with a 250 tonne electric crane, an Autonomous Inspection
Drone (AID), an electric module handling system (MHS), and two electric
work class remotely operated vehicles (WROVs) housed in a 350 square metre
internal hangar.
Owned by Rem Offshore, the vessel is set to begin an eight year charter
with DeepOcean upon delivery. During the contract, REM Ocean will support
Equinor's offshore IMR activities.

title: ERWC relaunches as EcoSymbia
content:
The European Renewable Energy & Wildlife Consortium (ERWC) has officially
rebranded as EcoSymbia.
The group consists of five ecological consultancies: Waardenburg Ecology
in the Netherlands, Écosphère in France, Nature Conservation Consultants
in Greece, Oikon in Croatia and Bioinsight in Portugal.
Including subsidiaries and partner companies, EcoSymbia is now made up
of 15 companies in total, with offices in nine countries.
ERWC was established back in 2024 to support wind and solar developments
bats and other wildlife.
The company’s work includes offshore wind projects, covering ecological
baseline studies, Natura 2000 appropriate assessments, and environmental
monitoring before, during and after construction.
The group uses a range of survey and monitoring methods, including ornithological
radar, bird tracking and telemetry, passive acoustic monitoring with towed
and moored hydrophones, eDNA sampling, and drone and aerial surveys.

title: Canada commits $100m to advance Nova Scotia offshore wind plans
content:
The Canadian Government has committed $100 million to support offshore
developments in Nova Scotia, including the Wind West offshore wind initiative.
The project is intended to develop offshore wind generation and the infrastructure
needed to deliver electricity within and beyond the province.
Wind West aims to generate enough renewable electricity to meet Nova Scotia’s
domestic demand while enabling additional power exports through new transmission
connections.
The project was referred to the federal Major Projects Office back in September
2025 as part of broader efforts to expand clean energy development across
Atlantic Canada.
Out of the funding announced, $5 million will be used to deploy floating
light detection and ranging (FLiDAR) buoys offshore. The buoys will collect
wind and ocean data to support project planning and help inform a Call
for Bids expected from the Canada–Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator
in winter 2027.
Natural Resources Canada is also providing nearly $3 million to Net Zero
Atlantic to expand transmission modelling for offshore wind exports from
Nova Scotia to Quebec, Ontario and other markets. The work will include
marine surveys to support future export cable routing.

title: Ecowende publishes offshore wind construction noise monitoring report
content:
Ecowende has released a report detailing the results of noise monitoring
conducted during the construction of its offshore wind farm.
Ecowende wind farm,Hollandse
Kust West VI,
is located off the Dutch coast, once completed it will have the operational
capacity of around 760 MW.
According to the report, six of the 52 monopiles installed by Van Oord
utilised two innovative installation techniques. Three monopiles were installed
using CAPE Holland's vibro hammer technology, while the remaining three
were installed using GBM Works' Vibrojet system, which combines vibro driving
and jetting.
Conventional impact piling was also used during construction, supported
B.V. monitored underwater sound levels at distances of up to 5 km from
the installation site.
The report includes processed sound-level data from the new installation
technologies and examines a range of noise mitigation measures, including
bubble curtains and the Hydro Sound Damper (HSD).
"By sharing our data openly, we help the sector and regulators make
better informed choices for porpoises and seals in the North Sea,"
said Pauline Roos, Marine Ecologist at Ecowende.
Ecowende said a second report providing a more in-depth analysis of the
findings will be published at a later date.

title: Apple’s Antitrust Settlement Talks Spur Worries Among Developers
content: As the U.S. Department of Justice negotiates a settlement of its antitrust lawsuit against Apple, app developers are fretting that any deal won’t go far enough in curbing what they see as Apple’s anticompetitive behavior, according to people familiar with the talks. Several developers, including PayPal and Epic Games, have discussed their concerns with the Justice Department about a possible settlement of the Apple case, the people said. In communication with developers, Justice Department officials have signaled their preference to settle the lawsuit rather than fight it, the people said. The department appears to be focusing on a deal addressing interoperability issues developers face with the iPhone. In its 2024 lawsuit, the Justice Department alleged that Apple maintained an illegal monopoly over the smartphone market by restricting how outside apps or devices worked on the iPhone. For instance, Apple’s smartwatch pairs with the iPhone more easily than competing smartwatches do. And while the company has begun opening the tap-to-pay feature, which used to work only with Apple Pay, to other payment apps, the feature still doesn’t work as smoothly with those rival apps. As part of its talks with developers, the Justice Department has asked them for a list of ways to improve the iPhone’s ability to operate with other devices, the people said. Many developers and antitrust lawyers are concerned that the Justice Department will offer Apple a settlement that imposes relatively light requirements on how its devices interact with other companies’ devices. Spokespeople for PayPal and Epic declined to comment on discussions with the agency. A Justice Department spokesperson also declined to comment, other than to say the department would “continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy.” Apple didn’t respond to requests for comment. Bloomberg reported on the early stages of the settlement talks in July. Dealmaking Preference After President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, he installed antitrust lawyer Gail Slater as head of the Justice Department’s antitrust division. Slater favored more aggressive antitrust enforcement and clashed with the Trump administration’s dealmaking inclinations, lawyers said. She stepped down in February, succeeded at least temporarily in June by Stanley Woodward, the third-ranking official at the agency and once a favored lawyer for Trump’s inner circle. The White House has nominated Adam Candeub to lead the division permanently. Candeub is awaiting Senate confirmation. In the meantime, Woodward has pushed for settlements because he believes they deliver benefits to consumers faster and cost the government less than taking a case to trial, which can take many years, according to antitrust lawyers. Some people involved in the talks have been surprised the negotiations have taken this long and had expected a resolution much sooner. But Candeub’s pending confirmation could be delaying a deal. This isn’t the first time Apple has held settlement talks related to its current conflict with the U.S. government. The company tried to settle with the Justice Department before the government sued in 2024, during the Biden administration. To avert a lawsuit, Apple promised to improve the interoperability of its products with other devices, one person familiar with the discussions said. Since the 2024 lawsuit, Apple has changed its products and policies in ways that address some of the complaints about its lack of interoperability. For instance, Apple has made it easier for Android phone users to message iPhone owners by integrating a messaging technology called Rich Communication Services, or RCS, into the Messages app. Still, Apple is likely to resist making substantial changes that open up its ecosystem the way many developers have demanded. As a result, there’s a chance the Justice Department and Apple won’t reach a settlement. The long-running Epic Games lawsuit demonstrated Apple’s intransigence on making major changes. Last year, for example, U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple willfully violated a 2021 injunction from the antitrust case and referred the matter to federal prosecutors for a possible criminal contempt investigation. Apple is appealing the ruling to the Supreme Court. “I have a hard time thinking that Apple would ever agree to terms of what a developer would consider a good settlement,” said Christine Bannan, senior public policy manager at Proton, a Swiss maker of privacy-focused online services that sued Apple last year over alleged anticompetitive App Store policies. Bannan said Proton had discussed the antitrust lawsuit with Justice Department officials earlier in the process and that the case seemed to be proceeding. But Proton hasn’t taken part in the latest settlement discussions because it is waiting for Candeub’s confirmation, she said. “But at this stage, I’m concerned that we’ll be waiting for too long, and the wheels are moving, and Apple’s pushing for settlement,” Bannan said.

title: The Party Is Still Going Strong for Private Tech
content: The sentiment gap between public and private markets could not be wider right now. Wall Street investors have been increasingly worried about overborrowing by AI-related companies, as evidenced by skyrocketing yields on CoreWeave bonds , a selloff in semiconductor stocks and the yanking of the IPO of Firmus, the Australian data center operator. Investors in private tech startups are still ebullient, blown away by how fast startups like Fireworks AI have grown. This bifurcation was evident to me this week at Morgan Stanley’s annual private tech companies conference. The mutual fund and other investors fanning out across a lush seaside resort in Dana Point, Calif., were aware of the red washing over trading screens. But that didn’t prevent them from rushing to meet the dozens of startup founders there, particularly if they were in the hot defense or inference sectors. “You can see there's a stark disconnect between the public markets and the private markets,” said Diana Doyle, Morgan Stanley’s head of technology equity and equity-linked capital markets on the sidelines of the conference. Doyle, who lives in Silicon Valley, notes that “in the private markets, growth still trumps all, and there is a license to pursue growth,” as well as a fear of missing out. “But we’ve seen this discipline in the public markets, where it’s no longer growth at all costs, and growth among public companies is hard to come by,” she said. Fueling Wall Street disenchantment was the prospect of higher interests, which risks squeezing companies that borrow a lot—such as cloud provider CoreWeave. But that wasn’t the only factor souring public investors. On Wednesday, as shares of CoreWeave and rival Nebius dropped sharply, attendees were anxiously checking with colleagues for a third-quarter update from Anthropic ahead of its initial public offering next month. They got their answer shortly after 3 p.m, when news broke that Anthropic recorded $16.8 billion in revenue in the third quarter. Investors in most five-year-old companies would have uncorked Champagne if the business hit that level of quarterly sales. But this is Anthropic, whose success selling Claude Code, Cowork and other tools boosted second-quarter revenue 140% from the first. Anthropic’s third-quarter report, up just a measly 45% from the first, instead came across as a worrisome slowdown. The news prompted some investors to nudge Anthropic’s bankers to lower its valuation target to under $1.5 trillion, rather than the $2 trillion those bankers had floated previously. They are already fretting over the sky-high valuations some debt-saddled data center firms such as Nscale are seeking for their public offerings. Nscale, for instance, has sought to raise up to $3 billion in an IPO at a valuation of more than $35 billion, according to the Financial Times. “I’m not sure how they can go public” at the valuations the data center companies want, one fund manager said. The grumpiness didn’t extend to the startups that seem happy to stay private for a while.  Investors at the conference were nearly tripping over themselves to meet with a coveted list of hot private companies the bank assembled such as Jeff Bezos’ rocketship company Blue Origin and Elon Musk’s brain company Neuralink. Plus, investors were eager to meet with young but headline-grabbing companies, such as chip startup Etched, Naveen Rao’s Unconventional AI and legal AI startup Legora. Some were particularly eager to catch up with defense tech startups, such as Anduril, Hadrian and Saronic, which have already raised money at multi-billion valuations. Many told me they were amazed by the businesses that Fireworks AI, Baseten and Fal AI have built. As we and others have reported , these startups, which sell access to AI models, have seen soaring demand as developers use more open-source AI models, which can often be cheaper than those from OpenAI and Anthropic. These investors are wondering when the first wave of these richly-valued AI-native startups will go public. While data center companies come with mounds of debt and revenue that hinges on yet-to-be built projects, the AI native companies don’t seem to carry such drawbacks. There are plenty of reasons for these startups to eventually enter the public markets. “Capital is an absolutely competitive weapon, similar to semiconductors and hardware companies,” said David Chen, global head of technology investment banking at Morgan Stanley, about the AI-native startups. “Going public does give you a significant advantage, because you have access to just a wide variety of additional instruments like convertible debt.” Assuming all goes well, of course. As Anthropic is showing, it’s hard for even A-list AI startups to show exponential growth every quarter. And public investors have a simple way of making their displeasure known. title: Did Anthropic Miss Its Peak IPO Moment?
content: It’s beginning to look like Anthropic waited too late to go public. Third-quarter revenue numbers disclosed to investors on Wednesday implied that its growth has slowed from the second quarter, which we reported is likely to put a ceiling on its IPO valuation. Anthropic might have been better off going public in June, when its growth was still spectacular. (Of course, a June IPO might have been impractical given that that’s when SpaceX went public.) As things stand now, Anthropic’s slowing growth may remind investors of a longstanding question surrounding the company: How much of a moat does it really have? Yes, its AI models are as good as they get, but increasingly, businesses don’t need really expensive frontier models. As we wrote earlier this week , developers are increasingly opting for other models that are good enough for most tasks. Anthropic’s aggressive pricing has prompted companies such as Microsoft to cut its spending on the former’s models, we reported 10 days ago . (This trend seems to be spreading ). And there are lots of alternative models available, mostly open source. TrustedRouter— a storefront for businesses wanting to tap any AI model—lists 665. And in China, at least, more companies are developing their own models, including Xiaomi, a smartphone maker, and Meituan, a food-delivery firm. That could easily happen here. Another problem: Given the growing safety concerns about state-of-the-art models, Anthropic’s ability to even release its best models is diminishing, as my colleague Stephanie Palazzolo pointed out in August. Layer on the $500 billion–plus in commitments Anthropic has taken on to secure computing capacity over the next decade, and the risks in owning its stock begin to mount. Our story on Wednesday night said investors thought Anthropic’s IPO valuation should be closer to $1.5 trillion than the $2 trillion bankers had floated in the past. “This IPO will need to price to sell,” said Jared Carmel, managing partner of Manhattan Venture Partners. He expects the company to go public at a valuation of $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion. That’s still a big number for a company that is not quite six years old. It would make Anthropic the ninth-biggest tech company by market value, below Broadcom and above Tesla. But it may well turn out to be Anthropic’s peak. Apple’s Value Growing questions about the value of frontier AI models suggest big tech firms such as Apple made the right bet in avoiding the costly race to develop their own models. It’s likely no coincidence that Apple stock has now risen more than twice as much as other big-name tech stocks so far this year. As of Thursday’s close, Apple shares were up 26% for the year so far, while Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Microsoft were each up 10% to 12%. Even more striking, Apple is the only one of that group to have seen its valuation, measured as a multiple of profits or sales, rise this year, according to Koyfin data. And yet Apple is growing more slowly than the other big tech firms. But given that most of those others are pouring a fortune into capital expenditures for AI data centers, Apple is increasingly looking like a healthier bet ( as we predicted ). In Other News • Apple is preparing to release its Apple Intelligence on-device AI service in mainland China in December, ending a lengthy wait caused by regulatory hurdles, Bloomberg reported Thursday . • Portland, Ore.–based startup Mueon raised $65 million to develop a new way to arrange AI server rack components. The company says its design could fit up to 10 times more computing capacity into the same amount of power as existing data center setups. This approach could ease constraints on global power and data center capacity for AI chips. • Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. said Thursday it will build another 3-nanometer chip factory in the Taiwanese city of Tainan, with production set for the first half of 2028. The move signals confidence that strong AI chip demand will last for years. • CoreWeave and Broadcom have objected to a request from OKXICE, a joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange, to list and trade their stocks on blockchain, joining a growing list of companies pushing back against crypto versions of their stocks. • Anthropic has now begun embedding AI evaluators within the company to assess and publish reports on safety practices and risks, Anthropic said in a blog post on Thursday. They’ll use company computers, office space and have access to internal tools and systems.
