title: Nick Wingfield Promoted to Co-Executive Editor of The Information
content: I am thrilled to announce three major editorial promotions for Nick, Abe and Meredith, along with some changes that recognize the incredible work of our newsroom and set the stage for more growth in what is shaping up to be the most exciting time in our history. Nick Wingfield has been promoted to Executive Editor , responsible for ensuring the high bar of all our reporting. Since he joined The Information eight years ago after working at the New York Times and Wall Street Journal, Nick has pushed us to think bigger in our journalism, overseeing our features efforts and some of our most important beats. When we heard whispers that Jony Ive’s personal life was becoming a distraction from his work at Apple, he and Aaron Tilley mustered a slew of reporting that turned into one of our most memorable crash leders. That’s what he has done again and again. Working with talented reporters to drive maximum impact, across coasts, beats and more. In his new role, Nick will run the day-to-day publication with me and Amir, with us all dividing up responsibilities for what we chase and ensuring the highest bar in what we publish while continuing to grow the team and build up new editorial areas. He will continue to manage his team of reporters. Abe Brown has been promoted to Features Editor, with responsibility for all our features at The Information. As Weekend editor, Abe has proven himself as something rare in media these days: a careful and skilled editor with a zest for trying new things. While managing a section, he has also jumped in any day of the week to help edit our biggest stories with a tireless work ethic and great attitude. While she has led all sorts of consequential coverage on ads, commerce, Musk and beyond, in recent months, she has helped our finance team carve out a huge lane around the financing of data centers and this turbulent moment. I’m excited to see how far she and the team can run against that massively important story. Meredith has also begun the work of bringing new talent to the team. I am thrilled to have her officially step into the role leading Finance, continuing to expand our reporting staff and find even more lanes where we can dominate. I am also happy to share that Martin has decided he wants to shift his focus to the Briefing and future related Briefing franchises and will become Editor-at-Large . Over twelve years, Martin has had a hand in every aspect of this business. I am thrilled he will be working with us full-time to focus on writing and how to expand the Briefing franchise, while continuing to coach and advise the newsroom. And there will be more time to celebrate more than a decade of Martin as co-Executive Editor. He will continue to edit The Electric and, in the coming weeks, reporters who report to him will transition to other senior leaders to free him up to go full throttle in his new role. We are making these changes now to celebrate the success of our incredible editorial leadership team, which remains unrivaled in the industry, and to prepare for the future. The next few years are going to demand a lot of news organizations. Sweeping changes to how audiences consume news are just beginning and I honestly think most news organizations will have no idea what hit them. Meanwhile, the onslaught of “information,” much of it biased and fake, has only begun. Our secret sauce—the high impact, ahead-of-the-curve, focused work no one else is doing—is exactly the right formula for this moment.

title: OpenAI Accelerates Ad Sprint With Meta Hires, Slashed Prices
content: As OpenAI has jockeyed with Anthropic to win over developers with new models and tools this year, its advertising business at times has seemed like an afterthought. Not anymore. Over the last few months, the company has unleashed a flurry of new products and tools to court advertisers, even as it has cut ad rates. That’s helped lure a lot more advertisers, new data show. The company has also gone on a hiring spree. Nearly half of the roughly 140 OpenAI employees working on ads joined between July and September, according to Crustdata, which tracks employees’ public profiles. Meta Platforms, where ad chief Dave Dugan spent 12 years, is the biggest source of talent. The hiring spree and some senior-level departures have contributed to a lot of internal change. OpenAI’s ad team has reorganized seven times since it launched in February, according to two people familiar with the matter. OpenAI is trying to make advertising, which is still small relative to the rest of its business,  a significant driver.  Since OpenAI started showing ads in February, annualized revenue from ads reached $1 billion in late August. In comparison, OpenAI neared a $50 billion annualized revenue pace for its overall business at the end of September, largely thanks to subscriptions to ChatGPT and related products, such as its Codex agent, as well as direct sales of its models. And despite growth in its ad revenue, OpenAI is likely to fall short of the lofty goals it outlined to investors early this year. The company then projected it would hit $2.4 billion in total 2026 ad revenue . Success recruiting more advertisers should boosting that growth. OpenAI had about 60,000 advertisers on its platform in early October, up from 20,000 in late August, according to Dan Salmon, partner at New Street Research, a Wall Street research firm. U.S. ad spending on ChatGPT is projected to increase 40% in October from September, estimates Sensor Tower, which tracks app and advertising activity and extrapolates using samples. OpenAI’s advertising has expanded to more than 60 countries. That growth has sparked a lot of curiosity among advertisers and agency executives about the business. Last Thursday dozens of people lined up to get a few words with Dave Dugan, OpenAI’s vice president of global ad solutions, after a packed session with customer Home Depot during New York’s Advertising Week. “We’re building the fastest-growing ads business in the world, and we’re hiring from a diverse range of companies across the industry, with no single company focus,” said Dugan later in a statement to The Information. “That breadth of talent keeps us shipping at pace and [turning] advertiser feedback into better products.” OpenAI is fighting an uphill battle to take a slice of a digital advertising market dominated by Google, Meta and Amazon. Most advertisers are still spending test budgets—typically 1% to 5% of annual ad spending—on ChatGPT, though a few have expanded far beyond that, according to people who work directly with advertisers. “It takes a while to write contracts, acquire new advertisers and gain market share,” said Kate Scott‑Dawkins, who runs the global research practice of GroupM, the media investment group of ad giant WPP. She expects Google will be the majority player in advertising inside AI chatbots and search for some time. But she said she hadn’t seen any ad channel grow as fast as OpenAI. Google, Meta Hires Fidji Simo, a Facebook veteran of more than a decade who joined in 2025, stepped back from her full-time role in early July. Since then, Dugan has restructured the team into vertical groups, each dedicated to an industry such as retail, travel or finance, and created a separate team that handles ad agencies. That setup resembles how more established ad sellers like Meta and Google organize their sales teams, said the people. A Meta spokesperson declined to comment. The senior ranks are sprinkled with former salespeople from Meta and its competitors, such as Vijaye Raji, who spent 10 years at Meta before becoming chief technology officer of OpenAI applications a year ago. Mitch Pilar, a 12-year Google veteran, and Andy Sinn, who spent about a decade at Meta, joined in July to sell ads to brands and agencies in Australia and New Zealand. And in late September, Mark Bambury, who spent a dozen years at Roblox and X, became OpenAI’s head of ads for Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Test Budgets When OpenAI launched its advertising pilot in February, it started by courting big brands and the agencies that buy ads for them, including Expedia, Target and Ford, along with ad agencies Omnicom, WPP and Dentsu. More recently, OpenAI has more aggressively been chasing small and midsize businesses —the type of customers that made Meta an advertising juggernaut. To entice those smaller advertisers, OpenAI is leaning on outsourcing firms to sell ads and help advertisers set up their campaigns. These include TP (formerly known as Teleperformance), Concentrix and consulting giant Accenture. Advertisers are slowly increasing their ChatGPT budgets as they learn how to use the platform, according to nine agencies and tech firms that run campaigns on ChatGPT. One big incentive: Ad prices on ChatGPT have fallen since the launch, when it charged some large buyers premium prices . A click on a ChatGPT ad costs about $5, versus $30 to $50 on Google for the same business software clients, said Cole Furrh, founder of InterTeam Marketing, an agency that works with advertisers. Filip Nakov, whose agency, Nakora, works with clients selling cybersecurity, AI and legal tech tools, said the ads were working surprisingly well: For $1,000 in spending, his clients get about 10 customers from ChatGPT, versus five from Meta and one from Google. Some of his clients have put up to 40% of their ad budgets, which range from $1,000 to $30,000 a day, into ChatGPT, he said. “When ChatGPT works, spend climbs to hundreds of thousands or more,” said Marcos Ciarrocchi, co-founder of the Graphite agency. Meanwhile, OpenAI has also expanded the type of ads shown to users. Its first ads, launched in February, appear as labeled sponsored ads below answers to queries, similar to Google search ads. These, known as last-click ads, target users who already intended to buy something. Currently about 20% of queries on ChatGPT signal a desire to purchase a product or a service, Dugan said last week. More recently, ChatGPT ad staff have focused on reaching people before they’ve started to query the chatbot about a purchase. Last week OpenAI announced a visual ad format that uses images to show how products and services could fit into people’s lives, and it has told agencies it wants to test a greater number of images and video, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. It’s also introducing more of the tools advertisers say they need to track the effectiveness of ads. Last week, it announced a string of partnerships with outside measurement firms that track what customers did after clicking an ad. But advertisers want more, such as tools that let advertisers compare a ChatGPT ad buy with a Google buy, said two people who work with OpenAI. Advertisers also complain they can’t see which conversations trigger their ads. “It’s a black box with no visibility whatsoever,” said Farhad Divecha, CEO of marketing agency Accuracast. That leaves advertisers guessing when they write the instructions that tell ChatGPT where to show their ads, he said. Some ads also land in the wrong place, according to Adthena, a company that tracks search and AI ads. In an analysis of about 187,000 ad placements, Adthena found that about one in nine ads was unrelated to the user’s question. A small number of these ads appeared inappropriately next to sensitive questions: An ad for push-up bras appeared next to a query about breast cancer, and an ad from a short-term lender showed up next to a query about debt relief. An OpenAI spokesperson said it was listening closely to feedback from advertisers and agencies and adapting its products, launching new features in response.

title: Why AI-Written Software Needs a Flight Simulator
content: As companies create more applications using AI, corporate officers say demand is rising for a new type of software that stress-tests those apps, simulating how they handle network problems and other disasters that humans may not think to test for—including cyberattacks by rogue AIs. Luis Chávez, CTO of coding assistant provider Replit, says his company uses an AI-assisted software known as a deterministic simulator, a kind of flight simulator for software. The deterministic part refers to how the simulator lets companies run the same disaster test again and again so they can try out different fixes for bugs that crop up during network failures or hacking attempts. Traditional stress-testing methods rely on developers guessing every potential problem that may arise. Merely using today’s AI models to evaluate code often produces false alarms or fake warnings, corporate executives say. Another issue is that AI models behave in a probabilistic manner, so they often won’t act the same way twice and are “very hard” to use to find all the problems in software, Chávez said. Some companies like Lumen and Pegasystems say they have developed their own software testing tools using AI products from Anthropic and Microsoft. Others are using software developed by startups focusing on the problem. Replit, for instance, uses one from Antithesis, a 200-person, Virginia-based startup. Founded in 2018, Antithesis’ other customers include Palantir and Datadog, according to its website. Antithesis’ simulator is powered in part by AI it developed in-house, said CEO Will Wilson. AI made writing software a lot simpler, but “checking to make sure the software actually works…did not get easier,” said Wilson. Other startups such as Gremlin and Chaos Mesh—not to mention big tech companies Microsoft and Amazon—sell software that tests how companies’ code handles potential problems through controlled experiments on their actual servers rather than in simulated environments. Microsoft is seeing an increase in customers using its testing software, according to a spokesperson. Wilson thinks Anthropic and other AI coding firms like SpaceX’s Cursor will eventually launch deterministic simulators. (Representatives of those firms didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.) Wilson said Antithesis added more revenue in the August quarter than in all of the preceding five periods, though he declined to provide figures. Antithesis raised $105 million in a Series A round at the end of 2025 led by quant fund Jane Street at a $525 million post-money valuation. It’s likely to raise capital again soon, seeking a considerably higher valuation, according to a person familiar with the firm. content:

Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
—Michal Luria, Aliya Bhatia, and Danah Boyd
Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.
The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15.
But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented.
Here’s what we ought to do instead to keep kids safe.
Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
—Jessica Hamzelou
I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated.
Almost 30 years later, pet owners have an expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing?
Read the full story on the promises and pitfalls of pet life extension.

10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Form Energy and its iron batteries
Form Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
As wind and solar power grow, utilities need cheaper ways to store electricity for longer periods. Form Energy aims to meet that need with batteries that can store energy for 100 hours.
The company has developed a new type of battery using iron, a far more abundant and cheaper metal than those used in many existing batteries. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting,” in which iron turns to rust as the battery discharges and back to iron when it charges.

title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
content:
More than 5 million people around the world with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) experience atrophy in their retinas. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones.
The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors
convert light into electricity,
bipolar cells
process that signal, and
ganglion cells
transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain. PRIMA replaces the photoreceptors.
BROWN BIRD DESIGN
Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.'s chief medical officer for ophthalmology.
BROWN BIRD DESIGN
Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing
capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a
fiber-optic cable
A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom.
BROWN BIRD DESIGN
projector
on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of
near-infrared light
directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the
and on to the
retinal implant
in the back of the eye.
The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an
electrode
photovoltaic cells
, which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery.

Los Angeles Times
reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

title: Love is infrastructure
content:
I. Meet cute
Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer.
When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress.
So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly.
A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host.
“Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.”
“Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well,
can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the
. And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.”
Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer.
For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring.
At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated.
“There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.”
Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point.
“St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. It drives me to gridlock.”
“I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.”
Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas. Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty.
“Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St. Barnabas again. I have better things to fuss about. Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.”
II. How they came alive
Everybody voted all the time. Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St. Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly.
A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets. Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.”
Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests. But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought.
Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.”
Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring. She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services. There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city. But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day.
Then there was Raeford, a bartender at the Wild Goose Chase in the middle of Gallery Row in St. Barnabas. He also listened to people’s problems from evening until the wee hours, and solutions came to him like clockwork when he woke at noon the next day. He saw St. Barnabas at night, so he knew the unsafe blocks that could use brighter streetlights, the places where hydroelectric jitneys drove too fast at 3 a.m., and the teens who needed an all-ages hangout. He also knew about the fish fry at the Black church in the Uptilt District that kept being disrupted by noxious smoke from the incinerator two blocks away. And the yarn store on the edge of Gallery Row that needed a disabled parking spot for its many customers with mobility issues.
People voted with their Quills, usually by saying or typing a short message and maybe including a photo or brief video. Voting was easy by design, and votes were public but anonymized to the point where even a statistics whiz couldn’t tie one vote to a specific person—same as with major elections. The votes went directly to the City Core, which tracked, tabulated, produced reports, and offered solutions with the help of workers in the city government.
Trees voted too, thanks to sensors in their bark, and so did birds and squirrels that had eaten special birdseed that monitored their gut flora harmlessly. But votes from humans provided the greatest insight into “quality of life,” that oh-so-nebulous concept, and thus counted the most.
There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing.
(Other cities in the region operated differently, of course. Like Turnbull City, where instead of expecting residents to volunteer every stray notion, the City Core gathered information via ubiquitous surveillance. Cameras and Quill sniffers, tracking devices on vehicles—the things privacy laws in both Mainspring and St. Barnabas had banned. A city like Turnbull tracked its people to meet their needs without their needing to say anything.)
Sandi and Raeford, as two of the people who voted the most, were among the earliest to suspect their cities were developing minds of their own. At first the clues were subtle: Raeford voted about a hazardous sidewalk crack, and instantly the vote had an annotation mentioning the Argentine ant colony under the cement, the local rainfall patterns, and recent trends in skateboard design—much too soon to be the work of a human. Sandi had ideas about the communal compost station on her block, and the Mainspring City Core made subtle adjustments to her proposal.
And then it became obvious to anyone who was paying attention, around the same time in both cities. One day, the number of votes nearly doubled in both St. Barnabas and Mainspring. People voted on a birdfeeder or a public toilet only to see a second vote, pro or con, within a split second—but also, some votes from months or years earlier suddenly had new upvotes or downvotes.
“The city is voting!” Raeford wrote on the City Core message board in St. Barnabas.
There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing, opinions that came from seeing the big picture and understanding that a street closure in one place might mean a traffic nightmare elsewhere, with everyone trying to get to the big game.
Some residents saw this as a problem to be solved; others wanted to throw their cities a big coming-of-age party. A week later, though, almost everyone had gotten used to the idea that they had a new friend.
III. Thrown together
Ask most people in either city, and they’d say that St. Barnabas and Mainspring weren’t quite rivals—but they certainly had some friendly competition. Before the dispute over the annual meeting of the World Geographical Society, they’d also vied for the same football team and major-league baseball team. St. Barnabas had pushed to have the Mainspring airport built close enough to serve both cities, but in the end St. Barnabas had ended up with its own small, dilapidated airfield.
The real static between them had to do with vibes. Mainspring was too buttoned-up, too full of corporate offices: tech, health care, publishing, transportation. St. Barnabas would be nothing without its three universities and all the cultural enterprises that had sprung up around them—not to mention the small biotech firms and other tech ventures near the campuses. People in Mainspring thought St. Barnabas was full of flakes; in St. Barnabas they referred to Mainspring as the Straitlaced City (and in the next breath, they’d add that at least it wasn’t Turnbull).
Both City Cores were shaped by the votes of their humans, so of course they absorbed all the prejudices and attitudes of everyone who lived within their city limits. But also, Barnabas and Mainspring simply … got on each other’s nerves.
After the geographer thing, Mainspring and Barnabas avoided communicating as much as possible. Some contact was unavoidable—like, they shared information about some nasty weather, and they both drew water from the Temple River. The two cities were close enough for people to go back and forth, and a few even commuted.
But for the most part, the two cities could ignore each other.
Until they couldn’t.
A new generation of leaders took office in both places, with words like “intercity cooperation” constantly on their lips. A high-speed rail line could shorten the trip between Mainspring and St. Barnabas to around 23 minutes, and the two cities could also pool more real-time information about the sudden weather events that kept happening. They could become a Regional Center of Excellence, whatever
meant, combining the innovations from Barnabas’s labs with Mainspring’s expertise in technical implementation. They could work together to attract tourism, conventions, sporting events, dreamleases, and all the other stuff they’d always competed for.
“It’s preposterous,” Mainspring complained to Turnbull. “I’m going to be saddled with a ridiculous partner who doesn’t even know their own mind. St. Barnabas will be the death of me.”
“I hope your human leaders come to their senses,” Turnbull said. “Or you can find a way to slow-walk this until they undoubtedly lose the next election. You’re a lovely city, and you have so much potential that mustn’t be squandered.”
Turnbull often mentioned how much “potential” Mainspring had: a recipe for anxiety. The word “squandered” conjured images of ruin, abandonment, being emptied out.
For their part, Barnabas kept muttering to themself that nobody had asked them—this was the disconnect between the small-scale democracy of constant voting and the major elections, which gave rise to local leaders with big plans. Big plans that invariably went wrong, leaving the City Core to repair the damage somehow.
Sandi went to St. Barnabas for one of those town hall meetings with residents of both cities. The previous meeting had happened in Mainspring, at the opulent City Lecture Hall, so this one was in St. Barnabas, at the biggest auditorium on the Griffin University campus.
A tall man with well-sculpted facial hair sat next to Sandi, nodding at everything the leaders of both cities were saying from the dais. During a lull when someone approached the podium to offer a comment, Sandi introduced herself and asked why he was so fired up.
“I’m Raeford,” he said. “I’m just thinking of all the new customers this could bring to my watering hole in Gallery Row.”
“You’re not worried about St. Barnabas losing its ‘unique character’?” Sandi whispered, parroting what a few commenters had said from the podium.
“Nah,” Raeford whispered back. “Cities change. It’s what they do. It’s one thing if people get kicked out of their homes. Or if your neighborhood gets wrecked by a freeway in your backyard. But ‘character’? You can’t eat character. And we need to compete with the bigger players.”
“I guess.” Sandi pursed her lips. “But what I like about Mainspring is the density. Easy to walk, lots of transit. And with this regional innovation zone or whatever they’re calling it, I worry it leads to sprawl, like we used to have.”
“They promised, though,” Raeford said. “They promised to preserve the greenbelt around both cities. We need all that farmland. The only change is adding some high-speed rail tracks.”
“I know, but …” Sandi sniffed. “People always make promises when they’re trying to start something. Doesn’t mean they follow through.”
“I just want to find my dog,” said a man sitting behind Sandi. “I live here, and my dog went missing. And now someone sent me a picture of Broomstick in Mainspring. Somehow he got a ride on one of the self-driving cargo trains. I know the Mainspring City Core could find Broomstick in a heartbeat, but right now the two City Cores won’t talk to each other because of ‘incompatible protocols.’”
“I hope Broomstick turns up,” Raeford said.
“I’ll ask around at the library,” Sandi said. “Send me a picture. I’ll put up a flier.”
Raeford invited Sandi for a drink at the Wild Goose Chase. The two of them hung out for a couple of hours, talking about everything and nothing. She tore herself away when she realized it was already after 10 p.m. and she had to get home to Mainspring.
One thing Sandi noticed? The volume of votes was spiking in Mainspring—and Raeford found the same thing happening in St. Barnabas. People shared every last observation with their City Cores, because they were either anxious or excited about the big changes afoot. Or a little of Column A and a little of Column B, probably.
IV. First date, second date
Who made the first move to bridge the distance? Neither of them could say. Barnabas developed a smidge of remorse for treating Mainspring like an uncultured lout. Mainspring stewed in their annoyance at Barnabas, until they realized there was something lovable about the obnoxious college town. Or maybe they both saw how many of their humans were happy about the possibility of their joining together.
“Hey,” Barnabas said to Mainspring.
“Hey,” Mainspring said back.
“Do you want to … hang out?”
“What did you have in mind?”
“I can host you. Show you the sights.”
And so Mainspring came to visit Barnabas. Or rather, Mainspring extended part of their awareness into Barnabas’s City Core, so that Barnabas could share what they perceived and experienced every day. They “visited” Armistice Park with its outdoor band shell, Gallery Row with its window-shopping families, the grain warehouses that had been converted into lofts, the artificial lake where swans and geese nurtured ancient, bitter vendettas. The fresh-doughnut scent that wafted half a mile from the Golden Circlet to the soccer fields, throwing players off their game. The life of the city.
“I can feel your love for these people, these patterns,” Mainspring said. “It’s both deep and intricate, which is quite a combination.”
Barnabas fluttered with pleasure.
Then Mainspring got to show off their own city—the gay nightclub with its cowboy nights, the labyrinthine Crestwood Park, the three-story used bookstore, and yes, the offices, coworking spaces, and startup incubators where people huddled together and came up with new products and new ways of doing things. The farmers’ market in the city center on Sundays, with street performers and stalls with games and local resources. And the converted storage space made of cement, where bands practiced and sculptors blowtorched.
“You’re full of surprises,” Barnabas said.
“I hope I keep surprising you forever,” Mainspring said.
“Me too.”
They exchanged little gifts. A new organic restaurant in Barnabas had won breathless coverage from foodie magazines, and Barnabas encouraged it to do a pop-up in Mainspring. Mainspring nudged a robotics firm operating out of the incubator space to bring a fancy demo to Barnabas; the robots were adorable and playful, and they could save lives after a disaster.
The two of them were talking constantly.
“Does it ever seem weird to you?” Barnabas asked Mainspring. “Being a living thing made of so many other thinking beings? Do you ever think of the city as your body, or the people as your bloodstream? Is there a metaphor that speaks to you?”
Mainspring pondered this question a long time—a whole picosecond.
“I don’t need a metaphor,” Mainspring said. “I
a metaphor. People compare other phenomena to me all the time. And I can’t imagine what it’d be like to be different. If the buildings collapsed, if the people left, I would cease to exist.”
“But,” Barnabas pressed, “what makes you
? What makes me
“I want to hear your answer to that question.” Mainspring sent good weather reports: a smile.
“I don’t have a good answer. I guess on one level, there is no ‘me.’ On another level, I’m a constellation, an anthill, a flock of geese on the wing in formation.”
“Ugh. Don’t mention geese,” said Mainspring, who had bill-snapping monsters of their own.
“Geese are cute!” Barnabas protested.
Talking to Barnabas was like when the sunlight hit the tallest buildings in Mainspring just right, putting a gleam on their tilted windows, a beacon to all below. But while Mainspring carried on this dialogue with Barnabas, they were conducting a second session with Turnbull.
“I can’t believe it,” Turnbull said. “I hate to see you doing this to yourself.”
“Doing what?” Mainspring protested. “Barnabas is a great city. And it’s not my idea—it’s my people. I’m making the best of their decision, like I always do.”
“Hmph.” Turnbull gave a burst of noisy data. “You wouldn’t believe how many impractical schemes my residents cook up. I’m constantly having to make sure people don’t get carried away. You can’t let them push you around.”
“You can’t?” Mainspring experienced a femtosecond of confusion. “I mean, my people need to get the things they vote for, as much as possible.”
“There’s your problem right there. All this voting, voting, voting. People don’t know what they want. Sometimes I have an election where a foolhardy proposition passes, and I have to waste energy making sure it doesn’t get implemented.” Turnbull sent Mainspring an invitation to come visit, the way they’d visited Barnabas.
Soon Mainspring was seeing the glistening web of Turnbull’s surveillance. Turnbull could track people everywhere they went, listen to everything they talked about, monitor their bodily functions in a way Mainspring did only for squirrels and birds. People didn’t choose to share ideas or things they’d noticed; instead, the city harvested it all automatically. It was beautiful. Turnbull and their city leaders protected people—gave them what they needed instead of what they wanted.
“The way you do things is so messy,” Turnbull said. “No offense. But if you and Barnabas got together? It would only make things harder for you.”
This hit Mainspring like a magnitude 4.3 earthquake.
“You know, you do have other options,” Turnbull said. “A beautiful city like you could do a lot better than that glorified college town.”
“Oh yeah?” Mainspring said. “Anyone in particular who might be interested?”
“Well, now you mention it …” Turnbull sent an image of their award-winning flower show: rows and rows of hardy perennials with bright petals. Mainspring had that earthquake feeling again, except now it felt nice, as though the ground shivered with pure possibility.
V. Caught!
Sandi brought her laptop to bed, which Raeford found charming and annoying in equal measure. He read a battered paperback of Karen Tei Yamashita’s
while she scrolled and poked. Cozy, peaceful—until she let out a yelp.
“What is it?” he asked.
“Trouble,” she said.
Everything the Mainspring City Core did was public by design. Not just how they processed the votes they received, but also their interactions with public officials and other cities. Sometimes you had to dig, however, and it didn’t hurt to be a reference librarian. Sandi poked around for ages until she found the logs.
“My city is sexting with bloody Turnbull,” she told Raeford.
“Cities don’t sext,” Raeford protested. “They don’t even have—”
She showed him the pictures: flowers, water features, new glistening tarmac, shining skyscrapers.
“Oh,” Raeford said. “I take it back. Cities do sext.”
“Mainspring is two-timing St. Barnabas. I’m embarrassed on behalf of my town.”
Sandi wanted to blow the whistle right away, but Raeford cautioned her to wait and try to find out more. For all they knew, Mainspring and St. Barnabas had an open relationship.
The next morning at the library, Sandi saw plenty of signs the Mainspring–St. Barnabas partnership was moving forward. Work had begun on the high-speed rail line, and the two cities were already pooling resources. When a big rainstorm missed Mainspring but flooded the streets of St. Barnabas, Mainspring provided disaster workers and extra help to triage all the damage reports. One of St. Barnabas’s biotech firms licensed some patents to a Mainspring company. They sponsored cultural exchanges.
And a man showed up with a dog in his arms: The man from the meeting, Jack, had found Broomstick with the help of Mainspring’s City Core, and he wanted to thank Sandi. She’d hardly done anything, but it was nice to see—and pet—a living reminder that these cities were good for each other.
Then Raeford messaged her, attaching some documents. “Don’t ask where I got these,” he wrote.
Sandi opened the attachments and let out a shriek in front of three patrons she’d been shushing a moment earlier.
The Mainspring City Core had shared a proposal with the city council and the mayor’s office: Maybe before they finalized this arrangement with St. Barnabas, they should consider a counterproposal from Turnbull. Sandi made sure nothing could be traced back to Raeford before she made the whole shebang public.
VI. The breakup
“I didn’t know I could be so happy,” Barnabas was saying to Mainspring. “I didn’t have a concept of happiness before, I guess. I had pleasure: People sometimes vote just to tell me something worked perfectly, or that I helped them. I feel pleased when I help solve a problem. But until now, happiness seemed a pointless abstraction.”
“You make me happy too,” Mainspring said, though they were also messaging Turnbull. “You make me believe the future could be weirder than I ever knew, which feels like a gift.”
“If it’s not weird, it’s not the future,” Barnabas chirped.
They were sharing happy images back and forth: roads being repaired, sewers flowing freely, solar arrays basking.
Mainspring was saying something else, but—
Barnabas’s alerts spiked. Not votes, not sensors. Something else. Messages from city officials, plus hits via some channel Barnabas had half forgotten.
Mainspring had stopped talking, as if they’d both received the same news at the same instant.
Barnabas felt stuck—couldn’t function—couldn’t react. Total core failure. Almost as if the city population had increased a hundredfold and everyone had voted at once. Barnabas waited to feel something, but all that came was emptiness.
Death struck all the time. Barnabas was used to the moment when a resident became a pile of flesh and bones, but also the passing of birds, trees, squirrels, bugs. Every passing registered as a blip in the homeostasis of the city, but also as a category of disaster that couldn’t be prevented or mitigated.
Seeing the logs of Mainspring flirting with Turnbull, Barnabas felt something like the awareness of death, at a much greater scale. A whole future had just died.
Several seconds had passed. Mainspring broke the silence: “Listen, I want you to know that I—”
Barnabas closed the connection.
VII. The darkest hour
“You’re better off,” Turnbull told Mainspring. “Barnabas couldn’t see you the way I do. You’re capable of greatness. You just need help to get there.”
Mainspring buzzed happily—but part of them couldn’t help thinking,
Barnabas thought I was already great
Turnbull kept saying things that gave Mainspring a double feeling—hot and cold at once. One instant, it was like the moment after a generous rainfall that left the reservoirs full, but a split second later that bountiful sensation was replaced by an unbearable pang of scarcity.
“You’re one of the best cities in the region,” Turnbull said, “but if you don’t make good choices, you’re going to fall behind.” See? Bounty followed by scarcity.
While Turnbull spoke, Mainspring was marinating in bad news. People were going to dismantle the rails they’d laid down for the high-speed train with Barnabas. The city councils of both Barnabas and Mainspring shouted accusations and threats of lawsuits, though a few people on each side pleaded for patience. The meetings had turned ugly. The votes were rotten.
Mainspring had sent so many messages to Barnabas but had no way of knowing if they’d been received.
“Your people seem to be giving you trouble,” Turnbull was saying. “You need to get them under control. I can help.”
“Under … control?” The syntax felt incorrect. “I don’t control my people.”
“That’s what I’m saying.” Turnbull shared their feeds. “See how peaceful everything is on my streets? People behave. Everyone is happier in the end.”
Mainspring had known Turnbull longer than they’d known Barnabas. But they were seeing Turnbull for the first time. The bounty/scarcity thing was becoming a loop. They ran a systems check but found no errors.
“Your people will be my people,” Turnbull said. “We’ll take such good care.”
A memory snagged in Mainspring’s mind: when they’d shown off their city to Barnabas. The buildings that were more than buildings. The park that was a wonderland.
“And …” Mainspring couldn’t keep from saying something foolish. “And we’ll love each other?”
“Love?” Turnbull said. “I don’t understand. We’ll have synergies. We’ll—”
Mainspring didn’t mean to sever the link to Turnbull. They just kind of … did it.
As soon as Turnbull’s voice was gone, the bounty/scarcity loop ended. But something lingered, a feeling of impending disaster—as if the generous rainfall had escalated into a deadly storm.
Mainspring couldn’t think straight. Votes piled up, people reporting issues but also shouting opinions about Turnbull versus Barnabas. For the first time in their life, they couldn’t bear to respond.
A memory snagged in Mainspring’s mind: when they’d shown off their city to Barnabas. The buildings that were more than buildings. The park that was a wonderland. And Barnabas had kept saying, “I had no idea. You’re so brilliant. I wish I’d known sooner,” and sending back their own recordings of Mainspring, all lit up and annotated.
Mainspring had never told Barnabas “I love you.” They hadn’t even known what they were throwing away. Now it was too late; Barnabas would never listen.
Unless Mainspring did something reckless—something a city had never done.
VIII. The grand gesture
Sandi sat at the information desk, feeling cruddy. It wasn’t like she’d single-handedly sabotaged the marriage between her city and St. Barnabas, but her snooping had only made matters worse. All around her, the vibes were rotten. People shared articles about what life was like in Turnbull City and wondered if they needed to move away. Sandi hadn’t heard laughter in forever.
A message appeared on Sandi’s computer, like a chat window—except there was no chat client on the library computers.
“I’m the city. I need your help. I made a mistake. I didn’t realize. I’m in love with Barnabas, and they won’t talk to me. Please. Please help.”
Sandi hesitated, then typed: “This isn’t funny.”
“It definitely isn’t,” came the response. “I can prove I’m the City Core. You voted 1,963 times last year.” A summary of Sandi’s votes followed—information nobody, not even the world’s best hacker, could have, because every vote was separately anonymized.
“Holy,” Sandi breathed, “cow.”
Her city was asking her, personally, for help. Because she was good at connecting people. Because everyone trusted her. Because she was a librarian.
“You’re … in love … with St. Barnabas,” Sandi said, still trying to catch up.
“I should’ve known sooner,” Mainspring said. “I never should have hurt them. I want to spend the rest of my existence making up for this mistake, if they’ll let me. I’m scared.”
Sandi was staring at a display of literacy tools, her mind whirling. She groped her way back to the only question that mattered.
“What do you need me to do?” she asked the city.
Five minutes later, Sandi was messaging Raeford. Plus every librarian she’d met in St. Barnabas, and anyone else she could think of.
Barnabas had not been able to escape that feeling of core failure since they’d severed the link to Mainspring. Death, nothing but death. Votes arrived, and Barnabas processed them with a minimum of attention. Maintenance issues piled up, and Barnabas filed them. Part of them wanted to let the city collapse, but they did their duty.
They tried not to think about Mainspring, but they remained trapped in that moment when happiness had gone sour.
A vote came in from a bartender named Raeford: “Mainspring loves you. They’ve cut off contact with Turnbull. They are sorry they were so wrong. They may not deserve another chance, but please give them one anyway.”
Barnabas filed that vote under “Not my problem.”
Another vote arrived, from Jack, the man who’d found his lost dog: Same message, different words.
Then more votes, saying the same. Dozens, then hundreds, then thousands. Tens of thousands in an hour—after two hours, there were nearly a hundred thousand. All from residents of Barnabas, all asking them to give Mainspring another chance.
Barnabas flagged the earliest vote, the one from Raeford, and appended a query: “What if I can’t? What if it hurts too much?”
Raeford did not respond for several minutes. Then he wrote: “That’s how you know it’s love.”
He added: “Listen, if Mainspring does you dirty again, I will tear up the light-rail lines myself. We’ll be watching, in both cities. Please, just talk to them.”
Barnabas sat with this for five whole seconds.
Then they reopened the link to Mainspring. “I’m listening.”
“I love you,” Mainspring said. “I didn’t know I was capable of love. I want to be with you, as close as you’ll let me be. I want us to be free together. I was wrong to think Turnbull could ever mean even a fraction of what you mean to me. I think … I think my people taught me how to love, but I still need to learn so much. I want to do right by you.”
Barnabas couldn’t process anything. They held a hundred thousand votes that needed to be resolved. They thought of a giant farmers’ market, a park that was also a maze, dreamers and performers. In their memory, Raeford repeated:
That’s how you know it’s love
. They were going to overheat. They were throwing up exceptions.
“I love you too,” Barnabas couldn’t help saying to Mainspring. “That’s what makes this so hard.”
“I promise if you give me another chance, this will become a fixed value for me: I love you and I’ll never take you for granted again.”
Barnabas hesitated a little longer, then marked all hundred thousand votes resolved.
They reached out to Mainspring and said: “Then let’s dance.”
Mainspring didn’t understand, until Barnabas sent a live readout: the water rushing through pipes underground, the storm cavorting overhead. The buses and trains stopping and starting, the aircraft landing and taking off, the power grid usage surging and subsiding, the constant motion of people and other living things. Mainspring saw all the places where their patterns met, touched each other, syncopated, all the points of light and heat that spoke back and forth. They were part of one system; they always had been.
The two of them danced and embraced, whirling and laughing, and they never wanted to let go.
Charlie Jane Anders
is the author of
Good Things Are Coming Your Way
a novel about time travel, coming in spring 2027. She’s writing
Star Trek: Zero Point
for IDW Comics.

title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it.
What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated.
There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing?
There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity. Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is
trialing
one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US. Others are
testing dog drugs
that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like
obesity and osteoarthritis
, and aging itself. There’s even a company focused on
longevity medicines for
domesticated cats.
I don’t know how or when Peppy died. But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it.
That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though.
I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement. In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal. It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing. It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs. In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go. This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin.
Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet. On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice. She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets. As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says. Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating. If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?”
Fair enough. But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different. It’s often the first time a child confronts death. Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood. I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced.
Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics. For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely. The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of.
, a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people. It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider.
With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero. Even those who work in the field acknowledge that the stored people and animals are unlikely to be reanimated. As things stand, there is no way to really and truly bring any animal “back.”
I miss Peppy. But given the chance, would I stick her in a vat of liquid nitrogen? Or get another cat to give birth to a genetically identical animal? No, I would not.
RIP to the one and only Peppy.

title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
content:
Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
Age gates can be staggeringly counterproductive, pushing kids to darker corners of the web. Closing loopholes will only make things worse.
Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15.
But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair.
Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age.
In our work, we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms.
Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world.
A less safe internet for kids
When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities. Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online.
It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks.
When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional, platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections. Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents. Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street. Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them.
A less safe internet for all
Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked.
Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences.
Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation.
What could work instead?
Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place.
For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want.
Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable. For example, keyword-based content filtering can enable a student who is targeted with a specific nickname or inside joke to block any post or comment containing it. Platforms are unlikely to know which word or term a child might want to block, nor can policy seek to address such dynamic types of harm. Policy can, however, offer tools that would put power back in users’ hands.
Poor privacy practices, anxiety-producing content streams, and a near-inescapable need to use digital technologies for everyday tasks, communication, and information-seeking have rightfully led parents and teens to want real change in how companies conduct business.
Circumvention shows where policy falls short. Stricter enforcement will mean yet more data collection, and it won’t meet kids and parents where they are.
Michal Luria is a senior research fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology, leading the organization's work on evaluating and designing sociotechnical systems. Aliya Bhatia is a senior policy analyst at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Free Expression Project where she leads policy advocacy and research on issues related to children’s safety online, multilingual technologies, and human rights governance of online platforms. Danah Boyd is the Geri Gay Professor of Communication at Cornell University, where her research focuses on the intersection of technology and society. Her latest book is Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census.

title: BTU macht die Lausitz fit für neue Fertigungstechnik
content:
BTU macht die Lausitz fit für neue Fertigungstechnik

Wissen zum Anfassen: Im chesco-Workshop lernen Beschäftigte regionaler Unternehmen den Umgang mit additiven Fertigungsverfahren. taf II macht daraus ein zertifiziertes Weiterbildungsangebot.
| Quelle:
Sascha Thor
| Copyright:
BTU Cottbus-Senftenberg
Download
Das Center for Hybrid Electric Systems Cottbus (chesco) zeigt mit dem erfolgreichen Projekt taf I – Transfer agiler Fertigungsverfahren, wie aus wissenschaftlichem Know-how ein innovativer Technologietransfer für die Lausitz entsteht – von unterschiedlichen 3D-Druck-Verfahren für Kunststoffe und Metalle bis zu neuen Weiterbildungsangeboten.
Jetzt legt die Universität nach: Mit dem Nachfolgeprojekt taf II fließen bis 2030 weitere 16,1 Millionen Euro aus dem STARK-Bundesprogramm in Technologietransfer, Weiterbildung und Vernetzung für die Region sowie die Begleitung des Neubaus der chesco Forschungsfabrik auf dem Gelände des Lausitz Science Parks (LSP).
Mit dem neuen Projekt „Transfer agiler Fertigungsverfahren (taf) II“ treibt das chesco den technologischen Strukturwandel in der Lausitz weiter voran und unterstützt regionale Unternehmen dabei, moderne und nachhaltige Fertigungsmethoden einzusetzen. Aufbauend auf den Erfolgen von taf I werden die bestehenden Strukturen zur Vermittlung, Vernetzung und Qualifizierung strategisch zu einem vollwertigen beruflichen Weiterbildungsprogramm ausgebaut. Gleichzeitig begleitet das Projekt die Weiterentwicklung der chesco Forschungsfabrik sowie deren Überführung in den geplanten chesco Neubau im Lausitz Science Park (LSP).
Getragen wird taf II ebenso wie das abgeschlossene Projekt taf I von der Zentralen wissenschaftlichen Einrichtung (ZWE) im Center for Hybrid Electric Systems Cottbus (chesco) der Brandenburgischen Technischen Universität Cottbus-Senftenberg (BTU). Die Idee: Forschungswissen aus mehr als 30 Fachgebieten der Universität direkt an kleine und mittelständische Unternehmen der Region zu tragen.
Wie taf I wird taf II über das STARK-Bundesprogramm gefördert, das nicht-investive Projekte zur ökonomisch, ökologisch und sozial nachhaltigen Transformation der Kohleregionen unterstützt. Dafür stehen dem Projekt in den kommenden vier Jahren bis Mitte 2030 insgesamt 16,1 Mio. Euro zur Verfügung.
„Mit taf II bauen wir das aus, was die BTU im Kern ausmacht: exzellente Forschung, die in die Praxis wirkt. Über 30 Fachgebiete unserer Universität bringen ihr Know-how direkt zu den Unternehmen der Region – das ist gelebter Technologietransfer und zugleich ein Beleg für die Innovationskraft der BTU Cottbus-Senftenberg“, sagt Prof. Dr. Gesine Grande, Präsidentin der BTU Cottbus-Senftenberg. „Mit dem chesco und dem geplanten Neubau im Lausitz Science Park stärken wir nicht nur den Strukturwandel der Lausitz, sondern auch das Profil unserer Universität als Motor für nachhaltige Fertigungstechnologien und als attraktiver Standort für Forschende, Fachkräfte und Unternehmen.“
Wissenschaftsministerin Dr. Manja Schüle sagt: "Die Lausitz hat sich auf den Weg gemacht, ihren Wandel selbst zu gestalten – und die Forschungsfabrik chesco zeigt, wie: mit Forschung und neuen Technologien, starken Partnerschaften und konkreten Perspektiven für Unternehmen und Fachkräfte. Das Projekt taf II knüpft dabei an die Erfolge des Vorgängers taf I an und baut den Technologietransfer, die Vernetzung und die Qualifizierung von Unternehmen weiter aus. Mit dem Aufbau eines modularen beruflichen Weiterbildungsprogramms entstehen zugleich neue Möglichkeiten, Fachkräfte gezielt für die Anforderungen moderner und nachhaltiger Fertigung zu qualifizieren. So geht erfolgreicher Strukturwandel."
Was taf II für die Region leistet
taf II baut unmittelbar auf den Ergebnissen von taf I auf und konzentriert sich auf drei außenwirksame Aufgabenbereiche: Sichtbarkeit und Vermittlung, Ausbau der Vernetzung mit Industriepartner*innen sowie (Weiter-) Qualifikation von Unternehmen. Ergänzt werden diese durch zwei Arbeitspakete zum Betrieb der Forschungsfabrik und zu deren Erweiterung im chesco Neubau. Im Fokus stehen:
- Transfer von Fachwissen zu Spezialthemen der additiven und subtraktiven Fertigung, Messtechnik und digitalen Technologien,
- Befähigung von Unternehmen zur Anwendung nachhaltiger Produktionsweisen, inkl. ressourceneffizienter Prozesse, Kreislauffähigkeit und digitaler Vernetzung (zum Beispiel Predictive Maintenance, Echtzeit-Monitoring),
- Erweiterung des Qualifizierungsangebots durch Ausbau eines modularen beruflichen Weiterbildungsprogramms mit Micro Credentials und zertifizierten Weiterbildungspfaden an der BTU.
Dabei verfolgt taf II das Ziel, dass Unternehmen nachhaltige Produktionsweisen nicht nur kennen, sondern aktiv einsetzen können.
chesco Neubau: Wissenschaftsstandort Lausitz dynamisieren
Ein eigenes Arbeitspaket begleitet in taf II die Überführung der bestehenden Forschungsfabrik in den chesco Neubau, der auf einer rund fünf Hektar großen Fläche im Lausitz Science Park (LSP) in Cottbus entsteht.
Der LSP soll künftig als zentrale Innovationsplattform fungieren, die Wissenschaft, Wirtschaft und Start-ups, beziehungsweise Strukturwandelprojekte der Universität – etwa chesco, Energie-Innovationszentrum (EIZ), SpreeTec neXt oder Innovationscampus Elektronik und Mikrosensorik Cottbus (iCampus) – zusammenbringt und den wissenschaftlichen, wirtschaftlichen und technologischen Strukturwandel der Region koordiniert. Bis zum Umzug bleibt die bestehende Infrastruktur am Standort Cottbus-Dissenchen mit Entwicklungs-, Fertigungs- und Testkapazitäten voll funktionsfähig.
Rückblick: Was taf I für die Lausitz erreicht hat
Ziel des ersten Projekts war es, regionalen Unternehmen – insbesondere metallverarbeitenden Betrieben der Lausitz – den Zugang zu agilen, modernen Fertigungsmethoden zu eröffnen und sie für den Aufbau nachhaltiger Produktionsweisen zu befähigen. Dafür wurde in angemieteten Hallen in Cottbus-Dissenchen die chesco Forschungsfabrik aufgebaut: eine Modellfabrik, die modernste Fertigungs-, Test- und Digitalisierungstechnologien miteinander verknüpft.
Die Bilanz nach knapp vier Jahren Projektlaufzeit:
- Die chesco Forschungsfabrik wurde am 24. Mai 2024 feierlich eröffnet mit zahlreichen Persönlichkeiten aus Wissenschaft, Politik und dem Mobilitätssektor.
- Zwei Tage der offenen Tür lockten mehrere Hundert Besucher*innen aus der Öffentlichkeit an.
- Die chesco Kontaktkonferenz hat sich erfolgreich als Vernetzungsplattform für Unternehmen der Region etabliert. In diesem Jahr fand die jährliche Konferenz zum mittlerweile sechsten Mal statt. In taf II wird die Veranstaltung zur Fachtagung weiterentwickelt.
- Am Standort in Cottbus-Dissenchen sind bereits realisiert: 65 Prozent der insgesamt 150 geplanten Maschinen für innovative Fertigungstechnologien, einer von acht geplanten Prüfständen für Komponenten und Prototypen sowie 43 Prozent der digitalen Kompetenzen (unter anderem Digitale Zwillinge, Netzwerkinfrastruktur und Cybersicherheit, Simulation und Analyse).
- In 2025 war das Projektteam bei insgesamt 37 Messen und (Netzwerk-) Veranstaltungen als teilnehmende Institution oder Gastgeberin vertreten und erreichte dabei rund 1.900 Personen.
- Das mit dem Netzwerk für den deutschen Mittelstand, BVMW e.V., gegründete Netzwerk „Innovationsdruck“ zählt inzwischen 60 Mitglieder.
- Insgesamt konnten über 30 Unternehmen und Institutionen für eine konkrete weiterführende Zusammenarbeit gewonnen werden; 28 schriftliche Absichtserklärungen zur Zusammenarbeit (Letter of Intent, LOI) mit regionalen Unternehmen wurden bereits unterzeichnet.
- Seit Projektstart wurden 21 Weiterbildungsworkshops durchgeführt. Fast die Hälfte der Teilnehmenden erhielten ein universitäres Zertifikat.
- Aus der praktischen Zusammenarbeit mit Unternehmen sind bereits verwertbare Ergebnisse entstanden: Im chesco-Pilotprojekt mit der Orthopädie- und Reha-Team Zimmermann GmbH wurde eine neuartige 3D-Druck-Struktur für individuelle Orthesen entwickelt, die sich derzeit im Patentverfahren befindet. Dem Cottbusser Unternehmen Negus CB GmbH konnte das chesco Team mit Messungen zu ihrem patentierten Produkt, dem „Comfort Booster“ helfen. Mit dem Start-up additiveStream4D GmbH kooperiert chesco, um die Hybridfertigung von Metall-3D-Druckstrukturen zu optimieren. Hinzu kommen Demonstratoren wie ein per Virtual Reality visualisierter Elektromotor sowie ein Prototyp für einen Vertikalrotor als Windturbine.
- Die mehr als 30 an chesco beteiligten Fachgebiete der BTU haben seit 2020 über 100 wissenschaftliche Veröffentlichungen zu ihren Forschungsergebnissen publiziert, die in den Transfer einfließen.
„Mit taf I haben wir gezeigt, dass in der Region großes Interesse und konkreter Bedarf an innovativen Fertigungstechnologien besteht und der Wissens- und Technologietransfer aus der Wissenschaft in die regionale Wirtschaft gut funktioniert. Mit taf II setzen wir genau hier an und entwickeln bedarfsgerechte Angebote zu nachhaltigen Produktionsweisen weiter, die Beschäftigte und Führungskräfte direkt in ihrer betrieblichen Praxis weiterbringen. Regionale Unternehmen erhalten noch gezielter Zugang zu Spezialwissen im Fertigungsbereich“, so Prof. Dr.-Ing. Klaus Höschler, BTU-Fachgebiet Flug-Triebwerksdesign. Gemeinsam mit Prof. Dr.-Ing. Georg Möhlenkamp, BTU-Fachgebiet Leistungselektronik und Antriebssysteme, leitet er die Zentrale wissenschaftliche Einrichtung im chesco. „Gleichzeitig gestalten wir im Rahmen des Projekts den Übergang der chesco Forschungsfabrik in den chesco Neubau, um noch effizienter an innovativen Technologien arbeiten zu können“, ergänzt Prof. Möhlenkamp. „Damit wollen wir dazu beitragen, die Sichtbarkeit der Lausitz im internationalen Wettbewerb zu stärken und den Standort als Region für Zukunftstechnologien und nachhaltige Industrie mit zu profilieren.“
Über chesco und das Projekt taf
Das Center for Hybrid Electric Systems Cottbus (chesco) ist eine Forschungs- und Transferinitiative der BTU Cottbus-Senftenberg und Teil des entstehenden Lausitz Science Park. Über 30 Fachgebiete aus den Fakultäten 1 bis 3 bündeln ihre Expertise zu innovativen Technologien für nachhaltige Mobilität – insbesondere Luftfahrt – und nachhaltige Produktion. Die chesco-Forschungsfabrik in Cottbus-Dissenchen bildet das Herzstück des Projekts taf und dient als Reallabor für moderne Fertigungstechnologien. Ziel ist es, Forschungsergebnisse zu hybriden und elektrischen Antrieben sowie innovativen Produktionsverfahren schnell in industrielle Anwendungen zu überführen und dadurch die Innovations- und Wettbewerbsfähigkeit der Lausitz zu stärken.

title: TUD-Studie: Nur fünf Prozent der Bauunternehmen in Deutschland kennen ihren CO₂-Fußabdruck
content:
TUD-Studie: Nur fünf Prozent der Bauunternehmen in Deutschland kennen ihren CO₂-Fußabdruck
Diesel, Strom, Zement, Lkw-Maut, Entsorgung: In den Preisen für diese Posten steckt heute ein CO₂-Aufschlag. Bauunternehmen zahlen darüber für ihre CO₂-Emissionen. Nur fünf Prozent der Firmen in Deutschland wissen jedoch, wie viel CO₂ sie tatsächlich ausstoßen. Zu diesem Ergebnis kommen Forscher der Technischen Universität Dresden (TUD) in einer repräsentativen Studie. Sie befragten dafür im Winter 2025/2026 bundesweit 601 Bauunternehmen. Aus Sicht der Wissenschaftler vergeben die Unternehmen Einsparpotential, denn wer seine Emissionen systematisch erfasst, sieht, wo sie anfallen, kann sie gezielt reduzieren und senkt damit seine Kosten.
Aus Sachsen haben 64 Unternehmen an der Studie teilgenommen. Auch hier gilt: Kaum ein Betrieb kennt seinen CO₂-Fußabdruck, aber jedes fünfte Unternehmen (20 Prozent) rechnet Kosten für CO₂-Emissionen oder Umweltkosten bereits in seine Projekte ein. Bundesweit sind es 22 Prozent der Unternehmen, kleine Betriebe zu gleichen Teilen wie große.
Bauwirtschaft liegt zurück
Im Branchenvergleich liegt die Bauwirtschaft klar zurück: Branchenübergreifend kennen in Deutschland rund 16 Prozent der Unternehmen ihren CO₂-Fußabdruck, in der Baubranche sind es fünf Prozent. Bei Bauunternehmen mit zehn bis 49 Beschäftigten kennen lediglich drei Prozent ihren CO₂-Fußabdruck.
Studienleiter Dr. Philipp Richter dazu: „Kleinere Bauunternehmen rechnen CO₂ genauso oft in ihre Angebote ein wie große. Ihren eigenen Ausstoß kennen sie kaum, obwohl die Daten in jeder Buchhaltung liegen. Es fehlt nur die Entscheidung, hinzuschauen.“
Hintergrund
Eine Pflicht, über die eigenen Emissionen zu berichten, trifft nach der EU-Omnibus-Richtlinie nur noch sehr große Unternehmen. Den Mittelstand erreicht das Thema trotzdem. Große Auftraggeber fragen Emissionsdaten bei Nachunternehmern ab, öffentliche Vergabestellen bewerten Emissionen mit einem CO₂-Preis, und Banken beziehen Klimarisiken in die Kreditprüfung ein. Ab 2028 verlangt zudem das Gebäudemodernisierungsgesetz für größere Neubauten eine CO₂-Bilanz über den gesamten Lebenszyklus.
Für die Studie wurden 601 Bauunternehmen aus allen 16 deutschen Bundesländern befragt. Die Stichprobe ist repräsentativ und entspricht in Größe, Umsatz und Eigentümerstruktur der deutschen Bauwirtschaft. Die meisten der befragten Betriebe sind klein, 89 Prozent sind in Familien- oder Gründerhand.
